To: Todd McCaffrey <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>
Subject: Fwd: THE KING'S GHOSTS typos, etc. - Chapter 12 - End

-------- Forwarded Message --------
Subject: THE KING'S GHOSTS typos, etc. - Chapter 12 - End
Date: Mon, 15 Nov 2021 20:16:02 -0800 (PST)
From: Susan Silver <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>
To: Todd McCaffrey <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>

Hi Todd,

Here are my observations through the end of the book.

I mentioned previously that the plural of SC is used two different 
ways... either SCs or SC's.  In these remaining chapters, it is written 
both ways. I'm sure you've already addressed this even though it doesn't 
show up in the version I downloaded.  Just throwing this out there since 
I did observe it.

*Chapter12*
Location 4956 - typo... her, not his .../Margaret replied cheerfully, 
bounding out of /her /seat./

Location 5107 - awkward sentence, not sure if you meant to say ./..relay 
a stream of conscious report of an SC that *is* thinking very loudly/ or 
possibly /...relay a stream of conscious report of an SC that *thinks* 
very loudly /or /if it's ...conscious report *to* an SC.../

Location 5147 - typo... I, not If  (*I* believe that it will be more 
meaningful...)

Location 5188 - typo... insert "would" (But what *would* you do in my 
position?)

Location 5217 - typo... Clio, not Cio

Location 5243 - not sure that *nearly* fits here unless it is supposed 
to be *just*. Maybe omit it completely? (...looked to Owami for 
confirmation, but Owami nearly waved her back to Cona).

Location 5347 - typo... on, not off (...co-pilot's hands so that they 
were centered *on* the self-destruct button...)

Location 5425 - "Admirals Branford" isn't correct. Janis is not a 
Branford, but he is an Admiral.

*Chapter 13*
Location 5572 - when onboard the ships, the British word lift is used.  
Actually, I think it works fine.  Just pointing out the use of British 
English.

Location 5588 -  May not be anything but... /You've been requested to go 
TDY to the NWC for the next week./ Not quite sure what this means. Is 
TDY Training Duty?  If so, my mind would read it better as /You've been 
requested to *do* TDY *at* the NWC for the next week./  Maybe this is 
how they speak and my non-military mind just has problems.

Location 5739 - Comma needed for If/then sentence: /Because if she were 
picked*,***it'd mean that.../

Location 5817 - typo... planted, not planet (...and by whom that 
bacterial assault was *planted* on Sparkle)

Location 5858 - typo... Rochelle, not Rachel

Location 5935 - Insert "said"... Fromer *said* as he strolled...

*Chapter 14*
Location 5962: typo... The, not They (*The* four of them fit..)

*Chapter 15*
Location 6488: tonnes - is it British for tons? (...there's /tonnes/ 
we're not seeing). I may have seen this somewhere else, but not sure if 
it was in this book or the first one, /Raw Space/.

Location 6724 - is this a typo... she, not he or is there someone else 
Owami is referring to? (She didn't want to joggle the Major's arm while 
*she* was conducing the assault...)

Location 6744 - typo... her, not him (Cona sent in *her* first team...)

Location 6772 - typo... her, not his (/Clip/, Cona ordered and *her* 
reserve squad moved out...)

Location 6824 - typo... outsider should be plural (... the name used 
with *outsiders* for /The King's Own Ghosts...)/

*Chapter 16*
Location 6966 (2nd paragraph of chapter) - This is a very long sentence. 
Suggestions: 1) move the comma from before to after "Scotty" and 2)  
drop the "when" along with the comma and put a period after Munchkin

Location 7032 - typo... on, not own ("So put her *on* alert," Rochelle 
said.)

Location 7088 - same confusing working for me: ...cadets were with us 
TDY to the NWC...  Guess it's just me.

Location 7159 - typo... Morton has a "w" on the end

*Chapter 17*
Location 7227 - typo whether, not when (... hard pressed to say 
*whether* her bedmate was male, female, or something else.)

Location 7244 - The math doesn't work. If Neff's sun is 700,000 times 
larger than Canaris Prime, it would be 14 million km in diameter, not 
1.4 km.  For 1.4 million km diameter, it would only be 70,000 times 
larger. (FYI - I did not check the mass calculations.)

Location 7279 - 1) typo... *Ophelia* is not possessive and 2) delete 
"said even" (...kneeling down to Ophelia's said even as she hit...)

That's all I have for you Todd.  Hope I didn't get this to you too late.
Susan

To: Jay A. Katz <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>, Alec Johnson <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>
Subject: Re: P Status/CONFIDENTIAL AND PRIVILEGED COMMUNICATION

Jay,

I'm so sorry to hear about your mother. It's always hard, no matter what 
the age.

I just turned 65 myself and am slowly climbing back down off the walls.  
Oi vey! 65! You don't look a day over 90!
I've just recently decided to target 100 as the intermediate phase and 
am hoping to get a full 200 (apparently that might be possible).
Certainly I don't feel the 65 everyone tells me I should feel.

I recall you told us about Heather Bellson's last name and stuff.  I 
remember looking her up on imdb.com and being reassured.

Fingers crossed, we'll get everything back on track soon.

I've been thinking that NYC would be one of my future travel 
destinations (NYC pizza, the Library Hotel, etc.).  I'm also eyeing 
France, particularly the Normandy graveyards as a bit of /homage/ to 
those who didn't return... and also as a bit of a nod to the likes of 
James Doohan and Sean Connery (who both survived D-Day).

Again, though, I'm sorry to hear about your mother. (At least she gets 
to spend time with Michael Collins.)

All the best,
Todd

Subject: Re: Trouble Blows West

Hi Monique,

Thank you for your patience, I read Trouble Blows West.

It did not work for me.  Permit me to emphasize, it did not work for *me.*
*
*
Here's why the book didn't work for me:

Ginny's character just didn't seem real to me.  It became less so as the 
book progressed. Her mounting anger and vengeance didn't have any 
rational background to support them and her unwillingness to listen to 
reason or learn finally killed any sympathy I might have had for her.

I also questioned the setting -- was this in the 1970s? 80s? 90s? 
Earlier? Later?

Ginny's love for her mare didn't work for me. I grew up with horse mad 
girls, and Ginny didn't fit.  It seemed to me that her horse was at 
about the same level in her affections as a rusted hand-me-down bicycle.

I began to notice the number of chapters.  There's an *awful* lot of them.

I also wasn't sure about the farm -- was it a cattle farm? Dairy? Crop? 
Mixed use?  That question nagged at me and helped pull me out of the book.

Cheers,
Todd McCaffrey

Message: Dear Brittany and Brianna, I realize that you most likely won't 
remember me, but that's okay. We first met at a WotF workshop in 
Hollywood in 2015 (I think). At the time I was teaching high school 
physics and English (SF/Fantasy Literature) at an all boys Catholic 
school in San Diego. I was mesmerized by the story of your development 
from "reluctant readers" to bestselling authors. Very inspirational for 
a teacher! At Comic-Con in 2017, I attended your panel and visited your 
booth on the Exhibit Hall Floor, where you graciously gifted me with 
your World Building guide (although that may have come from the 
workshop; I don't really remember) and an autographed copy of "The 
Strand Prophecy." For reasons I won't go into here, I will tell you that 
the book sat on my shelf for almost a year before I finally read it, and 
that the 2017 Comic-Con was the last one I attended--until this year. I 
was so happy to have gotten tickets for this year's Con, and so 
disappointed when it was cancelled. But here we are at Comic-Con at 
Home, and I am able finally to tell you both that I finally did read 
"The Strand Prophecy," and I really enjoyed it! My life circumstances 
have changed rather significantly since last we met, and I see that 
yours have as well. Brittany, I was shocked and sorry to hear about your 
vision loss, but I'm happy to hear you're still going strong. I now no 
longer teach high school physics and English to boys, but middle school 
science and literature to both boys and girls at a Catholic K-12 school 
in Indiana. VERY different climate from SoCal, and not just in terms of 
the weather! I was looking through your products offered on the 
Comic-Con at Home Exhibitor Hall website, and I had a couple of 
questions that I hope you can answer before I start purchasing (and 
thank you in advance for your time): 1. How many total volumes are there 
in the Twin Soul series, and how many of these are compiled in the 
Omnibus? Is this a series that would be appropriate for middle school 
students from conservative Catholic families? 2. Is Millennial Madness 
an autobiography, or is it a fictionalized story? I'd love to be able to 
share your ladies' story with my own students, IN YOUR WORDS. It's nice 
to be in touch with you again. I love your work! Looking forward to 
hearing back from you soon--hopefully before the Con ends and before you 
run out of merchandise! :) Be well! May God bless you both! Sincerely, 
Bob Weber P.S. I look forward to your email response, but feel free to 
call if you wish. I always have really enjoyed our conversations.

Hi Geoff,

As usual your Xmas missive beat my vague "I should write Geoff" by a 
long shot.

Congratulations on being a double grandfather!  And you got to see them 
both!  All good.

You know, for years now it's struck me that you have a marvelously 
humorous writing style.  If you ever thought of picking up a new hobby, 
writing humorous pieces would be a boon to the world.

Naturally, I've been reading a fair bit.  Writing a lot less than normal 
because of the "covid cloud."

This whole thing with the soon-to-be ex-President is rather appalling.  
I wish someone would provide us with quantified data on how much the 
Russians influenced the 2016 election.  We know they worked at it just 
as we know they worked to help the Leave part of Brexit (which will go 
down in history as just as major a self-inflicted wound as our 2016 
elections).

I've signed up for a lot of Domestika online art classes. I'm taking one 
on Photoshop and, despite years of experience, I am learning things 
about Photoshop that I didn't know.  I've signed up for the Advanced 
Photoshop course by the same instructor, as well as a nice class on 
cover design by a German woman who speaks passable English.

The twins -- my writing partners -- are both still alive which, given 
what's been going on with Brit (the alpha of the two) and her health is 
actually saying quite a lot.  We think the root problem for her is some 
sort of auto-immune disease but we haven't got it down to specifics. Her 
hemiplegic migraines are nearly synonymous with strokes (sigh).  She's a 
tough lady but these past four years have been physically exhausting for 
her.  What seems to be helping most now is an acupuncturist who is using 
herbals to calm her nerves (literally, nice big needles go to nerve nexi).

I'm thinking that "this too shall pass" and we'll see the end of the 
COVID tunnel but perhaps not fully until 2022 (sigh).  Our ancestors 
survived much worse... although that's scant comfort.

One thing I have grown to realize is how incredibly powerful an 
individual human being is.  Take Greta Thunberg as an example. In fact, 
take anyone who decides that they will change things (Rosa Parks, the 
students in Tienanmen Square).  I wonder why we fail to use our strength 
so often?  Is it because changing the world is pretty consuming passion 
and we choose to avoid it?

I also am in shock that too many of my fellow countrymen (and women) are 
willing to accept a con man for President and cede unto him all the 
powers of a dictator.  I really have a hard time adjusting to how *dumb* 
these people are.  It makes me very sad.

I recall reading an article not too long ago praising some young black 
kids for their genius IQs. It wasn't the color of their skin that 
intrigued me -- it was that one of the kids scored a 142 on the 
Stanford-Binet IQ test.  I scored a 156 at the same age.  That made it 
really strike home that I am genius (gush, shucks, folks!).  I have 
always held the belief that everyone on this planet is as empowered as I 
am; that given the right set of circumstances, they could accomplish 
whatever they set their minds to, that we were universal in our 
potential.  Now, with the whole mess of the last four years, I have to 
question that and that has been causing me a great deal of angst.

Television-wise, I am now particularly spoiled.  I acquired a marvelous 
ASUS 34" ProArt curved monitor which now graces my desk in my bedroom.  
Over the holidays I acquired a Amazon Roku Firestick and discovered that 
I can pipe TV signals through my HDMI2 port.  So I've been getting 4k TV 
from 18 inches. Whew!

I've been watching the new Star Trek Discovery.  The first season nearly 
killed it for me because every episode pretty much stopped dead when the 
Klingons came on.  Season Two was better and now Season Three is quite 
enjoyable (forgiving such complete inanity as "parasitic ice").

I watched the Mandolorian with a skeptical eye particularly as so much 
of it was just pure re-cast western. And there was one episode that 
stopped me for weeks but I was assured that things got better.

I've also been re-watching Dr. Who, starting with Eccleston who was such 
a marvelous Doctor.  I'm sorry he couldn't stick around longer (but 
maybe he would have gone stale).

Anyway, that's a taste of life at Dell Ridge.

Always glad to hear from you, my oldest friend!

Love,

Todd

steal all of Christmas from the town of Who-ville, figuring that the 
Whos will all be sad.  When the deed is complete and yet stillthey 
celebrate, he learns the true meaning of Christmas, repents, and returns 
the gifts.  This is a feel-good story.

As I thought about it more, I realized that Harry Potter and the 
Philosopher’s (Sorcerer’s, US) Stoneby J.K. Rowling is alsoa Christmas 
crime story.  In fact, multiple crimes are attempted, several 
committed.  At Christmas, Harry receives mysteriously an invisibility 
cloak which enables him to perform many capers and ultimately to track 
down the criminal who wants to steal the philosopher’s stone.  At which 
point, Lord Voldemort, co-inhabiting the body of Professor Quirrell, 
attempts murder.  Harry survives.  This is another example of a 
feel-good story.

The next book, Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secretsis also holiday 
related (Halloween), as is the fourth (Harry Potter and the Goblet of 
Fire) which reprises the Yule holiday.  And, of course, all the books 
involve unsuccessful attempts to murder Harry Potter.

with Peacocks,centers upon three weddings and a murder.  This is another 
example of murder and attempted murder. Also an example of a feel-good 
story.*

Faults with the first subscription page ("Step 1'):

- You didn't link your image to the hyperlink to your Step 2 page 
(https://subscribe.newscientist.com/default.aspx?prom=16450&pkgcode=T&term=3I),

just the "Subscribe" button.  You always want to make it easy for the 
customer to proceed to the next step.

On "Step 2" 
(https://subscribe.newscientist.com/default.aspx?prom=16450&pkgcode=T&term=3I)

Firstly, whatever you're using to switch between offer packages is 
clunky and slow (Javascript should enable you to generate a 
highlight/hover effect).

Secondly, your offers are "bad" and "worse."  Remember that your 
audience is mostly college educated, savvy people.

The first offer "Option 1" has the rate of $1.05 per week for 3 weeks 
(catchily reduced to $3.14 -- pi) with an automatic continuing rate of 
$49.99 per quarter. Sneakily below you say that this is a 85% savings.  
It is, but just for those 3 weeks. Not quite a "bait and switch" 
advertising tactic but damn close. I think less of you, your marketing 
department, and New Scientist in general for such sharp business 
practices.  Also, you fools, you're dealing with college educated people 
who tend to *think*. So you're insulting your potential subscribers' 
intelligence at the same time. Shame!

If you'd really wanted to woo me back, you'd have made the 3 issue "pi" 
deal which ended *without* automatic renewal at the usual (exhorbitant) 
rate.

"Option 2" -- $314.00 for 3 years with a "saving 70%" is too much.  I'm 
a prior subscriber to New Scientist but I stopped subscribing because I 
found the online version not as compelling as the print version (you 
didn't replicate formats, nor did you try), so asking me to take "a pig 
in a poke" -- to make a 3 year commitment to a product I'd previously 
declined -- is just too much.  If I had evidence that New Scientist was 
such a deal, maybe then but not right out the gate.

You make no other in-between offers that might give me a chance to 
determine whether New Scientist is now something I want in my media 
stream (which currently includes New Atlas, WIRED, The Economist, The 
London Times, The New York Times, and various others).

If you had some in between offers ("a third of a pi", "a slice of pi", 
etc.) that might have interested me.

In conclusion, you failed to get a new subscription and a large part of 
that is due to your poor marketing and arrogance.

Wishing you the best,

recommend the Apple TV show, "Home Before Dark." Seriously good acting 
all around.

Hannukah got a Amazon Roku firestick which means I get to watch 4k TV up 
close and personal.

New Year's Eve I took a shower and scratched an itchy ankle with the toe 
of my other foot -- and got it all infected.  By the second I was in an 
Urgent Care getting a prescription for Keflex which is a staph specific 
antibiotic.  I'm doing much better but I was appalled at how quickly the 
infection spread.

I am taking some Domestika courses, some on Photoshop, some on Book 
Cover Design, and all sorts of things.  They're mostly in Spanish with 
subtitles but I'm having fun.

I also signed up for Dean Wesley Smith's and Kristine Kathryn Rusch's 
"The Decade Ahead" bundle with the challenge of looking forward to 2029.

Dex and I speak semi-frequently.  He called me the other day to say that 
Jenna had totaled her car in a roll over accident.  I, of course, 
immediately recalled your Glen of the Downs accident.   She's okay but I 
asked her (via text) to be worried about possible concussions. (I 
attached a photo of her poor car.)

part with it.

which is alarmingly similar to the behavior of certain Presidents I 
could name.

Coming up soon, I get to apply for Medicare which is a bit more involved 
than I'd imagined.

I'm re-reading the /Bloody Jack/ series once again.  I started looking 
at the first book and just got caught up with the whole thing. It really 
was a lot of fun and it'd make a great TV series.

Here's hoping to a vaccinated New Year!

stock for sale, so I can’t afford to buy anything now and lay down new 
roots. The holding pattern I’m in is excruciating!

And I guess other aspects of my life, and the seemingly never-ending 
crises that are engulfing the earth, are all mixing together to fill my 
plate with a gloomy looking repast. I should stop reading the news.

Sleep is difficult; I’ve been wide awake for an hour and it’s not yet 
5am, so this day’s store of resilience is already fecked up. - I have to 
go to Owen’s girlfriend’s place today to help celebrate the “gender 
reveal” (slap me quick before I gag!) they have planned now that their 
gestating baby is 3 months along. It’ll be the first time I’ll be in the 
same air space as Geoff since we were in court getting our divorce 
decree; when I bawled my eyes out in front of everyone whilst giving 
testimony. Oy! Added to that, Owen has, frankly, been treating me like a 
piece of shit over the last few months so the strain is telling. I’ll be 
a big girl, though, go along to see what sex the baby will be and try to 
smile a lot.

About two weeks ago Geoff’s youngest sister, Edel, the main carer for my 
(ex?) mother-in-law, Joan, was in a terrible car crash while travelling 
to Cork for a weekend break with her boyfriend. She’s broken the bones 
in the top of her foot, and two vertebrae just above the tailbone. She 
literally broke her arse. Poor Mick, her boyfriend, is far worse off and 
will remain in hospital in Cork for at least another 6 weeks, undergoing 
another couple of surgeries on top of the 3 he’s already had. Fuck! What 
a nightmare, and no visitors allowed to see him. Poor guy.

And then a totally strange series of things have occurred recently with 
regard to my late sister-in-law’s husband, Noel. He’s a very successful 
businessman and a pub owner and has been trying to cope with the sudden 
death of his wife in June 2019, along with the grief their two (young) 
adult kids are experiencing, plus the lack of pub business due to Covid.

I’ve kept in loose touch with Noel ever since he asked me to write and 
deliver Maria’s eulogy. Over the last couple of years, through texts, 
he’s always suggested that we get together for a drink and catch up 
which I’ve always put down as pure politeness. Recently he suggested the 
same thing but in a phone call when he told me about Edel’s crash, which 
no one else in the Kennedy clan had informed me of.

Edel has always been close to Noel and she asked him to drive to Cork to 
be with her whilst she gave an official report to the Gardai regarding 
the crash. So here’s where it gets weird, Tig. Noel asked me to drive 
with him to Cork to collect Edel but suggested we go down the day before 
her release, have a nice meal, a few drinks and “a laugh”, and stay the 
night in an hotel before we retrieve Edel the following day. Whilst he 
was suggesting this plan I was uncommonly quiet on the other end of the 
phone and Noel said we would, of course, have separate rooms because he 
“wasn’t going to try and climb into bed with me”. The thought never 
crossed my mind! To be honest, I wasn’t sure what the fuck was going on 
but it’s been a very long time since I’ve been in the company of a kind 
man who wanted to hang out with me, so I agreed, thinking what harm 
could come of it.

with the Gardai in Cork and without discussing it with me, Noel changed 
his initial plan ‘to have a laugh’, and we simply drove to and from Cork 
on the same day to collect Edel. I reckon he possibly had a good think 
about what he’d proposed and decided against it. We had a pleasant time 
talking on the way down to Cork but I couldn’t forget the fact that I’m 
fairly certain he’d possibly made a pass at me. Or did he? I have no clue.

*way* too much time in my own head. I keep scolding myself to stop! but 
I’m lonely, and would like a man to like me again. I guess I’m just 
going to have to let time do it’s magical thing and allow it all to 
slowly fade away. Talk to me, Todd. Give me your take on this. Sorry 
this is so long but, hell! I’m long-winded.

Love,
Skin

**

*How I didn’t become a racist*

*

By Todd McCaffrey, BSME, MFA, SFWA, New York Times Bestselling author

I think it’s important to understand America’s underlying inclination 
toward racism. It doesn’t just come from our parents. It comes from our 
community, our society, from the people we grow up with.

I am an alien, so I think my point of view may be helpful. When I say 
I’m an alien, I’m an alien in Ireland: where I lived for my high school 
and college years. I describe myself as “mid-Atlantic and sinking.”

My journey toward racism started in late elementary and early middle 
school, before I moved to Ireland.

I moved to Long Island, New York, in time to enter third grade. The 
school was small and the community tight-knit. There were only two black 
kids in the whole school — they were brothers, a year apart. Nice guys. 
The younger one had a small bit of iris detached in the white of his eye 
which amazed everyone who saw it.  I remember constantly asking to look 
at it — it was just so cool!

My parents were determined to raise broad-minded children and when the 
chance came, introduced us to people from all  over the world, including 
a Nigerian who stayed the weekend with us, arriving in the marvelously 
bright Nigerian native clothing.

Still, in school hallways, there were the whispers. That blacks would 
beat kids up, that you couldn’t trust them.

This whispering became more apparent in middle school and I think, had 
it not been for my relocation to Ireland, that background whispering 
would have lodged firmly in my mind.

But, barring that lingering underlayer of fear, I like to think that the 
full implant of racism didn’t take with me.  And I think that’s because 
of my time in Ireland… and two people in particular.

In Ireland my classmates said: “I hate all Yanks!” to which was hastily 
added, “But not you, I know you.”  Such statements are examples of 
prejudice and bigotry. It was my first experience of prejudice directed 
at me.

The two people who broke the back of racism for me were strangers.  One 
was a classmate, the other an actor.

We’ll take the second first.  He is Lenny Henry — now SirLenny Henry.  
He is a black comedian. Hearing a very English accent on a black man 
broke the mold that society had tried to impose on me about black people 
— that they all spoke the same.  That was a revelation to me, a “Wait, 
what?” moment. Not all blacks are the same.  My fourteen year-old 
thinking went like this: “So… this notion that blacks are a threat or 
menace… that’s a lie!”

My second revelation came with my classmate, Obudan Obesan. Obudan, for 
me, will always be the primal proof that skin color means 
absolutelynothing!  Also, he proved that James Joyce was a second-rate 
author. I can’t remember when we read Joyce’s The Dubliners.  I’m pretty 
sure it was after I’d first been exposed to Mr. Obesan’s writing.  The 
thing is, Obudan gotthe feel of the Irish, the Dublin Irish, down pat.  
He had it better than Joyce. Waayyybetter than Joyce. Nearly fifty years 
later, my opinion has not changed.

Between Obudan and Sir Lenny Henry, I threw out that notion that black 
people were inferior.

With the benefit of hindsight, I can see how American society has a 
built-in underlying prejudice against people of color.  It starts as the 
whispers in middle grade and high school corridors: “You can’t trust 
them.” “They’ll beat you up.” It’s something that we should be aware of, 
should recognize... and banish.

Because black culture has imbued our society with somuch. Even while we 
derided it, it gave us rock’n’roll, starting with Chuck Berry. The black 
culture is more vibrant and alive than the old, tired white culture. We 
can and should learn a lot from it.  The first step is to recognize 
that. The next step is to embrace this difference, to grasp it and learn 
from it. Our society will grow stronger when we do.

*

whether the moon's gravity would be sufficient remains to be explored.)

push fully into space... and staying there.

invade" dystopian idea set on the asteroid belt (called "Minor's War" 
because it's a YA about asteroid miners taking back Earth) but my heart 
is never really in dystopian/apocalyptic stories.

A proper rotating space station would also be a great place to learn how 
to properly create self-sustaining environmental systems.  Also, we 
really need to start to learn how to build stuff in space instead of 
simply boosting it pre-built from Earth.

So... what do you think? 

I had to take a break for a bit and get in some light reading --
 Rick Atkinson's
 
Pulitzer Prize-winning 
An Army at Dawn

 and 
Day of Battle
.

I finished book 4 at 5 a.m. this morning.  I went back and
 re-read the last chapter at least twice just because I'm a sucker
 for such lines as:

“Combat Ops, Combat Ops, Navy One. Say again
 . . . Navy 
One
 .
 . .
 Over.”

Is there a Bible available?

I see that there are books 5,6, and 7
 although they seem to be anthologies, am I right?

And do we have a future timeline?

I was sad to see that the ISS was used up...
 that had been my first story idea.

Also, I thinking about the nature of the
 H7D3 infection, it would seem to me that one solution to the
 infected would be take advantage of their changed physiology --
 they're not quite 
homo sapiens sapiens
 anymore, they're
 a separate species.  In fact, unless John is planning on having
 baby zombies, they're genetically a sport (can't reproduce) -- a
 dead end.

I'm dubious about the current populations of
 infected still alive.  A human without clothing is a very naked
 ape.  A human eating only flesh will find all sorts of vitamin
 deficiencies -- scurvy and rickets are high on the list.  Add to
 that the return of lice (always a source of protein) and other
 parasites and I don't see the infecteds being very long-lived.

So, if formication is the start of the final
 infectious phase, presumably leading to brain swelling and
 necrosis of large amounts of the cerebral hemisphere, it might
 make sense to 
finish the job
 by releasing a virus that
 pushes the infected over the edge.

A simple method would be infected food --
 "poisoned" with something contagious and terminal.  That would
 leave all those rotting bodies however (that seems to be a given
 in any situation).

One possibility would be arranging a "trap"
 that included thistles (they itch like crazy) and let the
 infected itch themselves to a final death (nasty, I know).

Another possibility might be some sort of
 virus that attacks along the same pathways as the original H7D3
 but inactivates the infected's mitochrondria (the powerhouse of
 the cells) and let them die of lethargy (perhaps a bit more
 humane).  Make it infectious and the only problem is ensuring
 that regular humans (particularly those still lost) can't catch
 it.

Another possibility is to arrange a virus
 that makes the infected light phobic.  They won't come out at
 night and are afraid of bright lights.  Make them underground
 vampires.  I suppose adding excessive sound sensitivity to their
 ills might also reduce their population.  How about simply
 figuring out a way to make them afraid of regular humans?  And
 while we're at it, why can't we just engineer a virus that makes
 them hate the smell of normal humans?  Make it so that they stay
 away from 
homo sapiens sapiens
 and just let them die out
 in peace.  (I know this kinda walks around all the loud
 explosions and raining body parts but it makes more sense).

It would seem to me that, at the very least,
 arranging physical contact with the survivors in the CDC --
 presumably the largest concentration of biological knowledge
 left in the world, would be a high priority.

It would also seem to me that if I'm going
 to contribute, I'd best understand the other contributions
 already made -- no point in writing 10,000 words only to
 discover that that particular story has already been told.

From a recovery point of view, one of the
 first problems is going to be food.  Planting, harvesting,
 distributing something easy.  Probably any agriculture will
 include potatoes (easy to plant, maintain, dig up -- not a great
 source of protein).  I think you might also want to consider
 some varieties of "super-food" (like genetically enhanced
 potatoes that include more vitamins).

The other problem, after food, will be
 shelter, clothing, medicine, metal-working.  And maybe there
 should be some thought given to better methods of construction,
 production, etc.  This world has a humungous manpower problem
 which means that individuals will be able to charge very highly
 for their time, effort, and skills (like after the Black
 Death).  Rebuilding chains of production may be easier,
 particularly if there are some advanced production lines mostly
 intact.  Labor saving devices will be even more than a must than
 they were after the Black Death, so innovation will be highly
 prized (and paid).  I'd expect to see robots everything (ain't
 nothing stopping some reverse engineering using simple motors
 and ancient computers).

-- Todd

64 GB Corsair LPX RAM

2x 2TB Samsung EVO M.2 drives

1x 4TB WD Caviar Black HDD

ASUS 2060 RTX Video card

ASUS ROG STRIX 750 W power supply.

To: [REDACTED_EMAIL]
Subject: Crime Assign #1

**

*Is the movie Die Hard(the first one) a Holiday Crime story or not?*

*

Well… damn.

Die Hard(1988) is one of my favorite movies. The dialog, the pacing… 
everything in that movie just works. They not only handle the hero well, 
they handle the supporting characters well.

It used to be that you could go to Drew’s Script-o-rama 
<http://www.script-o-rama.com/>and read the screenplay (probably final 
cut). And that screenplay reads. Just reading it to yourself, on your 
own, and you get the pacing, the pull, the feel of the story. Good stuff.

So when the question comes, is it a holiday crime story, the answer 
seems obvious. It’s certainly a crime story -- bad guys want to steal 
hundreds of millions of bearer bonds and don’t care who (or how many) 
they kill to get them. And it does occur sometime in the Christmas 
holiday frame, probably one to two weeks beforehand (that’s the normal 
time for corporate office parties).

BUT… the test of a holiday story is whether you can take the story out 
of the holiday period and have it still work.

With that in mind, I considered other films that would be regarded as 
holiday films and how they worked.

Consider The Santa Clause (not a crime story), Elf(also not a crime 
story), and Home Alone(a crime story).

In the case of The Santa Clausethe whole premise is that our hero finds 
himself becomingSanta Claus. He transforms from a curmudgeon along the 
way into a person of character and soul. Can you move this story out of 
the Xmas holiday? Nope, no way. The story doesn’t exist without 
Christmas, specifically without the whole Santa Claus mythos. Elfis 
similarly constrained: no story without Christmas (and, in fact, our Elf 
saves Christmas).

With Home Alone, the question becomes more involved. Our young hero is 
accidentally left behind and finds himself defending his home against 
would-be robbers. The basic plot -- young hero left alone to fight 
against bad guys -- is not dependent on the holidays per se.  We could 
have placed this in the summer or spring break or a number of other 
holidays -- or even just played it out withouta holiday (albeit with 
perhaps more difficulty). But the robbers rely on automatic light 
systems and lots of empty houses to target. That spells holidays, and 
pretty much spells Xmas. Also, our hero has a bonding moment with Scary 
Shovel Guy which helps affirm his course of action and speaks to general 
human kindness. So… this would be difficult to make work without the 
Xmas holiday. In this regard, I’d consider this to be a Holiday (Xmas) 
Crime story.

When pondering Die Hardand the question of whether it is a Holiday Crime 
story, I asked myself firstly: Could I change the holiday? If I could, 
then perhaps the “Holiday” part of the “holiday crime” story was 
superfluous.

What if this was a New Year’s Eve story?  Consider inter-cutting between 
the New Year’s Ball falling in Times Square and Hans Gruber falling to 
his death.  Consider, instead of “Now I’ve got a machine gun! Ho-ho-ho!” 
having “Thanks for the party favor, now I can really make noise when the 
ball drops!”  And more.  I’d say that Die Hardcould easily be moved to 
be a New Year story.  In fact, that adds even more to the fundamental 
plot line -- because New Year’s marks new beginnings and the central 
personal question of the movie is “Will John McClane lose his wife and 
family?”  That could now morph into the side question, “What will the 
New Year hold for John McClane?”

[Also, let’s not forget that we’re talking about a Hollywood movie.  
They have to be pretty flexible in their details because no one can be 
certain when someone demands a change of location or timing.]

With this, then, the question becomes: Does this movie haveto be a 
holiday movie (let alone a Christmas movie).  Why can’t it be set in the 
summer?  The essentials -- a new building, corporate party (“great 
quarter”) do not demand a holiday, that could happen any time. The 
robbery could happen any time. In fact, the holidays are possibly a 
badtime for a heist (note, for example, that noneof the Ocean’s movies 
used a holiday), in that such times often come with increased delays and 
heightened security.

So, if we take the holiday out of this movie, does it fall apart? No. 
The fundamental story is not dependent on the time of year, season, or 
holidays. Therefore, this is NOT a HolidayCrime Story.

Hence my, “Well… damn.”

To: 'Les Johnson' <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>, Robert Hampson <[REDACTED_EMAIL]>
Subject: Space Stations

Hi Les, Rob,

I think, with this new administration, we should propose a bold space 
exploration initiative -- a new High Frontier.  I think our nation works 
best when challenged, the bigger the challenge, the better.

Listening to NASA experts on the biological effects of microgravity, it 
becomes clear that man cannot survive and thrive in a "zero-gee" 
environment. So that means we have to have gravity (how much is not 
clear, some say lunar gravity would do the trick).

I think, in terms of bold exploration we should move from the baby step 
of exploring space to the more profound concept of living in space -- 
that we should build rotating space stations which provide all the way 
up to 1.0 gravities.

Further that we should target the goal of completely self-sustaining 
space stations. We're going to need to know how to build completely 
self-sustaining habitats if we want to exploit the solar system.  And 
we're going to need to know how to build completely self-sustaining 
habitats if we're going to travel to the stars.

I read and well remember NASA SP-428: Space Resources and Space 
Settlements, as well as "Space Settlements: A Design Study," so I recall 
the state of the art in the 1970s.

We have over 20 years of understanding life in zero gravity, and we know 
how *assemble* a space station in orbit. What we don't know is how to 
build a rotating space station nor how much the coriolis effect will 
affect humans.

Building a self-sustaining rotating space station will also allow us to 
fully understand a closed-loop environment -- what we learn from that 
will be directly applicable to our issues with global warming and 
climate change (aside from offering a bolthole).

Building a self-sustaining rotating space station is the first step 
toward building habitats throughout the stars.  I would expect that we 
would plan on building more than one station, each one improving on the 
design of the former.  It should be possible to profitably move certain 
industries up to the stations (part of their self-sufficiency).

I wonder how hard it would be to pitch it to the President, 
Vice-President and Congress.

What do you guys think?

-- Todd

Dear Sqeej,

How are you?  How's the world in Ireland?

i am still holed up at Dell Ridge.  We did Hanukah, celebrating mostly 
at Brit's.  Brit has a "port" because she was getting so many IV 
infusions that it was messing with her veins. Now she gets it through a 
medically implanted thingie (I know, all so technical).  Also, with 
eight days, Hanukah is more stressful than Xmas.

Dex and I have been talking on and off.  He's decided to change majors 
(which was the reason for the first call).  He's thinking about 
anthropology which sounds like a good fit for him (he may be rethinking 
things after WW84).  Anyway, I think he's probably right -- Occupational 
Therapy never seemed like a good fit (I keep recommending art/writing 
where he's a natural but "it doesn't pay enough").  "Kids these days!"

I've been looking for good books, having pretty much re-read all the 
favorites to predictable tatters.  I recently re-read "Bridge of Birds" 
(still a classic) but I've read that book so much I could almost qualify 
for the Fahrenheit 451 "book" crew.

I got a marvelous Jacquie Lawson card from Richard. That was awfully sweet.

I'd managed to donate a lot to the last election and now the various 
fundraisers are treating me like their monkey.  I have quite forcefully 
disconnected myself from that -- there's something wrong with a 
democracy that requires $$ to elect.  It means that the biggest pockets 
generally win.  That's obscene. There must be a better way to handle that.

I've been signing up for many marvelous Domestika classes (they teach 
art, in Spanish with subtitles).  They're generally $9.90 and if you 
want to brush up your Photoshop skills or learn ZBrush, they're a good 
group to examine.

Did you know that Jeff won Illustrators of the Future?  (He's one of 12 
for the year, but even so!) I think it really validated his art.

Amelia tells me that your divorce finalized.  That's one of those 
bittersweet milestones, I know.  Just like all major changes, it'll take 
you about two years to fully process it.

Alec extended "the paw of friendship" (my quote) and I accepted. He's on 
Facebook all quite ready to criticize Biden. Sigh.

I am still waiting tenterhooks for the formal, official, and irrefutable 
change of presidency.

I'm glad we have got vaccines.

When the Spanish Influenza (called Spanish because they were the only 
un-censored newspapers back in WWI) ended, we got the Roaring 20s.  I 
wouldn't be surprised if we got the same when we finally kick off COVID.

Anyway, that's sort of news for now.

Love,

Todd

Yes, there is a bible, which I have attached. And
 there are two more novels that cover Tom Smith's story (Steve's

 main storyline. Chuck Gannon has a new novel coming out, which I
 just got in this week and haven't had a chance to read yet. 
 

And yes, there are two anthologies, which I have also
 attached. Sarah Hoyt is also working on a full novel, and
 Ringo has been plotting out the next "main" novel. It's a busy
 and nicely profitably universe (both anthologies continue to
 pay royalties and were published in hardcover, the last one
 debuting at #1 on the bookscan SF/F chart). 
 

As to your other questions... yes, there population of
 infected has been substantially reduced by the time of the
 new anthology (basically set in the first spring/summer
 after the Fall). However, even a "base brain" homo sapiens
 is a remarkably resilient creature. That said, this
 anthology is basically moving past the "zombie menace".

Ringo wrote a bit from the first State of the Union
 speech after the U.S. government has (sort of) reformed to
 use as the thematic base for the anthology: “Though we have
 much to do, the great threat has ended. The infected are but
 a background nuisance. The question becomes, where do we go
 from here? This I will tell you as your President. We shall
 not fall. We shall not enter ‘a thousand year night.’ We
 will triumph over this adversity as America has always
 triumphed. The Fall is ended. We shall Rise.”

 The “centerpiece story” of the next main line Smith book
 will be about saving the infrastructure, primarily in the
 Eastern United States. Dams, locks, bridges. That is the
 primary focus for the ‘Feds’. What’s everyone else doing
 wherever they are in the world is the focus on this
 anthology. 

Well, I'm adaptable.

But I gotta say... if you're rebuilding a country, don't start
 with outdated systems.  Dams, locks, bridges... why?

Dams I can see for flood prevention and energy generation but I
 don't see why the ideal should be re-inventing what existed before
 -- the trick is to step BEYOND that.  Again, the lack of
 population is going to demand labor-saving at all levels,
 particularly in agriculture (farming).  You aren't going back to
 the old ways, they won't work (they require a much larger
 population).  You've got to think smart, and different.

Solar and wind power are available (and the Dutch have been using
 windmills for centuries).

Why rebuild a road infrastructure?  Why not revitalize rails? 
 Why not automate rail transport, using roll-on-roll-off containers
 and automated movement systems?  And, for that matter, how much
 cargo is there to move?

The biggest issue is population sustenance and growth.  The US
 build up so well because there was a flood of immigration.  This
 time would be very different.

Is there conversation group for this?  One of my pet peeves is
 the desire to build a self-managed medical system.  You've a
 dearth of doctors, instead of following the old Johns Hopkins
 hyper-perfectionist model why not develop home-use systems that
 allow people to mostly tend to themselves?

In terms of agriculture, I'm thinking that highly-mechanized,
 localized systems are possibly best (I can it "a farm in a box"),
 something that's tightly integrated to the city, part of the city,
 so that there is no "rural vs. urban" issue anymore (you'd need
 it, you just don't have the manpower).

What is the thinking on global warming? Clearly with the
 population so based there isn't any major contributions towards
 the problem but the problem still exists and it will take time to
 reverse (unless you posit that runaway global warming has already
 started).  So you've got rising sea levels, so building right next
 to the shore is not a good idea.  You've got weather issues, too.

One thing you're going to want to get back quickly is a space
 industry, including launch capabilities (what happened in French
 Guyana?  Did SpaceX do a "soft landing"? (I'd think so, Musk is a
 smart guy)).

My opinion is that the older, less nimble corporations didn't
 anticipate the level of destruction leveled by the virus.  The
 younger, more nimble corporations were better suited to handling
 the disaster.  What about Virgin Galactic?  That might have
 survived (but who needs sub-orbital capabilities?).

If the question really is -- what next? Then let's talk.  What
 are the goals of the survivors of the US?  The same ol' same old? 
 Or something better?

What's the status of fusion?  I know there's at least one group
 in Canada thinking they've got a good shot now.  What if they
 succeeded and enough of them survived (in the cold)?

How hard is it to get a chip fabrication plant back online, given
 power?

What about the CDC?  If the crisis of the infected is mostly
 over, is Atlanta (mostly) habitable?  Are cities mostly wasted and
 useless (build new "cities")?

How much do you want me to lead and how much do you want me to
 follow?

You're going to want to get the internet back up, at least at the
 Wi-Fi and major datacenter levels.  Who re-starts Amazon? (Because
 there's a lot of stuff there and a good logistics system).

-- Todd

 in foster children and helps them flourish. The system,

 Bird’s Plea” blends elements of science fiction and fantasy to

 village, which she believes is being attacked by demons.

 a hulking amnesiac who, after being found naked in a parking
 garage by a local crime boss and hired on as muscle, finds
 something unexpected on his brutal journey of self-discovery.
 Beagle’s “Except on Saturdays” reimagines the French myth of
 Melusine with the story of a California high school history
 teacher who, after meeting a wheelchair-using woman on a bus,

 Parker’s “Habitat,” a local hero is tasked by a prince to
 catch and deliver him a living dragon. The hero delivers—with
 karmic results. There are no weak links in this anthology, and
 every selection is noteworthy in some way, but arguably the
 most memorable story is Ann Leckie and Rachel Swirsky’s “We
 Continue,” set on a planet where human colonists struggle to
 survive while dragons thrive in hivelike communities that

*

Hi Amelia,

Here's a quick partial brain dump to give you some more info about who 
your Dad is. Feel free to share with Eliza. I'll write more as I get the 
time. (I'm still REALLY sad about Chadwick Boseman - his is a great loss.)

We grew up in several locations in the US, all in the northeast:

 1.

 Montclair, NJ.  I left when I was two and have no memories.

 2.

 100 Danforth Place, Windybush, Wilmington, Delaware

 1.

 With one interruption, we lived there from the time I was 2
 (1958) until we moved to 369 Carpenter Ave., Sea Cliff, Long
 Island, NY in 1965

 3.

 369 Carpenter Avenue, Sea Cliff, Long Island, New York

 1.

 We lived there from 1965 until we (Gigi, Mum, and I) moved to
 Ireland in 1970

 4.

 In Ireland (just to continue the record), we first lived in:

 1.

  14 North Avenue, Mount Merrion (1970-71)

 2.

 Meadowbrook House, Dundrum (1971-72)

 1.

 Alec joined us there and became a trawler fisherman.

 3.

 Site 11 Rochestown Avenue (1972-73)

 1.

 Alec wasn’t here

 4.

 79 Shanganagh Vale, Cabinteely (1[REDACTED_PHONE]?)

 1.

 Nor was Alec here.

 5.

 Dragonhold, Kilquade, Co. Wicklow (1[REDACTED_PHONE])

 1.

 He visited here occasionally

 6.

 From there, Mum moved into Dragonhold-Underhill and lived there
 until she died in 2011.

I have many memories of Alec, some of which are great and some of which 
are not.

When we were in 100 Danforth, we all got kittens: Tasso (Alec), Tallabar 
(me), and Silkie Blackington (for Gigi with much adult supervision in 
the naming else the cat would have been simply “Blackie”).

Tasso was a tortoise shell.  He lost an argument with a car not long 
after we got him. Alec was devastated.

Tallabar was a multi-color, a mix of grays and oranges.  Quite the 
pretty cat.

Silkie was your average black cat.  She was sweet and her fur was very 
soft, hence the name.

Silkie and Tallabar went on to have many, many litters.  Tallabar was 
good at producing orange marmalade cats.

We also had dogs, starting with Wizard (a German Shepherd) followed by 
his son, Merlin.  Wiz decided that I was his human charge. We had a 
sloping hill outside our front door and it went down to join the street 
which formed part of the branches of a tee-junction (the other street 
tee’d into Danforth Place).  Wiz decided that I was not allowed to go 
down that hill when I was an infant and took to blocking me.

Our next door neighbors (to our left as you’re standing in the front 
door looking out) were the Estes.  Larry Estes was Alec’s age.  I think 
their daughter was close to Gigi’s age.  Alec and Larry hung out and I 
did my best to tag along, often successfully.

There was another housing estate being built across the railroad tracks 
beyond a small woods at the edge of Windybush and we used to trek there 
many a  time. The woods had some pretty decent undergrowth. One day 
Larry got a hold of his father’s machete (from WWII) and he and Alec 
took turns “clearing” the underbrush (think Indiana Jones in South 
America at the beginning of Raiders of the Lost Ark).  I must have been 
around six.  At one point Alec told me to stand back.  I did but, 
apparently, not far enough and the machete tore into my shin.  I think 
it was Alec who carried me back to the house. I went to the ER and got 
four stitches.

Another  time, when I was eight or so, we had a particularly hard but 
dry winter.  It was decided to go exploring (“mountain climbing”?) in 
the culverts at the upper side of the estate.  Alec had brought a hammer 
along to poke holes in the ice as handholds.  He told me (seems to be a 
pattern here) to get back and swung immediately after I said, “Okay” but 
before I could comply (well, that’s my story) and I got the claws of the 
hammer hitting my head -- just on the eye socket.  A bit lower and I 
would have lost the eye.  As it was, I got two stitches without novocaine.

Ah, the good years!

Alec and I fought often enough that I have many recollections of 
variously being forced to eat grass or dirt to escape being buried under 
him.

In 1962 we moved to Dusseldorf, Germany for six months because Dad had a 
job doing PR work for DuPont that required him to work there.  Overall, 
it was a marvelous experience.  Alec, Gigi, and I were all very 
nordic-looking and, when we didn’t speak, had no trouble passing for 
German (Dad’s family had roots in Schleswig-Holstein on the 
German-Danish border).  Mum place Alec and I in the local German 
school.  I can’t say how well Alec did but I flourished, having a 
teacher who could speak English (she was raised in England during the 
war) and I learned excellent “gekauft Deutsch” -- as Mum called it 
(“shopping German”).

We all adored the chocolate over there.  We took the tram everywhere, 
un-parented.  I recall once having some old Frau look at us and scoff, 
“Ach, Englander!” to which I replied, “Nein, Amerikaner!” -- that seemed 
to both affront and appease her, somewhat (the English had ruled the 
area after the war and weren’t particularly good at it).

They had these marvelous parades where they’d throw candy.  We all loved 
that.

We got a VW station wagon while we were over there and, when our time 
was up, drove around Europe (France, Germany, Holland, at least).  We 
took the ferry to England.  We were broke, so we camped one night all in 
the VW and discovered later the next day that we’d stopped outside an 
insane asylum.  We dropped the car off for transport to the States and 
headed to Gatwick airport (Heathrow was not then built), only to 
discover that there was some tax that we still had to pay before we 
could board the flight back.  This caused the parents immense distress 
until a nice American couple, hearing the panic, loaned us the money 
(there were Texans).

sister was drying explosives in the over."

sparklers for a school science project.)

I figured that it was such a good starting premise that I just /had/ to 
write the novel.

Anyway, one of my tertiary characters decided that, as she was going to 
gene-engineer her own child, she would name him from her favorite 
"pre-space" science fiction series.  And so, currently Engisn Millisor 
Rau is serving on HMAS Sparkle (laundry ship for the Navy).  He also 
becomes the OCTO - Officer Candidate Training Officer - for one of my 
heroines, the girl who turned him down when she was a teenager (/Oh, 
damn, the one boy I've ever broke and he's my commanding officer!)/

how do i delete from git

To delete things from Git, the approach depends on what you want to delete: a file, a branch, or a commit. Here's a clear breakdown:

---

 ️ . Delete a File from Git

 A. Delete a file from the repo and disk:
```bash
git rm filename.txt
git commit -m "Remove filename.txt"
git push
```

 B. Delete a file only from Git (keep it locally):
```bash
git rm --cached filename.txt
git commit -m "Remove filename.txt from tracking"
git push
```

---

 . Delete a Branch

 A. Delete a local branch:
```bash
git branch -d my-branch safe delete (only if merged)
git branch -D my-branch force delete (even if not merged)
```

 B. Delete a remote branch (e.g., GitHub):
```bash
git push origin --delete my-branch
```

---

 . Delete a Commit

 ️ This rewrites history. Only do this if you're sure.

 A. Undo last commit (keep changes unstaged):
```bash
git reset --soft HEAD~
```

 B. Undo last commit (discard changes):
```bash
git reset --hard HEAD~
```

---

 Bonus: Remove Untracked Files
To clean up untracked files (not in Git):
```bash
git clean -f delete untracked files
git clean -fd delete untracked files and directories
```

is there a way to get the Linux 'touch' command to recursively create directories

The `touch` command itself does not create directories; it only creates (or updates) files. 
If you try `touch path/to/file.txt` and the intermediate directories (`path/`, `path/to/`) do not exist, it will fail with: 
```
touch: cannot touch 'path/to/file.txt': No such file or directory
```

---

 What You Want: `mkdir -p` + `touch`

To recursively create directories and then create a file, you need two steps:

```bash
mkdir -p path/to/
touch path/to/file.txt
```

You can chain them:
```bash
mkdir -p path/to/ && touch path/to/file.txt
```

---

 If You Want a One-Liner Script

Here’s a shell one-liner that will do both in one go:

```bash
mkdir -p "$(dirname path/to/file.txt)" && touch path/to/file.txt
```

Or, for many files:
```bash
for f in path/to/file.txt path/to/file.txt; do
 mkdir -p "$(dirname "$f")" && touch "$f"
done
```

---

 Summary Table

| Task | Command |
|----------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| Recursively create directories | `mkdir -p path/to/` |
| Create an empty file | `touch path/to/file.txt` |
| Both, one-liner | `mkdir -p "$(dirname path/to/file.txt)" && touch path/to/file.txt` |

---

There is no direct `touch` flag to create directories—use `mkdir -p` as above.

 Option : With `dosunix` (Recommended if installed)

 Option : With `sed` (no new tools needed)

Then run as usual.

 Option : In VS Code or Sublime Text
- Open the file.
- In the lower right, click “CRLF” and change to “LF.”
- Save.

That error usually means your shell is using `sh`, not `bash`. 
`[[ ... =~ ... ]]` and the use of parentheses in the regex are Bash-specific features—they do not work in `/bin/sh`.

 How to Fix

. Shebang 
 The very first line of your script must be:
 ```bash
 !/bin/bash
 ```
 Not `!/bin/sh` and not missing.

. How you run it 
 Always run your script like this (so it uses Bash):
 ```bash
 ./prepDocker.sh
 ```
 or:
 ```bash
 bash prepDocker.sh
 ```
 If you run it as:
 ```bash
 sh prepDocker.sh
 ```
 It will use `/bin/sh` which does not support Bash features.

. Double-check script permissions:
 ```bash
 chmod +x prepDocker.sh
 ```

. If you must support `/bin/sh`:
 - Use `case ... esac` instead of `[[ ... =~ ... ]]`, 
 - Or just use plain `[` `]` tests (less powerful).

---

 Example
Wrong:
```bash
if [[ "$ACTION" =~ ^(prod|drd|local|custom)$ ]]; then
```
Right (bash only):
```bash
if [[ "$ACTION" =~ ^(prod|drd|local|custom)$ ]]; then
```
Right (POSIX, works in sh):
```bash
case "$ACTION" in
 prod|drd|local|custom)
 do stuff
 ;;
esac
```

---

 TL;DR

- Make sure your script starts with `!/bin/bash`
- Do not run it with `sh prepDocker.sh`
- Use `bash prepDocker.sh` or `./prepDocker.sh`

 Step : Define the `withdir` function

Add this to your shell config file (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, etc.):

```bash
withdir() {
 local index="$"
 shift
 local dir
 dir="$(eval echo $(dirs +$index))"
 dir="$(realpath "$dir")" || return 
 Replace {} with the real path
 cmd=()
 for arg in "$@"; do

 "${cmd[@]}"
}
```

```bash
python manage.py runserver 
```
This will run at `http://...:/`

 To specify both IP address and port:

```bash
python manage.py runserver ...:
```

- If your Dockerfile does not copy the file to `/`, the container won’t find it at `/wait-for-postgres.sh`.

Ophelia caught herself quickly, "I imagine the captain wants us to be prepared for anything." "It's customary that the officer in charge of midshipmen be the assistant tactical officer," Ensign Rau reminded her. "Or perhaps you weren't aware?" "Sorry, sir," Ophelia said, telling herself to control her temper and mind her words, "I had assumed that as a fleet auxiliary ship our tactical control would be under fleet command." Under certain circumstances, Ophelia's mind would go racing off to conclusions that seemed quite logical to her but quite impossible for others. This, apparently, was one of those circumstances. In rapid order she determined that Ensign Millisor Rau had doubtless been appointed midshipman to Sparkle upon his delayed graduation from the Academy – he was, after all, only a year younger than her sister – probably under the aegis of the same mysterious strings that had assigned Ophelia to the same ship her sister commanded. Someone had been very devious in that assignment – for there would certainly be questions asked if Midshipman Rau failed his middy cruise aboard a ship commanded by a long-time enemy family. Not that the Branfords had started the feud, nor had the Rau's – the name of Rau hadn't even existed until Milly – er, Ensign Rau – had been hatched; the name was the result of his parent's strange decision to combine the names of two fictional villains. Valeria Lawson, his mother, had been within her rights to do so and, as a naval veteran – albeit one forced out of the service under a cloud – she was supported by her generous pension. Of course, whatever it was that got ex-Captain Lawson beached had been under the same hush-hush secrecy that covered everyone else involved with the events leading up to the Battle of Canaris. The best that the children had ever managed to wheedle out of their father – he being more easily wheedled, particularly when his daughters ganged up on him – was that Captain Valeria Lawson "had been under a great deal of stress and might have made a poor call." This information had been acquired long before the two girls were old enough to recognize their Admiral father's phenomenal ability to dissemble.

"We know that James Walker, son of Daniel, was an ensign on one of the other Walkers under the Prince, so we can eliminate him," I said. Karl called up the passenger list on the main screen of the Comm console. Elodie moved close beside him to get a better view and, also, to whisper to him: "Did you tell him? Does he know?" Karl shook his head. Elodie hissed her displeasure. A beep from the main Comm console distracted them. Elodie glanced over at the telltale light, deftly called up a window on their main display and pointed to the stream of numbers: "See? Code groups." Karl glanced at them and grunted. "Going out on the data line." Elodie stole a quick look at Strasnoye, then muttered low: "We could decode it." Down in his cabin, Captain Zhukov carefully replaced his code generator in its secret compartment. There! That's done, he thought to himself. He smiled as he imagined his two first officers trying to decipher the gibberish he had sent out on the data link his real message was hidden in his verbal report to the combined Russian/European space exploration agency, Eurocos. "She's the oldest cruiser in the Navy and her captain's almost older," Nick grumbled by way of bragging. Captain Adrian Wardlaw was nearly two hundred years old, had seen combat with the old Pevencee pirates, and was famous for his refusal to accept higher rank or retirement. As he'd been personal friends with the first King and known the current King when he was only in diapers, there was no one who would tell him otherwise. His ship was also the command ship for the Home Fleet which put him at the beck and call of Admiral Omicron Katzelos – though it was rumored that it was mostly the other way around. Ophelia recalled only that her mother never said anything about the Home Fleet's admiral, and that all she'd heard in the Academy was that the admiral was "a great administrator." Given what she'd seen of Dean's behavior while they were training together, she was privately convinced that her classmate would prefer to work with the Admiral than with the Captain – and was quite likely to get his wish.

Silently I waited as he passed me by and obediently I fell in behind him, pulled the double doors closed, and made my way to the kitchen to obey his orders. I would not run away. Our eyes met and my hand went halfway to my neck as I looked at her left foot.

Captain Morton rose wearily from his chair, took his hat and said to my Master, "Then I see no point in continuing this discussion further, sir. I shall take my leave of you." The captain had not quite reached the double doors before Master Evans, clearly amused, nodded toward me once more. "Captain, suh," I said, "I think there might be a reason, suh." He stopped, turned his head and glared at me challengingly. "Well, sir," I continued, "I can think of several reasons why you weren't told and still sent here." He turned back toward me, waiting. "According to our information, the one who found Lieutenant Clarke's remains and buried them was Lieutenant Samuel Cattan, Sir MacAllister's apprentice." His eyebrows flickered with interest. "Well, sir, Samuel Cattan would have known Miss Walker," I continued. The captain frowned, not following me. "What I mean, is that if he'd found Miss Walker, why didn't he say so?" Captain Morton raised a hand to his chin and stroked it thoughtfully. Finally, he turned to me, "I'm afraid the answer is simple: you've never been in a battle so you wouldn't have guessed, but in all likelihood the body was too cut up for him to recognize." Goodness, this man was dull! Aloud, I said, "But if that were so, captain, then how did he identify the body as the lieutenant's?" The captain stopped stroking his chin and raised his head up straight, eyes wide with hope. Then he smiled at me triumphantly. "Yes!" he said. "That could be it, indeed!" He turned toward Master Evans. "Very well, sir, I shall engage your slave as you desire." Master Evans nodded, having expected nothing else. "I'll have the necessary papers drawn up, you can leave tomorrow if you wish. Tonight you'll be a guest at my table." "Thank you," the captain said, having expected nothing less. "I'll be able to catch a ship in Charleston."

Actually, Owami was sure that Bosun Ellis would order Purvis to get Ophelia's gear to the middy berth. Ophelia knew a dismissal when she heard one, even if it was from her own sister, and braced to attention before turning smartly and exiting the lift tube. Behind her the doors hissed shut as Owami – Captain Branford, she corrected herself – said, "Bridge." The deck was empty, a two-person wide corridor running most of the length of the ship, one of two which ran parallel on the main crew deck. Bridge deck was above while stores, engineering and various work decks were below that. For all her glib recital to her sister, Ophelia knew no more about the laundry ship than she'd managed to glean in the few spare hours between receiving her orders and reporting aboard the shuttle. She planned to catch up on her reading as soon as she could, paying special attention to her assignment in – "Milly, is that you?" Ophelia cried as she caught sight of the trim figure standing at the entrance to the midshipman's quarters. As soon as Ophelia caught the other's face, she realized she'd made a terrible mistake. As soon as she caught Ensign Millisor Rau's smirk, she knew it might be her last. "It's Ensign Rau to you, snotty," Millisor Rau replied in a cold voice, carefully working the smirk off his face. ‘Snotty’ was the derogatory – and discouraged but never forgotten – nickname for new midshipmen. ECLSS – Environmental Control and Life Support Systems – pronounced it 'Ee-class', was her assignment. Which made him her immediate superior. "Tactical?" Ophelia said, the question surprised from her. Why would a jumped-up tramp freighter need a tactical section? What could Sparkle do, threaten to over-starch the enemy's underwear?

"But these orders assign me to Sparkle." Lieutenant Commander Madsen raised his head for a moment, as if to confirm the identity of the whining newly-minted officer, sighed, and tapped a quick inquiry into his tablet. "You requested an engineering assignment," Madsen said, as he perused the tablet. "Sparkle has put in a request for an engineer. The computers made the match. You have your orders." He glanced up at her again. "I fail to see where there is a problem." He bit his lips before adding, with a twinkle in his eye, "Unless you are complaining about the ship." His Majesty's Auxiliary Ship Sparkle, in all honesty, was a glorified freighter. Her crew was a strange conglomeration of the traditional "dregs of the Navy" and assorted misfits, odd-balls, and those unfortunate enough to have earned the displeasure of their Lordships in some way. Her armaments were a few targeting lasers, a pair of missile tubes to deal with any asteroids or comets that might stray unavoidably in her path, and a pair of outdated mine-launchers that were added as a convenient way of hiding an accidental over-supply of the same by some unfortunate Ordnance Acquisition Officer who was later discovered to have financial relations with the selling company. On the other hand, for all her lack of speed, grandeur, and general sexiness, Sparkle was a busy ship, on a busy schedule and deemed a vital naval asset. Unlike her sister ship, Gleam, which provided the far-spread Fleet with ordnance and general supplies, Sparkle was tasked with more mundane but no less essential duties. To whit, she was the laundry ship for the Navy, or, as her commissioning orders read, "To provide fresh accouterments and auxiliary materials for naval personnel."

His ship was also the command ship for the Home Fleet which put him at the beck and call of Admiral Omicron Katzelos – though it was rumored that it was mostly the other way around. Only the torches were dim in the morning light and I could make out the smudge that was our carrier. Dart -- bless her! -- had valiantly risen to a full two thousand feet in our five hours’ flight in return. She had done it slowly, sometimes reluctantly, and occasionally dipping back downwards, as if reconsidering her disposition. But here we were. “Charles, if you look to your right you may spot some of the buildings that may become precious to you,” I called. I hadn’t heard from him in a while although once or twice I thought I heard snores. He would be the very first person to sleep on an airship, to my best knowledge. “Be careful, the sun’s rising on that side!” “Oh, indeed it is!” he called back a moment later. “Quite the glory it has, too! And, yes, I see some buildings below. Would you care to enlighten me as to their purpose?” “I believe that the owner would do a better job of that, if you’d permit,” I replied. “The famous Lieutenant Clarke of whom I have heard so much, perhaps?” he replied. “Also, no disrespect to your fine vessel, Captain, but I do wish it had a head.” “If you’re desperate,” I said, thinking quickly. “As you’re a man, you could probably just go over the side.” He was silent for a moment. “And I won’t rock the deck too much?” “Move slowly, keeping the stay line tied around you and stop at a safe distance from the edge,” I cautioned. “I would not, under normal circumstances, engage in any such activity -- will I be the first?” “That I can guarantee,” I told him, my own bladder now questioning the prudence of my gender. “Well,” he said, untying himself with a tone of relish in his voice, “you know, I always fancied the notion of peeing on England.” As he rose and the deck ducked, he added, “Scotland, on the other hand…” He moved closer to the edge and undid himself.

The Vice President, as might be expected given his predecessor's legacy, was not completely traditional. His Majesty's Auxiliary Ship Sparkle, in all honesty, was a glorified freighter. Her crew was a strange conglomeration of the traditional "dregs of the Navy" and assorted misfits, odd-balls, and those unfortunate enough to have earned the displeasure of their Lordships in some way. Her armaments were a few targeting lasers, a pair of missile tubes to deal with any asteroids or comets that might stray unavoidably in her path, and a pair of outdated mine-launchers that were added as a convenient way of hiding an accidental over-supply of the same by some unfortunate Ordnance Acquisition Officer who was later discovered to have financial relations with the selling company. On the other hand, for all her lack of speed, grandeur, and general sexiness, Sparkle was a busy ship, on a busy schedule and deemed a vital naval asset. Unlike her sister ship, Gleam, which provided the far-spread Fleet with ordnance and general supplies, Sparkle was tasked with more mundane but no less essential duties. Would you care to enlighten me as to their purpose?” “I believe that the owner would do a better job of that, if you’d permit,” I replied. “The famous Lieutenant Clarke of whom I have heard so much, perhaps?” he replied. “Also, no disrespect to your fine vessel, Captain, but I do wish it had a head.” “If you’re desperate,” I said, thinking quickly. “As you’re a man, you could probably just go over the side.” He was silent for a moment. “And I won’t rock the deck too much?” “Move slowly, keeping the stay line tied around you and stop at a safe distance from the edge,” I cautioned. “I would not, under normal circumstances, engage in any such activity -- will I be the first?” “That I can guarantee,” I told him, my own bladder now questioning the prudence of my gender. “Well,” he said, untying himself with a tone of relish in his voice, “you know, I always fancied the notion of peeing on England.” As he rose and the deck ducked, he added, “Scotland, on the other hand…” He moved closer to the edge and undid himself.

Recon ships were manned by the maddest of people, people hoping to find new planets or rare resources so that they could strike it rich. At least a few were cultists looking for another “promised land” but most were malcontents who preferred the vastness of space to the crowding of humankind. Cody had a certain respect for them.

This one! Cody said, pointing to the largest dot. The Maru.

A family, Ellaz told him. Five. Father, mother, three children.

That’s a light crew, Cody thought in surprise.

So is six, Other Cody reminded him.

But… warp watch! I mean, who could keep watch and —

The children were older than me, Gail replied. And they all had implants. The captain, Horace Mayhew, made a lot of money back at Quark but he also made a lot of enemies.

What else do we know about him? Cody wondered.

That’s it, Ellaz replied. There’s just not enough room in the computers for a lot of useless data. Anyway, what about the other two?

The Reliant disappeared earlier, Cody thought. But she was a solo crew. And the Doorman was later. He frowned. I don’t know. But, Ellaz, imagine if aliens stopped your ship and threatened your family unless you did what they wanted?

Why not just kill them all? Ellaz asked. Or kill some… and. Nasty.

Very nasty, Other Cody agreed.

Only if the aliens consider us worth living, Gail’s ghost thought. Sentient or whatever they would call it.

Any ship that bumped into them they’d either have to capture or destroy, Nora’s ghost added.

Which means, if that’s true, they know how to catch a ship in warp, Cody thought with a sinking feeling. I wish we’d known that earlier.

We made the best plan we could at the time, Other Cody consoled him.

And, if they don’t see us, they won’t know we’re there until we attack, Nora added.

From the rear, Gail reminded them with a wolfish grin.

So they sent out scouts and they caught these ships — or one of them — nearly two years ago, Cody thought.

Which means they’ve got a scouting shell two years ahead of them, Nora agreed.

So how many systems have they already scouted? Other Cody wondered.

“Shoot them with their own weapon,” Nora added. Then, “But you’d have to aim it just right —”

“No, use an arc, or even a — a cone,” Cody thought. “Sweep it in a wide circle so that it’ll have a better chance of —”

“Cody, that’s brilliant!” Ellaz said. “Huh, you’re not too stupid after all.”

“Thanks,” Cody said. “And it’s still mate in four.”

Nora glanced around in the virtual space and raised a hand to point, “Isn’t it cheating if you use a board for mental chess?”

“We’re in virtual space,” Cody reminded her. “And —”

“You’re not really trying unless you’re cheating,” Ellaz and Cody said in unison. Then, Ellaz added, “Quiet, this is difficult.”

They went quiet. For twenty-nine minutes. Cody used the time to update several courses, just in case. Nora checked on the systems, frowned at their fuel use but said nothing.

They all jerked when the alarm went off.

“Thirty minutes,” Nora said. She turned to Cody. “I’m going to let everyone know.”

“We’re here!” Gail cried as she entered VR. “Ensigns Eber and Falcon — what’s that?”

Well, if we’re lucky, it’s a warp mirror, Ellaz replied. Then she realized that the others couldn’t hear her thoughts. “If we’re lucky, it’s a warp mirror.”

“I thought you said reflector!” Nora protested.

“I was wrong,” Ellaz said. “And I’ve got us a possible approach, complete with a firing solution.”

“Twenty-nine minutes,” Gail said. “So…” she went silent, putting herself into a virtual command chair and wrapping herself in displays, moving them around with her fingers. Jacob spotted her and wrapped himself up similarly in the simulation space.

“This is the First Officer,” Nora said, calling over the ship’s intercom. Her voice echoed in the shuttle. “We are currently twenty-nine minutes from Deneb. We have revised our plan. We’re going to try a warp mirror to reflect back the alien ship’s warp lance at it and protect spacehab Elantra.”

“If this works,” Cody said, “we’ll destroy their ship, save the hab and maybe stop their attack.”

“All departments check in,” Nora ordered.

“ECLSS,” Mandy Barquess replied immediately. “All systems green, standing by.”

“Engineering,” Eric Doohan reported next, “All systems green, standing by.”

“My hair’s not even dry and you want to — what?”

“I’ve just found a signal from Carlow Ships,” Cody told her with a grin. “I’m going to volunteer to check it out.”

Ellaz considered that. “Okay…” she turned back to her computers and started typing. A moment later, she turned to him with a raised eyebrow. “And…?”

“Control, this is Wasp,” Cody called over the radio. “We’ve been checking telemetry and we think we found some more survivors…”

#

Five minutes before they were due to depart, someone rapped hard on the outside airlock. Cody checked the vids. It was Bamber. There were three people behind him, including the grizzled spacer they’d rescued and one of the young girls. Cody didn’t recognize the woman standing next to Bamber.

Fuming, he gestured at Ellaz to check it out.

“They want to come with us,” Ellaz reported. “They’ve got suits.”

“And the kid?”

“She’s got a suit, too,” Ellaz replied, opening the hatch and letting them aboard.

“You’re going to need crew for the survey, Captain,” Clive Bamber said as he came into the main cabin and peered around into the cockpit. “I’ve got us four trained hands, including myself.”

Cody nodded and smiled. What else could he do? “Welcome aboard Wasp.”

“I’ve got a skinsuit and tanks,” the grizzled spacer reported.

“This is my wife, Moira Collins,” Clive said, introducing the woman behind him. “And you know the other two.”

“My daughter, Jasmine,” the willowy old spacer said. “She’s had a few EVAs and she listens.”

“Glad to have you aboard,” Ellaz said. “Secure the hatch and let’s get cleared for departure.” She scrambled back to the cockpit to join Cody, giving him a shrug. He answered with an accepting nod and went back to his preflight checklist.

They took off at a steady one gravity, they didn’t need more. Besides, it gave Cody — and Ellaz — a chance to check out their new crew. Clive Bamber was an administrator with years of experience in ground control and logistics.
