“So you want to trust the fate of mankind on one ship?” Ellaz snapped.

“Okay… so what if we use the monitor?” Cody said.

“That’s tuned to the two of you,” Edie replied, taking another sip of her restorative drink. She frowned. “I suppose we could rework it for me. Or Jazzy. But…”

“Ellaz and Jasmine,” Cody said. “How do they pair?”

Edie considered that. “We can test, I suppose.” She didn’t sound enthusiastic.

They took a break for lunch and when they came back they tried all four combinations — Ellaz and Jasmine, Ellaz and Edie, Cody and Jasmine, Cody and Edie.

“The results are in,” Edie said. “Top match — Cody and Ellaz. Next, Cody and Edie, Cody and Jasmine, Edie and Ellaz, Edie and Cody.” Cody was surprised by that, thinking that he and Edie had made a better team. She made a face as she added, “I’m afraid it’s a plasticity thing — brain plasticity. I’m a bit too set in my ways to work well with anyone.”

Jasmine patted her arm consolingly. “When I get older, and we train together…?”

Edie smiled at her. “Then maybe we could work together.” She smiled at her daughter. “But I have to admit, it was great playing with you.”

“You just can’t fly a starship that way,” Ellaz murmured in a voice meant only for Cody’s ears. Then, louder, she said, “Could we make a monitor to pull you out if you fell into the Playground?”

Edie considered it. “Maybe,” she said. “But would it be fast enough? Quick enough to stop us from blowing out of warp?” She shook her head.

“Could we get more implants?” Cody asked. He waved around the room. “Isn’t this one of the places where they install them?”

“Yes,” Edie said. “But usually it’s done at a major hospital. This is just for repairs and tuning.” A moment later, she added, “And, you need trained specialists to perform the implants.”

“And it takes months for them to settle,” Ellaz added. “I had nightmares for months.”

“I still get nightmares,” Jasmine admitted.

“You do?” Edie said. “Oh, baby, you should have said! No one should ever go into a simulator with nightmares!”

“That would explain the incompatibility,” Ellaz said. “How long ago —?”

No one knew how fast the aliens could travel in warp. As it was, they’d been gone for twelve days now, and it’d be twenty-one before Hope would arrive at Deneb. At the earliest.

And there was no way that Cody could pilot the ship by himself. He glanced up as someone dropped a tray beside him. Ellaz. She gave him a nod and slumped into her chair.

“Sorry,” Ellaz said grumpily. “I’m worried. I didn’t sleep well.”

Cody nodded.

Tom Walker strode in, looked for Brenda Hogg and marched over to her, standing above her with his tray in his hand while he rattled off a quick bunch of comments.

Cody frowned. Brenda seemed to sag under Walker’s tirade. She spotted Cody, grit her teeth and shook her head — begging him not to get involved.

He didn’t have to; Clive Bamber and Moira Collins came over and started talking with Walker. A moment later, Clive and Tom left the cafeteria and Moira sat next to Brenda, patting her soothingly on the shoulder.

#

They ran through the usual list of space disasters — micro-meteor punctures, failed systems, problems with sanitation and hydroponics — the lot.

Nora and the four engineers handled them with growing confidence even as the three nursery attendants managed the twelve babies with aplomb. “Perhaps you’d care to tell us why we’re both on this ship?” Clive Bamber said, pointing to his wife.

“Also why we’ve got so many rations?” Brenda Hogg — Captain Hogg — added.

“Redundancy,” Edie Crump replied. “Jazzy and I are ringing the ship.”

“Ringing?” Moira repeated. “You mean, you’re handling the ring?” She glanced to her husband. “Why?”

“Because this is a single ring warp,” Edie said. “And while we’ve got two ships… that’s all we’ve got.”

“And we have to warn people,” Brenda agreed.

“And get help,” Clive added, waving a hand toward the distant moon, Nettles.

“Warp Nine is hard,” Edie said. She made a face. “In sims we discovered that Jazzy and I… well, we’re not up to Warp Nine.”

“So what can you handle?” Moira Collins demanded. “And is there anyone who can help?”

“No one here has implants,” Edie explained. “Just running the ring in VR won’t cut it, particularly as these rings are new.”

“And we couldn’t just build or use old rings?” Moira asked.

“We don’t have the time,” Clive told her.

“To warn the others?”

“Here,” Clive told her. “We can consume our rations here or we can take them with us. But, at some point, they’re going to run out.”

“So we need to get help,” Moira guessed. “So… what else?”

“We’re going to Quark,” Edie said. “We’ll go at Warp Five. We’ve got charts for that. Eighty-two days, twelve hours.”

“And Hope?” Clive asked.

“People who work in debris fields,” Cody said. He put the two seats back, secured them and looked around. “I’ve got two balloons still in the air. I’m going to keep us in microgravity until we’re certain.”

“Pressure is stabilized,” Ellaz reported, glancing to the ECLSS panels. ECLSS — Environment Control and Life Support Systems, usually pronounced “ee-class.” Cody grunted, turned and kicked himself back to the cabin.

He buckled himself in, pulled up the navigation system and checked their fuel levels. “If we go there, we won’t be much good after.”

“Unless we get refueled,” Ellaz agreed.

Cody nodded and ran a sweep of the debris near them. “Nothing here to refuel with,” he said, his hopes of finding a spare tank or something similar dashed. If the aliens — or really dumb space pirates — had been in a rush, they’d also been thorough.

“Okay, they’re alive,” Ellaz said, bouncing in her chair with glee. “See? I can see when they shut down their systems —”

“When?”

“It looks like — it looks like just about long enough for light speed from Xerxes,” Ellaz said.

Xerxes was one of the largest asteroids in the solar system’s asteroid belt. It was — or had been — inhabited and was a major mining and research center for the whole system.

“So either someone was looking or talking with them,” Cody guessed. He frowned. “Both observatories?”

“Everything went dark within five minutes,” Ellaz replied. “It was like someone threw a switch, it was so fast.”

“That doesn’t mean anyone’s alive,” Cody said with a grimace. “It could be that these aliens have fitl and they destroyed the bases first.”

“Fitl?”

“Faster-Than-Light,” Cody translated.

“‘Fitl?’” Ellaz repeated, crinkling her nose in disgust. “You call it ‘fitl?’”

“It’s easier than saying FTL or Faster-Than-Light,” Cody replied. “And everyone says it.”

“Well, how come I haven’t heard it before?” Ellaz challenged.

“I dunno, maybe you don’t have any friends,” Cody shot back with an evil grin. Ellaz’s face fell and she looked like she was frozen. “Hey! It was a joke!”

“I don’t have any friends,” Ellaz said in a small voice.

“Well, you’ve got me,” Cody offered.

“Me, too,” Cody said.

“Well, not to be mean, but you can’t be,” Ellaz said. “Your name is Cody, so you’re only the third in line, right?”

It was traditional to name clones alphabetically. The first would have an ‘A’ name, the second a ‘B’ name and so on. Only the Fords didn’t do it that way. It was a closely guarded secret that the first Ford was Zacharias.

“You said your mother was Elle,” Cody remarked.

“Well… yes,” Ellaz allowed. “We decided to stick with the same first letter until we —” she broke off abruptly and shook her head “— sorry, that’s classified.”

“I won’t tell anyone,” Cody said, waving to the debris surrounding them, pointing out that there was no one to tell. Then he had a thought. “So, is E for Engineering or Electronics?”

Ellaz hissed in surprise before admitting, “Energy.”

“Right, like your power converter,” Cody guessed.

Ellaz gave him a reluctant nod. Her panel beeped and she sat up excitedly. “Can you make the emergency signal?”

“Do you mean the Mayday squawk?” Cody asked her, moving to bring up another control panel on his displays.

“Squawk?”

“That’s what we call it,” Cody said, programming the emergency code and hitting the switch that broadcast it. “It’ll take about forty-five seconds at light speed.”

“Ninety round-trip,” Ellaz observed. Cody nodded and got busy, turning the shuttle toward the least time course for the farthest moon and checking his fuel levels.

Ninety seconds later there was a beep. Someone had replied.

“This is cargo shuttle Wasp from the freighter Hornet,” Cody said quickly in a calm, professional voice. “Two souls aboard. Air for two hours. Request vectors for approach.”

Ninety seconds later, on the same frequency, a voice replied, “Say intentions.”

“We need to refuel, resupply — we had an air leak — and then we’re going to search for any survivors,” Cody replied.

“Wasp, you are cleared to approach the Deep Space One, orbits and speed in data,” came the reply.

Ellaz followed him, took her seat and pulled up some displays. She frowned as she played with them.

“They’ve got enough life support for five hundred, they’ve only got… five hundred and twenty-three people, counting the survivors.”

Cody nodded. He had expected as much. “They’re not running a closed loop,” Cody added. “They get about twenty percent of their food — got twenty percent of their food shipped in.”

“Neither the second dish nor the data center have any excess,” Ellaz added. Then, “And they’ve got a fixed amount of fuel for ships and air.”

“Yup,” Cody said.

“What are we going to do?”

“Well, we can’t stay here,” Cody said.

“Which is why you wanted to sleep here,” Ellaz guessed. Cody nodded. “A shuttle is not a spaceship.” Cody shot her a look and she corrected herself, “I mean it’s not a starship. You use it to get from one place to another, not to live on.”

He waved a hand at her to continue.

“All the starships are wrecked,” Ellaz said. “And… well, how much —” she broke off and keyed in some commands. “They got the habitats, not the farms.”

“They got the orbiting farms,” Cody corrected.

“The food, yes, the fuel, no.”

Cody raised an eyebrow and nodded for her to continue. Then he raised a hand to stop her. “How many farms, how much fuel, and how much do they need it here?”

“Meath had anti-matter farms to fuel at least twenty starships every month,” Ellaz said. “Here, they use less than a hundredth of that.”

“We need to know more about these aliens,” Cody said, sitting up in his seat and typing furiously. “And then…”

“What?”

“We need to warn people,” Cody said.

“They already know,” Ellaz said.

“Not here,” Cody snapped. “The other worlds.”

“Deneb is twenty light years away,” Ellaz said. “I’m sure we can send them a message but… it’ll be a bit late, won’t it?”

“We need a starship,” Cody said.

“And where do you expect to find one?” Ellaz snarled at him. “They’re all gone.”

“Hmm, but when’s the next one coming?” Cody asked.

“We’ve got better on the ship,” Nora said as she sat beside him. “That was part of the plan.”

“We’re on schedule,” Cody agreed. “Fourteen hours.” He eyed Ellaz but she kept her head down over her tray, mixing the food around and occasionally taking a bite. Jacob was beside her, chattering gaily about their latest sims and how they’d beat Revenge on the readiness tests. Cody checked his tablet — Hope’s crew were only 0.05% better than Revenge’s, so it wasn’t a big issue.

“Cody —” Cody looked up to see Brenda Hogg looking down at him, her expression worried. “Can I speak to you? In private?”

Cody got out of his seat and followed her out into the corridor.

“What’s up?” Cody said.

“We can’t find Tom,” Brenda told him. “I’ve been looking for the past three hours but… no one’s seen him.”

Cody’s tablet flashed. So did Brenda’s. They pulled them up to examine them and swore almost at the same time.

“Unauthorized departure,” Cody’s tablet flashed.

“He’s taken a shuttle!” Clive Bamber said, skidding to a halt as he spotted them. “He’s going back to Nettles. He has all our plans.”

“He’s a traitor,” Brenda said sourly. “They can get back here in hours!”

“They could stop us,” Moira Collins said, racing to a halt just beside her husband. “And we’ve got another twenty-four hours — at least — before we can launch Revenge.”

“Gail!” Cody shouted, smiling at the others. Little Gail raced out to join them, still chewing a mouthful of food. “Operation Loop.”

“On the shuttle?” Gail asked, pulling up her wristcomm and tapping in a set of commands. She hit the EXECUTE button and then smiled at Cody, raising a thumbs up. “Done.” She glanced around, “Um, can I go back to dinner?”

Cody waved her off.

“‘Loop?’” Brenda said.

“Nothing fatal,” Ellaz said, joining the throng. “Just a twenty hour comm delay.”

“Pardon?” Moira Collins said.

“Initiating standard emergency comms,” Ellaz added a moment later, raising her arm slowly against the doubled gravity. Then she said, “What about the compensators?”

“Compensators?” Cody said to her.

“Didn’t you use the gravity compensators?” Ellaz demanded.

“Well, we’re on a shuttle,” Cody reminded her smugly. Then he relented and said, “Yes, I did. We’ve got a ten to one compensation ratio.”

“That’s… not great is it?”

“For a shuttle?” Cody said. “It’s amazing. For a starship… it’s pathetic.”

“I wish we had a starship,” Ellaz said, looking at her screens sadly. As if in answer, a light flashed and they heard a solid ping! “Got a life suit, bearing…”

And then they were working nonstop.

They pulled in twenty spacesuited figures. Ten of them were alive. One had just died in the last five minutes. Most of them were young, younger than Ellaz.

“Smaller lungs,” Cody muttered as they pulled a four year-old out of her suit and watched in relief as she gasped in fresh air. Her suit was just out of oxygen. Another two minutes and she’d be dead.

“There were thirty targets,” Ellaz said, snapping the seatbelt around an unconscious six year-old.

“When we left,” Cody agreed. He made a face. “You good here?” He turned to the cockpit. “I want to get us started —”

“Nothing above three gees, max,” Ellaz warned.

Cody shook his head. “We’ll see. No more than two, if I can help it.” He waved a hand around. “Hook them up, will you? We’ll need to monitor life support from the front.” In the cockpit. He left before Ellaz could nod.

Chapter Nine

Chapter Nine

“Nine… eight… seven… six… five… four… three… two… cut warp!” Nora called. In front of them space shimmered back into reality.

“I have the hab,” Cody called. “Rotating.” He turned Hope around so that it was facing backwards.

“I can spot the ship,” Ellaz reported. “We’ve got a good look. Prepare the mirror, Cody.”

“Roger,” Cody replied. “We’re going to bring up the forward bubble and put all power into it.”

“Then you’ll execute pattern Alpha,” Ellaz agreed. “In three… two… one!”

Hope engaged the forward part of her ring, projecting a circular disk two thousand kilometers in front of her.

“Got it!” Ellaz cried. “We’ve deflected their lance but… Cody!”

“I see it!” Cody replied, twisting the ship in space so that its shielding warp mirror twisted the alien’s warp lance around — and back on the alien ship itself.

“Impact!” Nora called. “Impact and — Jeez!”

The alien spaceship blew up. The virtual view screen went black as it dimmed to protect their eyes and only slowly brightened.

“We’ve got debris everywhere!” Nora called.

Cody! Ellaz thought to him. The spare shuttles!

On it! Cody replied, firing off all the empty shuttles and sending them out to intercept any debris coming toward the spacehab.

“I’ve got eyes on the alien ships!” Nora warned. “They’re… wait a minute! Wait.” Then she whooped with joy. “They’re leaving!”

“How many?” Cody said aloud.

“All of them!” Nora crowed with glee.

Cody! Ellaz warned him.

Cody looked where she was pointing in virtual space. Oh, shit!

“Eject, eject, eject!” Cody shouted, pushing the buttons that fired the remaining shuttles away from Hope. Those weren’t the right words, he realized. “Abandon ship!”

Wasp flew away from Hope just as a large chunk of debris bounced off her warp ring, shattering it.

Cody! Ellaz’s voice came to him. And then, it was gone. Just like Hope.

#

“Everyone got off, Cody, they’re safe,” Nora told him when he’d recovered. He looked at her and shook his head. “Who?”

“Ellaz,” he told her.

“Sorry,” she said. “What do we do now?”

“Unknown ship, unknown ship, this is spacehab Elantra on 121.5, state your intentions,” a voice came over the speaker.

“We’re on schedule,” Clive Bamber called out, entering the hallway and smiling at them. “That’ll be two days for the first and three for the second,” he said as he stopped in front of them with his wife, Moira coming up alongside. “We had to downcheck one unit which cost us a days’ time but the other three checked out fine.”

“Three?” Cody asked.

“It’s always good to have a spare,” Moira Collins assured him. She waved a hand to the Simulations Lab. “How’s it going?”

“Great!” Edie said. She patted Cody and Ellaz on the shoulders. “These two are a natural team!”

“Excellent!” Mr. Bamber said. “And my teams are working out great. We’ve got Engineering, including ECLSS all manned and training. As soon as we get the ships together, we’ll be able to start training.”

“How about training in Sims?” Edie suggested. “I know that there are programs available.”

“For freighters,” Moira corrected, “not for these lightships.”

“Half meggers,” Clive said, glancing at his wife. Cody got the impression they were trying to win converts for their favorite names for the ships.

“You mean Hope and Revenge?” Ellaz said. The two adults nodded.

“Lightmegs?” Cody suggested. Everyone shook their heads.

“Megships?” Ellaz added. More heads shook.

“Halfships?” Edie added. She winced as the looks of the other shot that down.

“Quarters?” Cody tried again.

“Quarships?” Jasmine said.

“This isn’t important,” Ellaz said. “We’ve got other things to do.”

“Yes,” Clive agreed, smiling at his wife. “But it is distracting.”

“You’ve got diaper duty in ten, you know,” Moira reminded him.

“How’s Nora doing?” Edie asked. She glanced down to Jasmine. “We’re ‘on’ down there in another thirty minutes.”

“Nora is doing fine,” Clive Bamber said. He glanced to Cody. “I think she should be the XO on one of the ships, truth be told.”

“And Walker on the other,” Moira added. She saw the expressions on Ellaz’s and Cody’s faces and added, “With Brenda on the Revenge, I mean.”

“We’ll take Nora,” Cody said immediately.

“You dropped down to eighteen shuttles,” Clive said. “Is there a reason?”

“We don’t need more,” Cody said. “We could take everyone with those.”

Clive and Moira exchanged looks. “Should we drop down on Revenge, too?”

“And hurry, we can’t stay here long,” the voice said. “Jazzy is having so much fun playing and I… Cody? Are you really here?”

There was something in the voice — Ellaz’s voice — something lost, hurt, worried.

“Yes, I’m here,” Cody said, because Ellaz needed him to say that. Needed him to pull her — them — all three of them back to — “I’ve got you, don’t worry.”

“Oh, thank you!” Ellaz’s voice came back. “Did you hear that, Jazzy? Cody’s got us!”

“Cody?” Jasmine’s voice came back, confused, uncertain. “I can’t — I see —”

“C’mon Jazzy, we’ve got you,” a new voice — Edie’s called out — “We’ve got what we need, sweetie. You were brilliant.”

#

Cody gasped as his vision went black. It took him a moment to recover then he snapped at his interface controls. He was back in the Wasp. Profile: Nominal.

“Edie?”

“They’re back,” Edie said. “And the extruders are running. According to this, we’ve got twenty hollow arcs with a flexible power cable to run through them and electronic couplings. We can slide them up or down — and the shape on the ring itself is —”

“Pretty cool,” Cody agreed. “It’ll throw a field forward and back. About one thousand kilometers forward, five hundred kilometers back.”

“So it sits near the stern,” Edie said. “And… Cody what’s this other thing? There’s a new file.”

“Oh! That!” Cody said. “Well, that’s the ship.”

#

“I’m going to leave Baker up in orbit with her cargo,” Cody declared as he approached the moon hours later. “I’ll send Able down first and then bring Wasp in.”

“Sounds good,” Clive Bamber said. “I’ll send you the coordinates.”

“Good, and the assembly?” Cody said. He’d looked over the plans that he and the two girls had made — apparently in an instant — when mind-linked. They worked. And the construction time — ten days. He still wasn’t sure how it all fit together but already he’d gotten Bamber to agree to let them fire up the bots and begin the initial assembly.

The bots had pulled one of the spare ECLSS — Environmental Control and Life Support System — out of storage and were prepping it.

Passage:
“We found food, and… well, you might want to come see what we’ve got,” Bamber said. Cody frowned, remembering Ellaz’s worries.

“I’m in the middle of something,” Cody said. “Can you just tell me? Or send an image?”

Bamber sighed. “We found the shuttle bay,” he said. “Rather we found the shuttle warehouse. There are about —”

Cody perked up, tapped a command into the computer systems. There were ten ships on the building slips which meant, with a crew of roughly one hundred, there had to be four shuttles for each ship. Maybe they weren’t all here but…

“Forty shuttles?” Cody guessed.

“Only about twenty in this warehouse, at a guess,” Bamber replied. “And they’re in mothballs.”

“Mothballs?” Ellaz piped up.

“I mean they’re not prepped, they’re wrapped up for storage,” Bamber replied.

“Then why didn’t you say so?” Ellaz murmured acerbically.

“Spacers know mothballs,” Cody said.

“Not this spacer,” Ellaz corrected him.

“So…” Cody typed in a series of queries, tied it in with Bamber’s location and said, “If you go from there across the field, you’ll find Warehouse Two. There should be another twenty shuttles there.” Of course they’d need fuel, charging, oxygen and… well, it was something.

“I’ll check it out, right after I pull up the systems in this other warehouse,” Bamber replied. “And Captain?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t fall asleep!”

Cody shook his head and looked back at the screens in front of him.

Plans. Tried-and-true. Because building a starship wasn’t just science, it was art, too.

They needed a power plant, no matter what. Preferably a “tried-and-true” plant and, more importantly, they needed one that was here, at the shipyards, ready to be installed. Only… there were only so many power plants lying around.

The power plant sized the ship. A big ship, a big power plant.

And all that depended on the size of the ship. There was no way they’d be able to build a two megatonne starship in less than four months. And they didn’t have four months. So, what was the biggest ship they could build in three weeks?
The computers didn’t have an answer to that. What was the fastest ship they could build?

Back in the flight deck, Ellaz shot him a look. He waved it away, pulling up the trajectory list and frowning. He shot her a copy silently and she started looking, hissing as she read the numbers.

“Largest first,” Cody said as he heard a group of people stomp aboard, pushing a supply trolley. He turned to wave at them and grinned, “Hey guys! Glad to have your help! Just top us off with anything you think we need but please hurry!”

“Yes, sir, we’ll be quick!” One of them answered. A couple of minutes later, they clambered off and Cody heard them securing the airlock.

“Detaching,” Bamber called. “You’re good to go, we’re raising you now.”

“Roger, ready to go,” Cody called back.

“And Captain… best of luck, sir.”

“Captain?” Ellaz murmured softly as the shuttle was bathed once more in the light of the distant sun and they were raised back up to the surface.

Cody grinned. “They… um… might think that they’re dealing with Daniel Ford, my father.”

“I thought he was dead.”

“Well, there was some confusion,” Cody said. “He might have been just undergoing regen.”

“‘Regen?’” Ellaz repeated, an eyebrow raised in disbelief.

“Well, they had no trouble dealing with Captain Ford,” Cody said. “I’m not so —”

“Wasp, you are cleared for departure,” the controller told them.

“Roger, initiating automated departure sequence one, shaping course for —” He shot a look toward the girl.

“Target Three,” Ellaz murmured to him.

“Target Three,” Cody finished.

“Godspeed,” Clive Bammber told them.

Cody turned to Ellaz. “How many gees are you good for?”

“Gees?” Ellaz said. She shrugged. “Three?”

“Life or death,” Cody reminded her.

“Maybe five,” Ellaz said. “But not for long.”

“Wuss,” Cody said, firing up the main engines and putting them to full power. Seven gees for twenty minutes. He eased back only when his relays from Ellaz’s co-pilot seat showed her approaching extreme distress. He pulled them back to two gees and turned to her. “You okay?”

She glared at him. He could see blood in the whites of her eyes where capillaries had broken under the strain.

I can’t guess, Ellaz replied. Are they more advanced than us? Do they think like us? How long have they had their tech? Can they build new things or are these ships the last of them? She shrugged. We just don’t know.

If they had it, wouldn’t they have spotted Hope when we defended Elantra? Other Cody asked.

Cody shrugged. Maybe. Or maybe they couldn’t react in time.

Or didn’t think that we’d be a threat, Nora added. Which may mean that the warp mirror was something they didn’t have.

Could they have it now? Cody wondered. And can we counter it?

They could, Ellaz agreed. And the best way to counter it is not to be seen.

Or make them look somewhere else, Cody thought.

How?

Make a big, splashy boom somewhere else, Other Cody thought. He smiled at Cody. I like it. Only… how?

#

“Forty-three hours, twelve minutes,” Georgie Cummings reported to Cody two days later. “It’ll be good to get out of this funky air.”

Cody nodded in agreement. The ECLSS had fouled the new filter and now they were on the last good filter but, because of the way that bacteria was clogging up so fast, Juan Suarez had suggested that they slow down the Environmental Control and Life Support System by eighty per cent.

“The system was designed for a crew of a hundred, and we’re just six,” Juan said, touting the latest excuse for why the system was misbehaving. They knew that one of the normal algaes used in recycling had overgrown, fouling the filters but they couldn’t say precisely why. Not even Ellaz and the other virtual people had a good idea. Worse, as Juan said, “This is why proper ships have at least two ECLSS. If one goes bonkers, we can purge it and restart it from the other.”

Fortunately for them all, if the ECLSS did totally pack it in, they could live in their shuttles on the canned air… for twenty-one days.

Which is why everyone was looking forward to planetfall at Quark. At the very least they could get a bunch of filters and work from there. Not ideal but… they’d live.

Chapter: OEBPS/Cody's_War_-_Flight_of_the_Wasp_12pt_5x8-10.xhtml

Passage:
“Pirates!” Other Cody snorted, shaking his head at Ellaz. Cody was used to Other Cody — as he called the simulation — and somewhat hopeful that if anything happened to him, his alter-ego would be able to help Nora raise their kids. Of course, that wouldn’t be this Cody because if anything happened to Wasp it would undoubtedly destroy their computers, too.

“They couldn’t be very good, given that they’ve stolen nothing from us,” Georgie said. Ellaz and Other Cody exchanged looks. Georgie noticed. “What?”

“Nothing,” Cody said, “just an inside joke.”

“Okay,” Georgie said. “So, we’re ruling out pirates?” The others nodded in agreement. “Refugees? That’s still a possibility?” Cody nodded. “So what are they looking for? A new homeworld?”

“Why would they attack ours if that was the case?” Gail’s ghost asked. “If they’re running, why would they slow down to hit us?”

“They’re aliens, they don’t have to make sense,” Ellaz said.

“No,” Cody said. “I think they do.”

Georgie, who’d turned her attention back to her 3D chess game with Ellaz, tipped her king over and said, “Show me.”

Ellaz grinned at her, righted the king and showed the next three moves that ended with the king in checkmate.

Georgie sat back, stared at the board, stared at Ellaz’s ghost and nodded. “Good, good,” she said to herself. “Want another?”

“Sure,” Ellaz said and the board was reset with the pieces all back in their starting places.

“Where’d they come from?” Cody said. “They seem to be — were they on a straight line course when they attacked Meath?”

“We don’t know,” Ellaz said. She pursed her lips and shot a look to Georgie. “Something might have distracted them. Maybe they —”

“They’re denying us to their enemy!” Gail said with sudden certainty. “They don’t care about us, they just don’t want the others to get us.”

“Others?” Georgie said, moving her piece. “Now there are two alien species? In three hundred years of space travel, we haven’t found any.”

“What if one of the aliens was destroying the others?” Gail asked. “I mean, look at Meath — a hundred years from now, will anyone know that it was inhabited?”

“I can’t say,” Cody admitted. “And what are you doing with that camera?”

“Looking,” Jasmine said with a shrug. “So this Ellaz, what’s with her?”

“She’s my sister,” Cody said, remembering their cover story. “She’s okay with shuttles but —” he shrugged “— I think she wants to do more.”

“Well, I mean flying a shuttle, how hard is that?” Jasmine asked. Cody felt his face go red. Jasmine noticed and added quickly, “I mean I’m sure that it’s terribly important and all but… don’t they have autopilots?”

Cody shook his head. Then, “Don’t they have robots to turn warps?”

“No, they don’t,” Jasmine answered immediately. “A robot might be able to produce a first order approximation but… you wouldn’t want to fly a ship that way.”

“Contact!” Bamber called out. “Multiple contacts! Jeez, they’re —” suddenly he cut off.

“Mr. Bamber?” Cody called back. He shot a look to Jasmine who shrugged and turned back to her camera display.

“I’m going in,” Ellaz called. A moment later, she called back, “Cody, Jasmine, you need to get here. And Miz Collins.”

“Why?”

“It’s a nursery,” Bamber called back. “One teenaged minder and twenty babies from months to years.”

“Let’s go,” Cody said, unbuckling himself.

“I’m staying here,” Jasmine said. “There’s…” she turned to her displays and waved him off.

“Miz Collins?” Cody called.

“Twenty-one more mouths to feed,” Moira Collins said, shaking her head. “What are we going to do?”

Cody didn’t have an answer.

#

“Why didn’t they get us?” Nora Wright asked when they’d settled all the babies in the main cabin. “They got everything else, why not us?”

“I’ll bet they used a mass reading,” Ellaz said. “Or a thermal level.” Cody shot her a look. He was trying to come up with a makeshift diaper for a very soiled little girl but… it was his first time. Fortunately, Moira Collins was able to guide him.

“You’re saying that anything too small they didn’t notice?” Clive asked. Ellaz nodded. “That explains all the kids you found.”

“Kids aren’t a threat,” Jasmine added. “At least, I’ll bet that’s what they thought.”

Ellaz followed him, took her seat and pulled up some displays. She frowned as she played with them.

“They’ve got enough life support for five hundred, they’ve only got… five hundred and twenty-three people, counting the survivors.”

Cody nodded. He had expected as much. “They’re not running a closed loop,” Cody added. “They get about twenty percent of their food — got twenty percent of their food shipped in.”

“Neither the second dish nor the data center have any excess,” Ellaz added. Then, “And they’ve got a fixed amount of fuel for ships and air.”

“Yup,” Cody said.

“What are we going to do?”

“Well, we can’t stay here,” Cody said.

“Which is why you wanted to sleep here,” Ellaz guessed. Cody nodded. “A shuttle is not a spaceship.” Cody shot her a look and she corrected herself, “I mean it’s not a starship. You use it to get from one place to another, not to live on.”

He waved a hand at her to continue.

“All the starships are wrecked,” Ellaz said. “And… well, how much —” she broke off and keyed in some commands. “They got the habitats, not the farms.”

“They got the orbiting farms,” Cody corrected.

“The food, yes, the fuel, no.”

Cody raised an eyebrow and nodded for her to continue. Then he raised a hand to stop her. “How many farms, how much fuel, and how much do they need it here?”

“Meath had anti-matter farms to fuel at least twenty starships every month,” Ellaz said. “Here, they use less than a hundredth of that.”

“We need to know more about these aliens,” Cody said, sitting up in his seat and typing furiously. “And then…”

“What?”

“We need to warn people,” Cody said.

“They already know,” Ellaz said.

“Not here,” Cody snapped. “The other worlds.”

“Deneb is twenty light years away,” Ellaz said. “I’m sure we can send them a message but… it’ll be a bit late, won’t it?”

“We need a starship,” Cody said.

“And where do you expect to find one?” Ellaz snarled at him. “They’re all gone.”

“Hmm, but when’s the next one coming?” Cody asked.

“Boom!” Edie cried. “You didn’t dodge fast enough! And your warp core shredded.”

Shredded? Cody thought.

“You died,” Jasmine explained.

So what do we do? Ellaz thought.

“Whenever you find yourself in a warp stream like that, the smart course is to offset your course and stick to it. It means you’ll have to recompute your astrogation, of course.”

I thought the routes were safe, Cody replied.

“They’re safe at Warp Five,” Edie explained. “Everything comes faster — and thicker — at Warp Nine.”

Why aren’t there routes for Warp Nine? Ellaz wondered.

“If there are, only the military has them,” Edie said. “Regular freighters don’t need them and mapping such routes… it’s expensive.”

In time or in ships? Cody wondered.

“Both,” Edie told them. “Okay. Again. Warp Nine.”

They did two more runs before Edie pulled them out. She and Jasmine passed them drinks.

“You are getting it,” Edie assured them.

Cody and Ellaz exchanged looks. “Excuse me,” Ellaz said, “but as near as I can tell, all we’re getting is dead.” Cody nodded in agreement.

“But you’re getting really good at that!” Jasmine teased.

#

Outside, Jacob and Gail waited with lists of disasters. Although, Cody noted, some of the disasters were crossed off his list. He glanced to Ellaz’s list and smiled.

“What?” Ellaz demanded, still grumpy from their exertions.

“Our aides are doing their work,” Cody said, pointing to the eliminated items.

“We talked it over,” Jacob admitted, “and asked ourselves what you would do.”

“Good work,” Ellaz told him with a grin. She gestured for his touchpad and peered down at it. “Now… we’ve got the supplies, the diapers, the formula. What about water?”

“Handled,” Cody said, pointing to his list. “What about soil?”

“We won’t be needing that until the ECLSS units are complete,” Gail said. “And that’s not for another three days. And then they have to power them up —”

“And where are we on power?” Cody asked, looking at his list.

“Not for a month,” Ellaz said. Cody shot her a look. “Well, smartass, as you could hack into the network, I could download the manifests of all the space stations. The next ship is the Twilight Star, scheduled to arrive from Earth in twenty-nine days.”

“Shit.”

“Well, if you’re going to imagine the worst —”

“Ninety-two,” Ellaz corrected. “I doubt we’ll survive here long.”

“How long did it take the aliens to destroy everything?” Cody said. “Less than a day, certainly. So… if they’ve got fitl that we don’t understand, they could destroy us all in another ninety-two days.”

“That’s assuming they don’t have more ships and haven’t already attacked elsewhere,” Ellaz reminded him.

“Okay,” Cody said. “So we need to get out of here.”

“We need to build a starship,” Ellaz said.

“Yup,” Cody agreed. He frowned. “What if we could take the tanks from one of the farms? That’d give us fuel.”

“We still need a ship,” Ellaz said.

“We have a ship,” Cody said, waving a hand around them.

“A starship,” Ellaz reminded him. “I mean, can you make a shuttle into a starship?”

Cody frowned. Then he turned to her, “Whirly, can you?”

Ellaz was silent, tapping on her keyboard. She glanced over to him. “The fastest a starship has ever been built was twenty-two days. And that was at the Lunar yards in orbit around Old Earth. Cody considered that. Then he said, “We need to get out of here.”

“Yes,” Ellaz agreed.

“We need to go to Carlow, to the bases,” Cody said.

“But they’re gone, we saw that!”

“You said the aliens attacked the habitats,” Cody replied.

“I said the attackers destroyed the habitats,” Ellaz corrected. “You said they were aliens.”

Cody ignored her, typing frantically on his keyboard. A moment later he sat back and smiled at her. “You ready for a trip?”

“‘Regen?’” Ellaz repeated, an eyebrow raised in disbelief.

“Roger, initiating automated departure sequence one, shaping course for —” He shot a look toward the girl.

“Target Three,” Ellaz murmured to him.

“Godspeed,” Clive Bammber told them.

“Gees?” Ellaz said. She shrugged. “Three?”

She glared at him. He could see blood in the whites of her eyes where capillaries had broken under the strain.

“Jeez!” Hanlan swore, shaking his head. “There are seven billion people here.” He glanced to Cody. “What do you propose?”

“We have a plan,” Cody said. He made a face. “We’re two ships short but —”

“I stay here,” Hartman said. He glanced to the system President. “Hermes is going to stay on guard.”

“One ship —”

“One ship drove the attackers off at Deneb,” Cody interjected. “And, if we’re lucky, there will be no attack here.”

“How?”

“Because we’re going to get them before they get here,” Cody said.

Ed Hanlan considered that and then nodded to the large conference table. “Tell me everything.”

#

Ed Hanlan blew out a long sigh when they were done, sat back in his chair and looked up to the ceiling in thought. Finally, he leaned back down, pressed his comm and said, “Okay, here’s what we’ll do —”

He didn’t get any further as someone began pounding on one of the double doors to the room.

“If you don’t let me in right now —!” Nora’s voice boomed through the door. She kicked it for emphasis.

“She’s with us,” Cody said, rising and rushing to the door. He opened it, saw two angry guards trying to restrain Nora, glared at them and said, “She’s with us.” Then he pulled Nora inside.

“You haven’t done anything stupid, have you?” Nora said, glaring at him. Then she broke down and wrapped her arms around him tightly.

“No, nothing more than usual,” Cody told him, turning the two of them around so that he could face President Hanlan. “This Commodore Wright, my second in command —”

“And mother of your children!” Nora added gruffly, pulling away from him.

Ed Hanlan jerked in surprise. “Little lady, aren’t you a mite young to be —”

“Ew!” Nora said. “Not bio-birth! We’re talking artificial wombs.”

Hanlan raised his hands defensively.

“Three,” Nora went on, releasing herself from Cody but still holding onto a hand as she led them to the table. “One of him, two crosses. And the three others, of course.”

“Oh, of course!” Hanlan said, barking a laugh. “Because half a dozen new babies is no problem for —”

“Actually, they’ll have lots of helpers,” Don Hartman broke in. Hanlan shot him a look. “Grateful helpers.”

With that error? We might just go scooting by, Cody said. Then, What if we let them hit us?
What?

We know they want to hit the hab, what if we put us between them and it?

Calculating, Ellaz said. Cody frowned. That sounded more like a computer than the girl he’d known. For just under three weeks. Maybe she said that and he’d never heard her before. Or maybe… Cody gave himself a mental shake.

It could work, Ellaz said minutes later, it could also mean that parts of this ship would crash into the hab and destroy it anyway.

How likely?

Sixty-five percent, Ellaz replied.

“What are you two doing?” Nora Wright’ voice came to Cody’s ears.

“You’re supposed to be resting,” Cody snapped to her.

“Well, I’m not,” Nora said. “I managed to get him to sleep but she was just all ants.”

Ants? Ellaz thought. Then, “Ants?”

“Like ants in your pants, antsy,” Nora explained. “So what are you doing?”

“Playing 3D chess,” Cody said.

“And what else?” Nora demanded. She slipped into the co-pilot’s chair and tapped his shoulder. “I’m going VR.” She pulled on her headset and a ghostly version of her joined them in the simulation. She glanced at the clock which now read fifty-nine minutes. Then she pulled up a virtual console and ran through the ship’s logs. Cody hadn’t thought of that, she’d doubtless see — “Two kilometers?” Nora groaned. “And you’re thinking — what? Interpose Hope between them and the hab?”

“We could abandon,” Cody said. “Anyway, five hundred million souls.”

“Against twenty-four,” Nora finished. “But then what?” Cody shot her a look. “So we die gloriously? What then? If the aliens scarper, what then? Just Elantra, right? No docks, no shipyards, nothing.” She blew out a sigh. “Ellaz, I want a better solution.”

“Yeah,” Ellaz said. “And if you’ll give me a chance to think, maybe I’ll come up with one.”

That sounded more like Ellaz, Cody thought to himself.

“What about the mirror?” Cody asked. “I mean, if we used that, and mirrored —”

“Reflected!” Ellaz objected. “How many times do I have to tell you?”

Cody smiled to himself. “Reflector, then.”

“And you’re alive,” Cody said. Again, the rolled eyes. “The alien shot you. It shot Martin and he turned to dust.”

Ellaz patted her shirt. “Energy converter.”

“What?”

“I’m wearing a portable energy converter,” Ellaz said. “It’s experimental, of course.” Of course. Because the Whirly family was famous for their experiments. Then she pointed to the displays, “There. That’s major structural failure. We need to go. Can’t be certain how long the core will hold.”

Cody agreed. He thumbed the freighter’s emergency airlock controls and the cargo hold door blew out. Then he tapped the cold jets once, enough to start the shuttle out of the disintegrating cargo bay. Once outside, he tapped a series of quick thrusts that set the shuttle tumbling like it was out of control. And then, to make that real, he shut down their active systems.

“Holy shit!” Ellaz cried, pointing behind them. “They got everything!”

Cody followed her finger with his head and his jaw dropped.

The freighter Hornet was docked at Parminter Station Number One, the largest of four orbiting cargo stations for the planet Meath. Meath was a planet of over a billion people, with orbital satellites providing homes for another half billion. Was.

Parminter Station One and the dozen freighters that had been docked were only shards of metal and smaller objects floating haphazardly in the light of the planet’s star.

“They got the orbitals, too,” Cody said, pointing to a smaller object in the distance. The orbitals were — had been — giant circular space stations — habitats for the half billion people who preferred to live in their own artificial atmosphere. He made a face. “I can’t tell about the planet —”

“Infrared,” Ellaz said.

“We can’t use power,” Cody said.

“Passives,” Ellaz replied, tapping a command into the shuttle’s computer only to have her hand smacked away by Cody.

“No power!” Cody hissed at her.

Ellaz put her fingers in her mouth and glared at him. “You don’t know —”

“I don’t!” Cody agreed. “And until we do, we’re going to be a piece of debris.”

“If they can track IR, they can see our heat,” Ellaz said.

“Which is why we’re staying close to the freighter,” Cody said. “We’ll be in the thermal shadow.”

“And the other twenty-five?” Eric Doohan asked. “What about them?”

“Probably not,” Eric said. The others looked at him and he shrugged. “Well, if we had one, wouldn’t we have used it to defend ourselves?” Around him the others nodded. He glanced to Cody. “I’m assuming that you have an idea how to find this alien ship?”

Cody nodded. “Not only that but we have figured out how to detect ships in warp. That’s why we know that they have twenty-six.”

Nora raised a hand. “Well, we don’t know, precisely,” she said. “We have three sigma confidence in that number.”

“So… twenty-six plus or minus zero,” Thomas said with a chuckle.

“And if this grav lance fails?” Eric asked.

“That’s why we’re here,” Cody said. “Because if it fails, there are twenty-four of us and over five hundred million on the spacehab Elantra, which we think will be the last target.”

“Okay,” Scott Ellis said, “And?”

“You want to ram them, right?” Eric Doohan guessed. He shook his head.

“We’ve got the shuttles,” Gail pointed out. “We can abandon ship and pilot her remotely.”

Or let Ellaz pilot it, Cody thought grimly to himself. He didn’t have his helmet on so no one could hear him.

“And then we’ll be in shuttles, in the middle of a war,” Scott said. He frowned. Then nodded. “I’m okay with that.”

“I’d like for us to vote,” Cody said.

“All in favor?” Nora called out, raising her voice and then pouting apologetically at the baby in her arms.

Eleven arms rose at once. Cody had kept his down, certain that his own vote was already known. The babies didn’t get a vote. Of course, they would be put on a shuttle.

“All right,” Cody said. “So, I’ll be taking Gail, Jacob, and Nora with me on Wasp.”

“No you won’t!” Nora said. “You’ll be taking Gail. I’m not leaving my Phoenix.”

“I can’t say,” Cody admitted. “And what are you doing with that camera?”

“She’s my sister,” Cody said, remembering their cover story. “She’s okay with shuttles but —” he shrugged “— I think she wants to do more.”

“Well, I mean flying a shuttle, how hard is that?” Jasmine asked. Cody felt his face go red. Jasmine noticed and added quickly, “I mean I’m sure that it’s terribly important and all but… don’t they have autopilots?”

Cody shook his head. Then, “Don’t they have robots to turn warps?”

“No, they don’t,” Jasmine answered immediately. “A robot might be able to produce a first order approximation but… you wouldn’t want to fly a ship that way.”

“Contact!” Bamber called out. “Multiple contacts! Jeez, they’re —” suddenly he cut off.

“Mr. Bamber?” Cody called back. He shot a look to Jasmine who shrugged and turned back to her camera display.

“I’m going in,” Ellaz called. A moment later, she called back, “Cody, Jasmine, you need to get here. And Miz Collins.”

“Why?”

“It’s a nursery,” Bamber called back. “One teenaged minder and twenty babies from months to years.”

“Let’s go,” Cody said, unbuckling himself.

“I’m staying here,” Jasmine said. “There’s…” she turned to her displays and waved him off.

“Miz Collins?” Cody called.

“Twenty-one more mouths to feed,” Moira Collins said, shaking her head. “What are we going to do?”

Cody didn’t have an answer.

“Why didn’t they get us?” Nora Wright asked when they’d settled all the babies in the main cabin. “They got everything else, why not us?”

“I’ll bet they used a mass reading,” Ellaz said. “Or a thermal level.” Cody shot her a look. He was trying to come up with a makeshift diaper for a very soiled little girl but… it was his first time. Fortunately, Moira Collins was able to guide him.

“You’re saying that anything too small they didn’t notice?” Clive asked. Ellaz nodded. “That explains all the kids you found.”

“Kids aren’t a threat,” Jasmine added. “At least, I’ll bet that’s what they thought.”

Go on! Ellaz thought with a mental wave to him. And Pawn to Queen Four.

When Cody came back, he reported, “Downstream, T+3, all systems nominal.”

“Roger,” Nora’s voice came back immediately. “We’re good here.”

Cody turned back to their view of space at Warp Nine.

Two hours later, after winning two games of chess, Ellaz said, Are we there yet?

Cody laughed.

Cody jerked when someone touched him. He pulled up his helmet. “You need to eat,” Gail said to him, passing him a hot tray.

Cody nodded in thanks and started gulping down his food.

“And I’m bored,” Gail added five minutes later when he’d finished and passed her back his tray. “Also, when are you going to sleep?”

Cody fumbled for an answer but Gail waved him off. “I’ll tell you,” she said, turning to back out of the hatch. “Ellaz needs to eat, too.”

Cody smiled at her and pulled back on his helmet. Chow time!

Ellaz took a moment to respond. What?

Chow time, Cody replied. He frowned. What were you doing?

Updating the system, Ellaz replied. Is — oh, someone’s poking my arm. I guess I should go.

Go!

Okay, now you need to sleep, Cody thought to Ellaz, thirty minutes after he woke up from his four hour “nap.” I’ll call if I need help.

I’m not sleepy!

Get your helmet off, crawl back to bunk and lie down, Cody ordered. Close your eyes, get some sleep.

Can’t I sleep here? Ellaz half-begged.

No, Cody replied, you need to lie down, get some shut eye.

Okay, Ellaz replied glumly.

Cody waited a moment then reached over to tap her hand. I said go.

He felt Ellaz rise and the cabin shake as she moved back to the main cabin. She patted his arm as she left.

And Cody was alone with the command of a starship moving at Warp Nine. He checked on their monitor program and came to the conclusion that it was bored.

#

Are we there yet? Cody thought to Ellaz when he plugged back into the mind-link two days later. I never thought that space could be this boring.

Don’t jinx it, Ellaz warned. You good? I want to take a break.

Cody found Ellaz already asleep when he came to the dorms for sleep. Jacob was sleeping in the bunk next to her. Cody sent Gail off to change, checked his latest updates, and then swapped with her, sending the little girl to the bed next to his. As he changed, he smiled at how fierce the two kids were with their “officers.” Gail was conscientious and tended to work herself too hard. Jacob was about the same. Ellaz could be difficult — what was that at dinner? — but she cared for the two kids, cared for everyone in her own, taciturn, grouchy way.

Cody got into his bunk, called the lights out and went to sleep.

He woke up sometime in the middle of the night. Jacob was giving Ellaz a glass of water. She saw Cody’s eyes and frowned at him, waving any questions away. Nightmares, Cody guessed. Well, Edie had thrown everything she could at them and… they were flying an experimental ship, aliens had wiped out over fifteen hundred million people in this system, and they needed to get going.

Tomorrow they would be three days from launch.

#

Cody sent Gail off to change, checked his latest updates, and then swapped with her, sending the little girl to the bed next to his. As he changed, he smiled at how fierce the two kids were with their “officers.” Gail was conscientious and tended to work herself too hard. Jacob was about the same. Ellaz could be difficult — what was that at dinner? — but she cared for the two kids, cared for everyone in her own, taciturn, grouchy way.

Cody got into his bunk, called the lights out and went to sleep.

He woke up sometime in the middle of the night. Jacob was giving Ellaz a glass of water. She saw Cody’s eyes and frowned at him, waving any questions away. Nightmares, Cody guessed. Well, Edie had thrown everything she could at them and… they were flying an experimental ship, aliens had wiped out over fifteen hundred million people in this system, and they needed to get going.

Tomorrow they would be three days from launch.

Passage:
“This Captain Ford is too tired not to take all the help he can get,” Cody said with a breezy wave of his hand. “Ellaz, can you fire up the sensors, see what we’ve got?”

She shot him a look — they knew what they’d get — but she nodded and played along.

“Nothing from the target,” Ellaz reported back a few minutes later. “We should go in for a closer look.”

“Yes,” Moira Collins agreed. “In fact, let’s see if we can find a pad, then we’ll get out and take stock.”

Cody brought the shuttle around in a long slow sweep over the nearest landing pad. They spotted the remains of several shuttles. Some looked intact.

“Did they target only the living?” Clive Bamber asked. He was following their displays on the remotes in the main cabin.

“It sure looks like it,” Edie Crump agreed. Then, “You know, if we wanted more lift, that might be a good thing for us.”

“Yeah,” Moira Collins said numbly. “At least…” she broke off.

Cody and Ellaz exchanged looks. Ellaz turned her head back to the main cabin. “You did the math.”

“Before you, I’ll bet,” Moira Collins replied.

“Twenty-five more mouths —” Edie Crump added.

“Plus we were never designed to be self-sustaining,” Clive Bamber added. He unbuckled himself and moved forward to the entrance to the cockpit, standing in the doorway. “So… what’s the plan?”

Cody considered his options and went with the truth. “We could take one of the fuel farms, steal the tanks —”

“That gets you the fuel,” Bamber said. He waved a hand around. “But I don’t see a ship, do you?”

“We haven’t looked yet,” Edie Crump said. “Let’s get down and scout.”

“We’ve got to warn the others,” Cody said, pressing on with his answer.

“What others?” Moira Collins demanded.

“The other worlds,” Ellaz said.

“We’ve got to fight the aliens,” Cody added.

“What aliens?” Edie asked.

“I saw one,” Cody said. He heard Clive Bamber hiss in surprise. “It was fuzzy, like a caterpillar but much bigger — man-sized — and it stood on its butt.”

“Did you get any imagery?” Moira asked.

“No,” Cody said. “But I’ll bet we can search for some.”

Passage:
A large, wrenching metallic sound followed immediately by a sigh energized Cody as nothing else could. The ship was tearing apart. He raced around to the side of the shuttle, pounded on the airlock release and rushed inside.

“Wait!” A small voice cried out. He turned just in time to be slammed into by a small person. The girl. “Now, go, go, go!”

Cody didn’t need a kid to tell him, he raced to the pilot’s seat, plopped down… and looked at it in confusion.

“Don’t you know how to fly this thing?” the girl cried at him, dropping into the co-pilot’s seat. She hit a number of switches, the engines came to life, the airlock slammed shut and the shuttle twisted around, facing the bay doors.

“I know how to fly it!” Cody growled. “I’m just thinking —”

“Well, think faster!” the girl cried.

“We need to wait,” Cody said, taking grip of the joystick in front of him.

“Wait?” the girl cried. “The ship is coming apart all around us!”

“And we’re in a shuttle, we’re safe,” Cody told her, forcing himself to ignore his hammering heart which was busily questioning his sanity. “If we fly out — powered up —”

“They’ll see us and blast us,” the little girl concluded glumly.

Cody turned to her. Short-cropped strawberry blond hair, freckles, intense blue eyes. “You’re a Whirly!”

“Yes,” the girl said, “how astute of you!”

“But — but — you were shot!”

“Again, your perceptions amaze me,” the girl said. Well, Whirly’s were known throughout space to be some of the smartest people ever — and also some of the most sarcastic. Apparently, they started early.

“Cody Ford,” Cody said, glancing at the sensors, trying to get a feel for what was going on outside the steadily failing freighter. “As soon as we see enough debris, we blow the cargo bay door and fall through, powered down.”

The girl considered this. “Good plan,” she said finally. Then, “Ellaz.”

“Huh?”

“Ellaz Whirly,” the girl said, rolling her eyes at him.

“You’re not on the roster,” Cody said. He’d spent some time memorizing the crew and passenger rosters.

“‘Child, age eight,’” Ellaz replied. “Not listed on primary passenger cargo.”

Anything!

Your daughter?

Ellen Whirly, Ellaz said. Pick the variants you think are best. Raise her for me, please?

Okay, Cody replied immediately. Absolutely.

One other thing, Ellaz thought. And you can say no.

Shoot.

Okay, so what if there was no plating? No ribs?

How to do that?

“Ellaz?” Cody called. “What’s the most intact ship? Here or in orbit?”

“I’ll check,” Ellaz said. “But… I wouldn’t expect to find anything. They were thorough.”

Yeah, they were. Well, scratch that.

“Mr. Bamber?” Cody called. “Could we set up a base here? A hab?”

“Maybe,” Bamber said. “But… I don’t think we could get enough people to build it and a ship at the same time.”

Yeah. Then, “We could use the shuttles.”

“I suppose,” Bamber agreed. “But they need to be powered up, charged with air.”

Cody nodded. How long did it take to outfit a shuttle? To get it out of storage and make it operational? He queried the computers. Three days.

“I bet I can get it down to one,” he said to himself. He knew shuttles. Of course, he’d never taken one out of mothballs but — he switched frequencies. “Ellaz, could we use the shuttles?”

“For what?” Ellaz shot back. Cody heard a wail in the air behind her and guessed that she was diapering a baby. That was probably new — and stressful — to her.

“We make a swarm,” Cody said. “Just put them all together —”

“And what?” Ellaz demanded. “Where do the rings go? How much life support do they have?” Not enough. “Also, you need an ECLSS, right? And power.”

“They’ve got their own,” Cody protested.

“For months?” Ellaz snapped. But then, “We could set up a distribution system. If we get the power.”

“See?”

“And the warp rings? How do they work surrounding a bunch of —” Ellaz broke off. “Okay, you need to get with Edie. Or, better, with Jasmine.”

“Jasmine?”

“She’s young, she thinks outside of the box,” Ellaz said. Cody got the impression that she felt he thought outside of the box, too.

“Ellaz?” Cody said, suddenly shaking with a brilliant idea. “Could we use your —”

“No!” Ellaz said immediately. “It’s experimental! And, beside, I don’t want —”

“Okay, okay! Keep your shirt on!”

The heat will dissipate and the other two segments will expand, Cody thought. The field’s a bit off so compensate on — he tried to recall which segment was the opposite of five. The twenty segments were numbered from zero to nineteen — Segment Fourteen —

Kk, Ellaz replied, putting more cooling into the opposite segment. This will make the warp smaller.

Only a little, Cody thought.

Warp Nine, Ellaz thought a moment later. Fuel!

I see it, Cody replied. They were using more fuel now because they had to divert more power to the cooling sections than planned.

“Day Five!” Edie called out.

The sensors shifted again. They were nearly at their destination. They were coming up on —

Ring failure! The monitor flashed to them. Ring failure in five…

Warp Two! Cody ordered. Immediately they slowed down. Heat up nine and zero! Compensate!

Cody watched as the measures of the rings surged and faded. Segment Five dropped to ten percent… then zero.

Fourteen out! Ellaz called. Adding power.

Warp Five! Cody called. He switched their astrogation to the standard Warp Five Astro charts. He drew a breath as he watched their approach and, finally —

“Unknown ship, unknown ship! This is Deneb Approach! Say intentions!” The voice was Edie’s, of course. “Well done, Hope! You made it!”

Cody and Ellaz pulled off their helmets and grinned at each other.

“Good thinking to surge the segments like that,” Edie said as she handed a drink to Ellaz. Jasmine had another waiting for Cody’s parched lips. “We couldn’t do that with a regular ring.”

“What would have happened with one?” Ellaz said.

“Well, there are two rings on a regular ship,” Edie reminded them. “But… a ring failure? That’s the number one reason ships don’t make it.”

“So these segmented rings, we could put them on regular ships?” Cody wondered.

Edie shook her head. “You’d need a ring watch — at least two ringers — to handle that.” She pursed her lips. “More, if you used two rings.”

“But… why use two?” Ellaz wondered. “I mean, we’ve proven that one works just fine!”

“In sims,” Edie reminded her.

“Well, we’ll know soon enough in five days,” Cody said.

Chapter Eight

Chapter Eight

“I wish there was some way we could warn them,” Cody said as he woke up and smiled at Gail who held a cup of coffee in front of him. He took it with a grateful nod and sipped it. “How long was I out?”

“Hours,” Gail said airily. “We’re two hours out.”

“They’ve started their attack,” Cody guessed.

“Yes, and we think we’ve got readings on them,” Gail replied. She made a face. “It looks like they’re using your plan.”

“Not my plan,” Cody objected, appalled at the notion.

“Get dressed, get moving,” Gail said, reaching a hand out to help him up. She was way smaller than Cody. He shook his head at her and stood on his own. She made a face. “Look, you smell. You need to wash off, change clothes, and eat before you put on that smelly helmet of yours again.”

“Smelly?”

Gail wrinkled her nose. “Well, it was! I cleaned it,” she admitted. “Again.”

“Thanks,” Cody said, moving past her to the restroom. Five minutes later he was out, dressed, presentable, and hungry.

Gail intercepted him with a tray. “This is cold,” she apologized. It was a set of protein bars. Cody smiled at her, pocketed one and opened the other.

“What about you?” Cody asked. He waved toward stretched out chairs. “Shouldn’t you get some rest?”

Gail scoffed. “Now? Do you think anyone can rest now?”

“Rest, yes,” Cody said. “Sleep, no.” He pointed to the nearest bed. “You stay here. I’ll call you when we’re thirty minutes out.”

“I’m not —”

Cody pointed to himself. “Captain.” He pointed to the bed. “Rest.” He smiled as he passed her and went into the cockpit. He politely “threw” Jacob out of his seat and set him to rest, “And make sure she’s resting, too!”

He pulled on his helmet after he climbed into the pilot’s chair. Then he tapped Nora on the shoulder to let her know he was on duty. In the simulation, Cody waited for Ellaz’s tap. He glanced around when he didn’t feel it. Ellaz?

Here! Ellaz’s voice came back to him. Sorry! I was watching — well, take a look.

“Cody, Cody, Cody!” A voice woke him up, sounding urgent.

“Hi!” A young voice came to him. “Who are you?”

“I’m Cody,” he said. “And you are?”

“How many AMCs and how many tachcomms?” Cody wondered.

“Well, I’m a bit worried about how we’d hook one on,” Georgie said. “For that matter, how we’d drop them off, too. And we’d have to deploy this brand new tachcomm sensor array. Which is untested —”

Georgie agreed with a nod. “I’d say, let the wonder team tackle the issue,” Georgie said. She yawned. “If you don’t mind —”

“Unknown ship, say type and origin,” A voice called back.

“Wasp and the convoy are experimental craft out of Deneb,” Cody replied.

“Hey, jerkface! Who let you on the comms?” Captain Don Hartman called. “Didn’t you retire?”

“Who is — unknown caller —”

“Cut it, Ed, you know who it is!” Don Hartman said. “And, I’ve gotta say, it’s good to hear your voice.”

“We got reamed,” Don Hartman said. “We got attacked by ships we’ve never seen before —”

“How many? How’d you fight them off?” ‘Ed’ asked.

“We didn’t,” Don Hartman replied. “Elantra is all that’s left. And it’s only alive because Cody Ford here and his crew damn near suicided to defend us.”

“That’s only because we’re the last two alive in this system!” Ellaz said. She shot him a hot look. “And don’t think that we’re going to do any repopulating. I’m a clone from a long line of clones.”

“Me, too,” Cody said.

“Well, not to be mean, but you can’t be,” Ellaz said. “Your name is Cody, so you’re only the third in line, right?”

It was traditional to name clones alphabetically. The first would have an ‘A’ name, the second a ‘B’ name and so on. Only the Fords didn’t do it that way. It was a closely guarded secret that the first Ford was Zacharias.

“You said your mother was Elle,” Cody remarked.

“Well… yes,” Ellaz allowed. “We decided to stick with the same first letter until we —” she broke off abruptly and shook her head “— sorry, that’s classified.”

“I won’t tell anyone,” Cody said, waving to the debris surrounding them, pointing out that there was no one to tell. Then he had a thought. “So, is E for Engineering or Electronics?”

Ellaz hissed in surprise before admitting, “Energy.”

“Right, like your power converter,” Cody guessed.

Ellaz gave him a reluctant nod. Her panel beeped and she sat up excitedly. “Can you make the emergency signal?”

“Do you mean the Mayday squawk?” Cody asked her, moving to bring up another control panel on his displays.

“Squawk?”

“That’s what we call it,” Cody said, programming the emergency code and hitting the switch that broadcast it. “It’ll take about forty-five seconds at light speed.”

“Ninety round-trip,” Ellaz observed. Cody nodded and got busy, turning the shuttle toward the least time course for the farthest moon and checking his fuel levels.

Ninety seconds later there was a beep. Someone had replied.

“This is cargo shuttle Wasp from the freighter Hornet,” Cody said quickly in a calm, professional voice. “Two souls aboard. Air for two hours. Request vectors for approach.”

Ninety seconds later, on the same frequency, a voice replied, “Say intentions.”

“We need to refuel, resupply — we had an air leak — and then we’re going to search for any survivors,” Cody replied.

“Wasp, you are cleared to approach the Deep Space One, orbits and speed in data,” came the reply.

“That’s only because we’re the last two alive in this system!” Ellaz said. She shot him a hot look. “And don’t think that we’re going to do any repopulating. I’m a clone from a long line of clones.”

“Me, too,” Cody said.

“Well, not to be mean, but you can’t be,” Ellaz said. “Your name is Cody, so you’re only the third in line, right?”

It was traditional to name clones alphabetically. The first would have an ‘A’ name, the second a ‘B’ name and so on. Only the Fords didn’t do it that way. It was a closely guarded secret that the first Ford was Zacharias.

“You said your mother was Elle,” Cody remarked.

“Well… yes,” Ellaz allowed. “We decided to stick with the same first letter until we —” she broke off abruptly and shook her head “— sorry, that’s classified.”

“I won’t tell anyone,” Cody said, waving to the debris surrounding them, pointing out that there was no one to tell. Then he had a thought. “So, is E for Engineering or Electronics?”

Ellaz hissed in surprise before admitting, “Energy.”

“Right, like your power converter,” Cody guessed.

Ellaz gave him a reluctant nod. Her panel beeped and she sat up excitedly. “Can you make the emergency signal?”

“Do you mean the Mayday squawk?” Cody asked her, moving to bring up another control panel on his displays.

“Squawk?”

“That’s what we call it,” Cody said, programming the emergency code and hitting the switch that broadcast it. “It’ll take about forty-five seconds at light speed.”

“Ninety round-trip,” Ellaz observed. Cody nodded and got busy, turning the shuttle toward the least time course for the farthest moon and checking his fuel levels.

Ninety seconds later there was a beep. Someone had replied.

“This is cargo shuttle Wasp from the freighter Hornet,” Cody said quickly in a calm, professional voice. “Two souls aboard. Air for two hours. Request vectors for approach.”

Ninety seconds later, on the same frequency, a voice replied, “Say intentions.”

“We need to refuel, resupply — we had an air leak — and then we’re going to search for any survivors,” Cody replied.

“Wasp, you are cleared to approach the Deep Space One, orbits and speed in data,” came the reply.

Cody didn’t need to be told twice. He pointed to Ellaz’s helmet. “We need to go in,” he said, pulling his helmet over his head.

They entered a dark world.

Edie? Cody thought. He felt Ellaz’s “hand” touch his in the simulation and he gave hers a quick comforting squeeze in response.

In the distance, they heard giggles. Cody “tugged” Ellaz behind him as he raced toward the sound.

We can’t get caught! Ellaz warned him just as he was about to jump down a hole that appeared suddenly before them.

Edie! Cody called out. “Edie!” he said out loud. “Can you hear us?”

Play, play, play! Laugh, laugh, laugh! It sounded like two voices, singing in chorus. Cody turned toward Ellaz and imagined her in front of him.

What do we do? Ellaz said.

Rope, Cody said, pulling a rope out of the air. Tie it around me, I’ll go in.

Ellaz considered his suggestion and started tying one end of the rope around her waist. This is a really stupid idea, you know.

What’s yours? Cody asked.

Build a bot to find them, Ellaz replied, snugging her knot tight.

Okay, Cody thought back, raising his hands out in front of him and sketching out a shape. Ellaz nodded, moved to join him, adding arms and a head. In a few moments they created a standard hand bot. Okay, boy, go find Edie! Bring them back to us!

Only the bot came back moments later holding one of its arms with the other. When Ellaz and Cody noticed it, the bots head fell off its shoulders and it collapsed into nothingness.

They got swords? Ellaz asked.

I’m going, Cody declared, imagining a shield on his right arm.

I’m following, Ellaz said, pushing him forward.

They went down the hole. They fell for a long time, following the sing-song voices.

When they landed, they found themselves on a pile of old diapers.

Ew! They thought in unison. The voices weren’t too far away.

They found two little girls in a meadow throwing leaves at each other and singing, Ring Around the Rosie, Pocket Full of Posies! Ashes, Ashes, We All Fall Down!

What’s that song? Ellaz said. I feel like I know it.

“Nursery,” little Franny Harper piped up, “we’re ready. Babies are ready. Is it okay if we seal off from the ship?”

“Actually, I think you should wait,” Nora replied.

“No,” Ellaz said, “seal off. Be ready to deploy. Set your controls to automatic.”

“Is Jacob…?”

“On my way!” Jacob Falcon piped up. “Captain —?”

“Go!” Cody told him. He wasn’t happy with just the three of them but, if Jacob survived, he might be able to tell their story. And that might help the survivors. “Take a complete copy of our log with you.”

“Okay,” Jacob replied, his voice distinct from his VR voice.

“We’re going to have to do some snappy maneuvering for this to work,” Ellaz said aloud.

Cody grinned. “Aren’t you glad I’m a shuttle pilot?”

“What?” Ellaz said, surprised. “I was talking about the computers.”

Beside him, Nora snorted in amusement.

“We’re going to need to fire up the RCS on the shuttles,” Cody said.

“Yes, yes, I know!” Ellaz snapped back. Then, in a slightly more subdued voice, she added, “And I don’t suppose it’d hurt to have you ready, if we need you.”

“Thanks,” Cody said. “Nora, let’s get the preflights up and running.”

#

“Eight minutes,” Cody said unnecessarily. Ellaz had refined their readings, they’d seen the destruction of the space docks, the moons, and now… the spacehabs. Four had been destroyed.

“I want us to start a track on the shipyards,” Cody said. “I want to know what we can find out about what’s intact, what we can use to —”

“Build more starships,” Ellaz said approvingly. “Working.”

“You sound like a computer,” Nora complained. Then she hushed, embarrassed.

“I’ve been told that a lot of times,” Ellaz replied, sounding unperturbed. “Cody? Didn’t you say mate in four?”

Cody’s eyes went wide. They’d finished that game. He’d beaten her just as predicted.

“I can play you,” Nora offered.

“But —” Ellaz broke off. “Oh! We finished that game! I didn’t — I mean, I was distracted.”

“We’ve got under eight minutes,” Cody said, “can you play a timed game?”

“No,” Ellaz replied. “I think I’d best… I’d best keep an eye on things.”

“Yup, high on our list,” Clive Bamber agreed. “But if we can’t build a spaceship —”

“Oh, well then we’ve got nothing to worry about!” Ellaz said with a grim smile.

#

Carlow Shipping was the name of the spaceport, the city, and the industry. It had been set up by the magnate William Buckley over thirty years before, Cody saw from the data entry on it. Carlow Shipping had produced over forty starships, mostly in the two megatonne range. It had the reputation of making good, moderately priced ships.

When Cody looked at the displays of the ground beneath them, all he saw were wrecks. The main dome was shattered, as were all the corridors connecting to other habitats, workshops, power plants, hydroponics gardens — anything where humans might live.

His instruments warned him of several radiation hotspots, including one huge mess that had been a ship dockyard.

“They nuked the Nautilus,” Edie murmured from behind him. “That ship was nearly flight ready.” She examined her displays more. “Huh, they didn’t spend any effort on the new builds, though.”

“Why?” Cody asked.

“My guess?” Clive Bamber said. “They were raiders. They came in quick and left quick.” He made a face. “Which is why we’re here.”

“But not for long,” Ellaz said, starting up a new tracking routine. “Even without the extra mouths —”

“We know,” Clive said, jerking a hand toward young Jasmine.

Ellaz scowled. “She’s just two years younger than me and I’m pretty sure she can do the math.”

“Less than a year,” Jasmine piped up. “Even with the original five hundred, that’s all they’ve got. They’re not rigged to be self-sustaining.”

“What would it take to do that?” Cody wondered. “I mean —” he waved a hand toward the shattered hydroponics dome “— we’ve got soil here.”

“You need bacteria,” Moira Collins pointed out.

“The compost tanks,” Ellaz said. “We could pull from that —”

“You need transport, fuel and —” Clive added grumpily.

“Wait one!” Cody said, turning the shuttle sharply around and descending. He pointed to one side and had the displays updated with a red circle where he pointed with his hand. “What’s that?”

They spotted a light, blinking.

“That’s Morse,” Ellaz said. “It’s SOS.”

Chapter Six

Chapter Six

“H minus 6, Captain,” Gail Eber called cheerfully the next morning. “All systems are green. We are go.”

Cody felt his heart pound as he lifted his head from the cot. He looked over to Ellaz and saw that she was still sleeping. So was little Jacob.

Well, they’d had a fright — two frights. Both caused by traitors. Of the two, Tom Walker was the lesser. Cody couldn’t imagine him being willing to kill fifteen hundred million people just to — kill an inventor. Cody drew in a quick breath — that’s what the alien had done — he had killed Elle Whirly, the inventor of the energy converter. Did he know about Ellaz? Or did he think she didn’t know enough, or was too young to understand her mother’s secret? Did he know that Ellaz had an implant? Cody made a note to himself to ask later.

Things were moving fast. He got up, got dressed, grabbed breakfast and then suited up to go out and check on Hope.

“She’s looking good,” Moria Collins said as she spotted him in the airlock. “You can go and have a look, if you want, but don’t get too close — we’re lifting her for the rings. Uh, ring.”

Two hours to get the ring installed then a mad four-hour dash to get all the crew and consumables in place. After that, a pair of tugs would haul her up into orbit and then — they’d see whether the whole thing worked.

Cody watched the assembly for twenty minutes, then Gail called to him and he spent the next several hours dealing with all the last-minute details that no one had thought of.

The eighteen shuttles were all attached, their connecting tubing pressurized and tested. Two failed the first test but it was only because some of the tubing needed to be freed of lint and dust — Cody remembered polishing his fuel intake valve so many days ago. Then all systems were green.

“Ellaz,” Cody called over his comm, “we’re ready to board.”

“Coming out through Tube Three,” Ellaz reported. “Where are — what are you doing down there? Get up here, now!”

Cody blushed, turned and headed back into the airlock.

“Ellaz,” Cody said when they came back to the dorms. “Can you come with me to the Lab? We haven’t practiced in a while and I think we should.”

Ellaz made a face. “Now?”

“Yeah, now,” Cody told her, waving a hand toward her. “I wanted to show you something.”

“Okay,” Ellaz grumbled, following him with dragging steps.

The Lab was clear, Cody had checked.

“So what do we do?” Ellaz demanded as Cody sat in one of the seats in the center table.

Cody smiled at her, winked, and pulled his helmet on. With a sigh, Ellaz did the same.

Okay, now what? Ellaz demanded.

Now no one can hear us, Cody replied. I was thinking —

!!

Don’t joke, Cody said. Here, in the mind-link, I can show you.

Show me what?

In answer, their world shimmered, shook and — resolved itself into a cargo bay. The cargo bay on the Hornet.

Now you can see what I saw, Cody thought to Ellaz. And you’ll know that I wasn’t crazy.

Okay, Ellaz said as Cody relived his memories.

#

There was a noise from outside in the cargo bay. Cody froze. He listened. A faint whine and a thud. Was that normal?

Cody put down his rag and slunk down under the shuttle, leaning to one side of the curving hull to look around.

A coverall-clad spacer raced into view — and disintegrated, leaving only black dust where he had once been. Cody stifled a hiss and ducked back, hoping he hadn’t been spotted.

Who the hell had a blaster like that? And why kill on a freighter? Pirates? Was that what that lurch had been earlier? Had they been boarded?

Cody turned his head toward a sound that came behind him. He caught just a glimpse of something — green, furry, tall. It looked sort of like a caterpillar but standing on its butt, upright. The caterpillar bulged at its midsection and a blue flash shot out. There was a cry and Cody spotted a small figure slump down to the deck and lay still. A girl. Maybe seven, maybe eight.

“People who work in debris fields,” Cody said. He put the two seats back, secured them and looked around. “I’ve got two balloons still in the air. I’m going to keep us in microgravity until we’re certain.”

“Pressure is stabilized,” Ellaz reported, glancing to the ECLSS panels. ECLSS — Environment Control and Life Support Systems, usually pronounced “ee-class.” Cody grunted, turned and kicked himself back to the cabin.

He buckled himself in, pulled up the navigation system and checked their fuel levels. “If we go there, we won’t be much good after.”

“Unless we get refueled,” Ellaz agreed.

Cody nodded and ran a sweep of the debris near them. “Nothing here to refuel with,” he said, his hopes of finding a spare tank or something similar dashed. If the aliens — or really dumb space pirates — had been in a rush, they’d also been thorough.

“Okay, they’re alive,” Ellaz said, bouncing in her chair with glee. “See? I can see when they shut down their systems —”

“When?”

“It looks like — it looks like just about long enough for light speed from Xerxes,” Ellaz said.

Xerxes was one of the largest asteroids in the solar system’s asteroid belt. It was — or had been — inhabited and was a major mining and research center for the whole system.

“So either someone was looking or talking with them,” Cody guessed. He frowned. “Both observatories?”

“Everything went dark within five minutes,” Ellaz replied. “It was like someone threw a switch, it was so fast.”

“That doesn’t mean anyone’s alive,” Cody said with a grimace. “It could be that these aliens have fitl and they destroyed the bases first.”

“Fitl?”

“Faster-Than-Light,” Cody translated.

“‘Fitl?’” Ellaz repeated, crinkling her nose in disgust. “You call it ‘fitl?’”

“It’s easier than saying FTL or Faster-Than-Light,” Cody replied. “And everyone says it.”

“Well, how come I haven’t heard it before?” Ellaz challenged.

“I dunno, maybe you don’t have any friends,” Cody shot back with an evil grin. Ellaz’s face fell and she looked like she was frozen. “Hey! It was a joke!”

“I don’t have any friends,” Ellaz said in a small voice.

“Well, you’ve got me,” Cody offered.
