“Warp Four, out and back,” Edie called out.

This time it was easier because they had experience.

“Warp Six, but watch the ring,” Edie told them when they’d come back.

It was a lot, watching the systems and the ring.

Can we create a monitor? Ellaz thought. Cody got an image of something constantly checking on pressure, temperature, deformations.

Sure, Cody thought. He tightened his grip on Ellaz’s “hand” and started thinking furiously. They fell into a small space of time between everything else they were doing to play a game of building the monitor.

“Cody! Ellaz!” Edie called to them urgently. “What? Where are you?”

Here, Cody thought back. We were just —

“Don’t take your mind off the ring!” Jasmine cried. “You’ll blow up!”

— building a monitor, Ellaz said, pulling their new software interface into their view. Hang on, it’s going to POST.

“POST?” Edie repeated.

Power-On Self-Test, Cody translated.

“What’s it for?” Edie asked. Then she must have pulled up the schematics. “You’re going to trust a computer with the — huh, this could work!”

POST complete, all systems nominal, the software replied.

Engage, Cody and Ellaz thought together. The new display in their virtual world blinked to life with data flickering on its console. Ellaz and Cody pushed the software monitor into their command code — and it took over monitoring the warp ring. They’d built it so that it would alert on caution and act on emergencies — pulling power, balancing thermal output, and regulating the anti-matter flows.

“You two are three sigma, you know,” Edie observed moments later.

Compatible? Cody thought.

“Yes, and that’s really good,” Edie said. “You’ll probably get better the more you work together.”

Ellaz’s ghost hand squeezed his. He squeezed back.

“Okay, ready for Warp Eight?” Edie asked.

Sure, they thought together.

“Here, drink this,” Jasmine said, passing a water to Cody. Edie was doing the same for Ellaz. “It’s electrolyte, you lost a lot of moisture.”

“Why?” Cody asked, after draining the drink in one long gulp.

“Well, you were in there for six hours,” Jasmine said. “And it’s work.”

“Pirates!” Other Cody snorted, shaking his head at Ellaz. Cody was used to Other Cody — as he called the simulation — and somewhat hopeful that if anything happened to him, his alter-ego would be able to help Nora raise their kids. Of course, that wouldn’t be this Cody because if anything happened to Wasp it would undoubtedly destroy their computers, too.

“They couldn’t be very good, given that they’ve stolen nothing from us,” Georgie said. Ellaz and Other Cody exchanged looks. Georgie noticed. “What?”

“Nothing,” Cody said, “just an inside joke.”

“Okay,” Georgie said. “So, we’re ruling out pirates?” The others nodded in agreement. “Refugees? That’s still a possibility?” Cody nodded. “So what are they looking for? A new homeworld?”

“Why would they attack ours if that was the case?” Gail’s ghost asked. “If they’re running, why would they slow down to hit us?”

“They’re aliens, they don’t have to make sense,” Ellaz said.

“No,” Cody said. “I think they do.”

Georgie, who’d turned her attention back to her 3D chess game with Ellaz, tipped her king over and said, “Show me.”

Ellaz grinned at her, righted the king and showed the next three moves that ended with the king in checkmate.

Georgie sat back, stared at the board, stared at Ellaz’s ghost and nodded. “Good, good,” she said to herself. “Want another?”

“Sure,” Ellaz said and the board was reset with the pieces all back in their starting places.

“Where’d they come from?” Cody said. “They seem to be — were they on a straight line course when they attacked Meath?”

“We don’t know,” Ellaz said. She pursed her lips and shot a look to Georgie. “Something might have distracted them. Maybe they —”

“They’re denying us to their enemy!” Gail said with sudden certainty. “They don’t care about us, they just don’t want the others to get us.”

“Others?” Georgie said, moving her piece. “Now there are two alien species? In three hundred years of space travel, we haven’t found any.”

“What if one of the aliens was destroying the others?” Gail asked. “I mean, look at Meath — a hundred years from now, will anyone know that it was inhabited?”

Passage:
Chapter Six

Chapter Six

“H minus 6, Captain,” Gail Eber called cheerfully the next morning. “All systems are green. We are go.”

Cody felt his heart pound as he lifted his head from the cot. He looked over to Ellaz and saw that she was still sleeping. So was little Jacob.

Well, they’d had a fright — two frights. Both caused by traitors. Of the two, Tom Walker was the lesser. Cody couldn’t imagine him being willing to kill fifteen hundred million people just to — kill an inventor. Cody drew in a quick breath — that’s what the alien had done — he had killed Elle Whirly, the inventor of the energy converter. Did he know about Ellaz? Or did he think she didn’t know enough, or was too young to understand her mother’s secret? Did he know that Ellaz had an implant? Cody made a note to himself to ask later.

Things were moving fast. He got up, got dressed, grabbed breakfast and then suited up to go out and check on Hope.

“She’s looking good,” Moria Collins said as she spotted him in the airlock. “You can go and have a look, if you want, but don’t get too close — we’re lifting her for the rings. Uh, ring.”

Two hours to get the ring installed then a mad four-hour dash to get all the crew and consumables in place. After that, a pair of tugs would haul her up into orbit and then — they’d see whether the whole thing worked.

Cody watched the assembly for twenty minutes, then Gail called to him and he spent the next several hours dealing with all the last-minute details that no one had thought of.

The eighteen shuttles were all attached, their connecting tubing pressurized and tested. Two failed the first test but it was only because some of the tubing needed to be freed of lint and dust — Cody remembered polishing his fuel intake valve so many days ago. Then all systems were green.

“Ellaz,” Cody called over his comm, “we’re ready to board.”

“Coming out through Tube Three,” Ellaz reported. “Where are — what are you doing down there? Get up here, now!”

Cody blushed, turned and headed back into the airlock.

The heat will dissipate and the other two segments will expand, Cody thought. The field’s a bit off so compensate on — he tried to recall which segment was the opposite of five. The twenty segments were numbered from zero to nineteen — Segment Fourteen —

Kk, Ellaz replied, putting more cooling into the opposite segment. This will make the warp smaller.

Only a little, Cody thought.

Warp Nine, Ellaz thought a moment later. Fuel!

I see it, Cody replied. They were using more fuel now because they had to divert more power to the cooling sections than planned.

“Day Five!” Edie called out.

Ring failure! The monitor flashed to them. Ring failure in five…

Warp Two! Cody ordered. Immediately they slowed down. Heat up nine and zero! Compensate!

Cody watched as the measures of the rings surged and faded. Segment Five dropped to ten percent… then zero.

Fourteen out! Ellaz called. Adding power.

Warp Five! Cody called. He switched their astrogation to the standard Warp Five Astro charts. He drew a breath as he watched their approach and, finally —

“Unknown ship, unknown ship! This is Deneb Approach! Say intentions!” The voice was Edie’s, of course. “Well done, Hope! You made it!”

Cody and Ellaz pulled off their helmets and grinned at each other.

“Good thinking to surge the segments like that,” Edie said as she handed a drink to Ellaz. Jasmine had another waiting for Cody’s parched lips. “We couldn’t do that with a regular ring.”

“What would have happened with one?” Ellaz said.

“Well, there are two rings on a regular ship,” Edie reminded them. “But… a ring failure? That’s the number one reason ships don’t make it.”

“So these segmented rings, we could put them on regular ships?” Cody wondered.

Edie shook her head. “You’d need a ring watch — at least two ringers — to handle that.” She pursed her lips. “More, if you used two rings.”

“But… why use two?” Ellaz wondered. “I mean, we’ve proven that one works just fine!”

“In sims,” Edie reminded her.

“Well, we’ll know soon enough in five days,” Cody said.

Ellaz shot him a look then sighed. “Okay, not all boys are stupid.” Cody blinked. “There have to be some somewhere, right?” She smiled when she caught his reaction and then her smile faded. She moved closer to him. “Thanks for that,” she said in a lower voice, “I don’t think we could have got out.”

“Yeah,” Cody said, knowing that she meant their mind-link. “But we got good plans and now we have a chance.”

“And we know what the attackers used,” Ellaz agreed.

“What the aliens used,” Cody corrected her.

Ellaz shook her head. “We don’t know that for certain.”

“Why would humans destroy the whole solar system? Kill nearly two billion people?”

“I don’t know,” Ellaz said. “But humans have done evil things before.” Ellaz looked around. “Let’s see how Seth is with a bottle.”

Seth, and Simon, it turned out, were very good. Sammy and Stan kept the babies, diapered and clean, Seth and Simon kept them fed and burped.

“We could make a fortune,” Nora said, looking around their makeshift nursery with a glowing expression. “Auto babysitters, why didn’t anyone think of that?”

“Because they’re super expensive,” Ellaz said. “You’re looking at — what? — twenty million?”

“So?” Nora said. “Worth it.”

Cody smiled. “Nora, do you need to rest?”

“Please,” Nora said, racing back to a chair, putting her feet up in another and closing her eyes.

“If you head upstairs you can get a real lie down,” Cody said. “And some food.” He waved a hand around. “We’ll watch them for you. And call you when we have to move on.”

“Really?” Nora said wistfully. Cody nodded. Nora smiled at him, then at Ellaz. “Okay,” she said, rising from her seat and squaring her shoulders, “Let me know if you need anything.”

“Sure,” Cody said.

“You can rely on that,” Ellaz agreed. She waited until the girl had left before racing over to the makeshift cot and settling into it. “Wake me if you need anything.”

“Well, did you program first aid into the bots?” Cody asked.

Ellaz’s eyes flew open. She checked his expression, trying to determine if he was joking. “No.”

Chapter Two

Base Commander Trudy Wilson worked in an office marked Administrator Wilson. Apparently, the emergency had changed things.

“Yes, Captain, we’ve activated our site-wide emergency protocols,” Wilson said when Cody had glanced at the sign. “And, may I say, you are looking extremely good. Youthful. Did you say it was a shuttle accident?”

“Yes,” Cody lied smoothly. “Fortunately, the ejectors worked brilliantly.”

“And your son?” Wilson asked.

Cody made a sad face. “He didn’t make it.” He put a hand on Ellaz’s shoulder. “We’re the only survivors of our line.” Well, that wasn’t quite a lie — just the number of clone lines involved was greater than one.

“And you saved twenty-five souls,” Wilson said, sounding pleased but not looking it.

“Yes, ma’am,” Ellaz said. “And we’re happy to —”

“What?” Wilson demanded. She shot an accusing look to Clive Bamber, like the controller was responsible for all the trouble.

“Commander, what are the immediate plans?” Cody said.

“We’re still taking stock,” Wilson said. “And, if you’ll excuse me, I’ve got a lot of work to do —” she gestured toward her desk and the various flashing screens on her displays. “I’ll leave you with the controller, he’ll handle your needs.” She waved them away, adding, “Later, we might want to formally recognize your generous deeds.”

Or not, Cody thought to himself. Between him, Ellaz, and the survivors they’d rescued, they’d added twenty-five more mouths to be fed. On a base that was designed for scientists, researchers, and a small, itinerant population.

“We’re still trying to square away quarters for you,” Bamber apologized as they headed toward the main cafeteria.

“We could bunk on the Wasp,” Cody offered.

“Don’t you want a shower and a change of clothes?” Bamber asked solicitously.

“That’d be great,” Cody agreed. “But… don’t you have a gym? We could shower there.”

Bamber considered the request and nodded. “But… well, we’ve got your sizes on file, we can fit you out with a change and launder your current clothes.”

“Great!”

#

“Sleep on the shuttle?” Ellaz said sourly as they closed the hatch to the Wasp. “Why?”

“You figure it out,” Cody said, striding into the cockpit and firing up the controls.

Chapter Four

“What’s that?” A voice cried as it rushed up to the command center. One of the new kids. Moira Collins had returned with all of them, nineteen more mouths to feed.

“What’s that?” Another voice — a young boy’s — called, pointing to another display in the command center. “Is that a warp ring? Where’s the other? And — are you guys building starships?”

“Kinda small aren’t they?” An older voice said. That was Tom Walker. He was the eldest, sixteen years old. His father had been First Mate on the Waldron, one of the freighters docked at Parminter One, the same station where Cody’s Hornet had been. He looked more closely at the plans. “Where are the quarters?” He frowned. “You’re not using shuttles as living spaces?”

“Yes, we are,” Ellaz said, frowning at him and shooting a pointed look toward Cody. “We’re going to finish them in seven days —”

“Seven days! That’s impossible!” Tom exclaimed.

“No, it’s not,” Cody said, swiping the display to throw the image into a holo view. He expanded the holo view in front of them and pointed to the construction details. “We’re ahead of schedule, as you can see.”

Tom Walker peered into the details in the glowing image in front of him. After a moment, he nodded, “Looks like. But — one ring? Who’s going to be nuts enough to fly that?”

“Me,” Ellaz said, making her displeasure obvious. “Cowards can stay behind.”

Tom bristled at the implication. “Look, it’s all untried. New. And one ring?”

“It works,” Edie Crump said, coming into the command center, attracted by the voices. She held out her hand. “Edie Crump, ring tuner.”

Tom eyed her warily then broke into a grin. “I’ve heard of you! You were speaking at the Symposium, weren’t you? ‘The Possibilities Of Single Ring Warp Drives,’ right?” He pointed to the ghost image of the ship in the holo view. “This is yours?”

Edie nodded.

“Impressive,” Tom said. But it sounded, to Ellaz, like he was using someone else’s word. He pointed to the windows and the view outside. “And you’re building two of them?”

“Yes,” Cody said. “We need crew for the second.”

“You mean you’ve found enough for the first?” Tom asked incredulously.

“Do the math, Whirly,” Cody snapped. She looked at him, considered it and nodded. “Unless they’ve got an atmosphere —” he broke off and rushed to the cockpit.

“What?” Ellaz called after him.

“Scanning!” Cody called back. “Come up here and run thermal, if you want to help!”

Ellaz looked around the cabin. “Can’t!” Too many of the kids needed her, needed the medpacks, needed… to live.

#

Two hours — and one miraculous rescue of five spacers trapped in an airlock later — they turned back to the farthest moon and DS1.

Fortunately, the five were older and able to look after the youngsters. One grizzled spacer tried to pull rank on Ellaz but Cody cut her off.

“You don’t know the parameters,” he told her bluntly. “And they need you back there.” He didn’t add the obvious fact that Ellaz was utterly exhausted. She closed her eyes and was asleep before Cody had finished talking.

They made their way back at one gee, relative. Because the thrust was from the rear, the cockpit was “higher” than the main cabin, so no one came forward. Cody set up more searches, just in case, but he was afraid that the chances were too low.

“Deep Space One, this is Wasp, twenty-three souls on board,” Cody radioed. “Returning to base.”

The reply took over two minutes to get back. “Roger, Wasp. Understand twenty-five?”

“Yes, we got lucky and found five trapped in an airlock,” Cody said.

“Come on back,” Bamber replied. “Can you send us the particulars?”

“Wilco,” Cody said. It would take them six hours to get back the farside of the moon Nettles; he figured that he’d wake Ellaz in three.

“Yes, Mr. President,” Admiral Cartwright replied. He turned to Cody. “And, admiral, I hope you’ll forgive me for earlier. It’s just —”

“There’s been any number of morons trying to pull the wool over our eyes,” President Hanlan interjected. He shot a look to Don Hartman, “Including some seated here at this very table.”

“You bought it and you made a profit,” Don Hartman said in his defense. Nora shot him a look and he nodded to her, “I’ll tell you later.”

“So, Admiral,” President Hanlan said to Cody, “your ship is down until we can pull your ECLSS and replace it with something better.”

“Yes sir,” Cody agreed. “But —”

“Your people aren’t bad, they’re probably just rusty,” Admiral Cartwright said. “As I said, I got a report from the dock and they say that they think the problem is because that ECLSS unit is overpowered for your crew. Six, right?”

Cody nodded.

“And it’s rated for one hundred,” Admiral Cartwright replied. He turned to Nora. “And your ship, Commodore?”

“We’re fine, sir,” Nora said. “But we had a newer unit, too.” She shot Cody a look. “The admiral insisted on taking the last of the inventory list.”

“We still lost two ships,” Cody murmured.

“They’re not officially gone until a year is up,” Captain Forster reminded him. She turned to the Quark admiral. “We could send a couple of SARs out down their route, sir.”

“How much air time do they have in their shuttles, assuming that their ECLSS units also packed in?” Admiral Cartwright asked, spreading the question between Cody and Nora.

“Standard freighter shuttles, sir,” Cody replied. “They’re good for about thirty days on canned air.”

“That’s with a full complement, right? So, twenty-five people. And you had six?”

“And three shuttles,” Nora added. “So they might have gone to one shuttle or all three.”

“So… more time,” Admiral Cartwright said. He glanced to Emma. “Our rules are clear — we offer SAR whenever we have a possibility of saving someone.” He nodded to Cody. “We’ll send some units out.”

“We can’t send many,” Emma objected. “We’ve got four ships —”

Edie nodded in understanding. Ellaz shot a look to Cody, “The last I heard, only one per cent test into implants.”

“Actually, half a percent,” Edie corrected her, smiling at Cody.

“And Jasmine?” Cody asked.

Edie’s smile twisted. “I may have rushed it,” she admitted. The other two blinked in surprise. “Oh, there’s nothing showing up on tests but… sometimes… well, it’s a mother’s right to worry!”

“Abnormal implant rejection symptoms include violence, extreme paranoia, and catatonia,” Ellaz recited.

“Also AI imitation,” Cody added.

“‘Lost in the clouds,’ we call it,” Edie said in agreement. “But Jazzy’s passed all her tests and —”

“She helped you with this new ring design,” Ellaz guessed. “It’s wider than the regular rings, right?”

“Wider and formed,” Edie said. “Instead of a simple ring, it’s got a parabolic curve forward, less so to the rear.”

“To project the fields,” Cody guessed. Edie smiled and nodded at him. He frowned. “If you extended the field far enough forward, could you make a lance?”

“A lance?” Ellaz said. “You mean an energy lance?”

Cody nodded.

“Possibly,” Edie said. “But why would you — oh!” She gulped down her food and glanced to the other two. “Are you coming?”

They raced back to the command center, put on their helmets and linked in to the main computer systems.

Five minutes later, they each pulled off their helmets, their expressions ashen.

“Warp lance,” Cody said.

“They used a warp lance,” Ellaz agreed. “They tore everything apart.”

“What about the planet?” Edie asked.

“The lances warped the atmosphere,” Cody said. “No one below had a chance.”

“If the gravity didn’t twist them to pieces, the radiation was instantly fatal,” Edie said. “But — did you see the size of them?”

“I only caught glimpses, just the edge of the lances,” Ellaz confessed.

“Interpolating from the lances to the warp, the ships had to be massive,” Edie said.

“I counted twenty-six,” Cody added.

“That’s the double of a prime number,” Ellaz said. Cody shook his head at her. “Well, it is!”

“Doesn’t mean anything,” Cody told her. “But I got a timing… I think. From first shot to last was less than two hours.”

“That’s not counting what they did out at Xerxes,” Edie added.

Cody found a layout of the shipyard and examined it. There were twenty slips — building sites — of which only ten had been occupied. One was gone with the nuking of Nautilus, three were holding the hulks of other nearly-finished ships that were torn to shreds by the alien attack, while the other six had ships in various states of construction ranging from skeletal ribs to partially skinned hulls.

The ten slips were divided into two groups, each controlled by its own main computer system. Cody had no luck with the first computer so he went out to the second section. He had to figure out the power connections but he managed to get the system to reboot after two hours. He was hot, hungry, tired, scared… and thrilled.

The main screens came to life and he tapped on the nearest keyboard. Then he had to crack into the system. This was easier than it would have been because he was able to physically get into the computer systems and because there was no one to stop him. Also, he found no less than three different passwords taped in various locations through the computer center.

“Ellaz,” Cody called, “can you connect to this?”

“Sure,” Ellaz chirped, “switch to frequency four. I don’t want us gabbing away at everyone else.”

Surprised, Cody switched frequencies. “Ellaz?”

“I don’t trust them,” Ellaz said immediately. Cody could tell from the echoes that she had her helmet on.

“Trust who?”

“The adults,” Ellaz said. “I think Nora’s right. They’re going to abandon the babies.”

“Okay,” Cody said in a talking-to-a-crazy-person tone. “Why?”

“Simple math,” Ellaz said. “There are too many babies for us and not enough food.”

She was right.

“So what do you propose?”

“I’m not killing babies,” Ellaz declared. “Either by leaving them or… worse.”

“What if we all die?”

“Then we all die,” Ellaz said. “We’re lucky to be alive. I won’t have their blood on my hands.”

“Okay,” Cody said. “And the best way to avoid that is —”

“Maybe we should send them back,” Ellaz said.

“Who?”

“The adults.”

“Well, don’t we need Edie for the tuning?”

“I could do the tuning,” Ellaz said.

“How many times have you built and tuned warp rings?” Cody asked.

“We found food, and… well, you might want to come see what we’ve got,” Bamber said. Cody frowned, remembering Ellaz’s worries.

“I’m in the middle of something,” Cody said. “Can you just tell me? Or send an image?”

Bamber sighed. “We found the shuttle bay,” he said. “Rather we found the shuttle warehouse. There are about —”

Cody perked up, tapped a command into the computer systems. There were ten ships on the building slips which meant, with a crew of roughly one hundred, there had to be four shuttles for each ship. Maybe they weren’t all here but…

“Forty shuttles?” Cody guessed.

“Only about twenty in this warehouse, at a guess,” Bamber replied. “And they’re in mothballs.”

“Mothballs?” Ellaz piped up.

“I mean they’re not prepped, they’re wrapped up for storage,” Bamber replied.

“Then why didn’t you say so?” Ellaz murmured acerbically.

“Spacers know mothballs,” Cody said.

“Not this spacer,” Ellaz corrected him.

“So…” Cody typed in a series of queries, tied it in with Bamber’s location and said, “If you go from there across the field, you’ll find Warehouse Two. There should be another twenty shuttles there.” Of course they’d need fuel, charging, oxygen and… well, it was something.

“I’ll check it out, right after I pull up the systems in this other warehouse,” Bamber replied. “And Captain?”

“Yes?”

“Don’t fall asleep!”

Cody shook his head and looked back at the screens in front of him.

Plans. Tried-and-true. Because building a starship wasn’t just science, it was art, too.

They needed a power plant, no matter what. Preferably a “tried-and-true” plant and, more importantly, they needed one that was here, at the shipyards, ready to be installed. Only… there were only so many power plants lying around.

The power plant sized the ship. A big ship, a big power plant.

And all that depended on the size of the ship. There was no way they’d be able to build a two megatonne starship in less than four months. And they didn’t have four months. So, what was the biggest ship they could build in three weeks?
The computers didn’t have an answer to that. What was the fastest ship they could build?

Hope shimmered in the space around it and then the ship slipped away from normal space and time.

#

“All systems nominal, thirty minutes into flight,” Nora reported. Then, “Whee!”

Cody grinned and smiled at Ellaz who nodded back, muttering, Amateurs.

Cody ignored her as they pulled more and more warp around them until they were finally registering Warp Nine.

“Five days,” Cody reported.

“Roger, five days,” Nora said. Then, “I don’t know about you, but I need to pee.”

Me too, Ellaz thought. Can you manage for a few minutes without me?

I’ve got the monitor running, Cody said in agreement. He felt Ellaz pull out of the comp-link and concentrated more on the “space” ahead of them, looking for any of the darker clumps that indicated a dangerous mass. The way was clear.

They were taking the standard Warp Five route out of Meath, only they were going much faster, of course. Warp Five was a mere 214 times the speed of light, they were traveling more than seven times faster than that. Fifteen hundred and sixteen times the speed of light.

Cody looked at the ring readings on his displays. All were green. Fuel consumption was… huh! A bit lower than imagined. He verified that they really were at Warp Nine but… yes, they were. So maybe the ring was more efficient than they’d guessed.

He pulled up a schematic of the warp bubble around them and grunted in approval when he saw that the end of the forward spindle was a good fifteen hundred kilometers in front of them. The rear was only a thousand kilometers behind them. And little Hope, not more than two hundred meters in length, was cocooned inside.

He felt Ellaz appear beside him. She grabbed his hand quickly and he squeezed back. It had become their secret handshake, here in the mind-link.

A-OK, Cody reported.

Good, Ellaz replied. I figured you could manage without me for a minute or two.

We’re going to have to sleep sometime, Cody reminded her.

You wish! They watched the ring temp, watched the energy flow, examined the warp bubble and were silently amazed. Warp Nine.

Yeah, Cody thought back.

Two hours later, Cody thought, Are you okay? I have to pee.

“Because we need to shape the ring,” Edie said. “We’ve made a composite, sliding system. We’d have to re-size it for this smaller ship anyway but because we didn’t know the parameters, we wanted to avoid having one fixed size.”

“So it can slide open?” Cody said. He turned to Ellaz. “How is that possible?”

“Well…” Ellaz said, turning to Edie, “You’d have to have compensators at each junction to smooth out any flux —”

“Variance,” Edie agreed. “We do.”

“But you need to size them for the field you’re going to generate,” Ellaz continued. “And we need Warp Nine or this is all a waste of time.” Ellaz shot a look to Cody and snapped, “Don’t you have a starship to build?”

“Don’t let us stop you,” Ellaz said, turning back to Jasmine and motioning for her to put on her helmet. She turned to Edie, “Can you pull us out if —?”

“‘If?’” Cody repeated, looking to Edie just as Jasmine and Ellaz slid on their helmets.

“If they get lost,” Edie said. “Stuck.”

The trouble with mind-link was compatibility. Incompatible minds were so different that they couldn’t mind link at all. Minds with slight compatibility came across as harsh and high-pitched, draining. Ellaz’s mind was just right. She was still Ellaz, warts and all, but they weren’t painful warts.

Good connection, Cody told her. Her “hand” — it was imaginary — squeezed back in agreement.

“Okay, so acceleration? Direction? Navigation? Control?” Cody asked. Each question was answered by an overlay of displays. “Power?” Another display. “Astrogation links?”

Why is that different from Navigation? Ellaz asked.

“Because navigation shows where you are, Astrogation shows where you want to go,” Jasmine’s voice came back in answer.

“Almost, sweetie,” Edie said. “Astrogation includes warp buoys and other pointers. Particularly, you know that it’s problematic to warp through large masses, right?”

The greater the speed, the smaller the mass, Cody replied through the mind-link. We don’t want to bump into something that might smash us out of warp.

What if we do? Ellaz asked.

Three possibilities, Cody replied. We drop out of warp, we drag the object behind us and slow down, or — we go boom!

Okay, so let’s not do that, Ellaz said.

“Now, we’re going to do a quick run,” Edie said. “Set course for Deneb, power up to Warp Two then reverse course to Meath.”

Why Warp Two? Ellaz asked.

Baby steps, Cody told her. Ready?

Ellaz’s ghost hand squeezed his. Control and Power.

Cody didn’t need to hear more to know that she was going to handle the power and the controls. He checked their astrogation screen, verified with the navigation display and set their speed to Warp Two.

It took them a while to get the hang of Warp Two. At that speed, a lot of the stars were still visible. And, when in warp, they streaked by in an amazing display of reds and blues — reds where the stars were approaching them, blue where they were receding behind them.

“Very good,” Edie said. “And how’s the ring?”

Nominal, Ellaz replied. Cody agreed with her. The ring, taking anti-matter and twisting it into something that warped space, was not overheated, nor was there any sign of buckling or twisting which could render it inoperable.

ead mille Failte

hen I was nine years old, I started reading science fiction. My first book was 
Space Cat
 by 
Ruthven Todd. I really loved the whole 
Space Cat
 series. I loved it so much that I decided to write a fan letter to the author. He never replied. My mother was upset by that and vowed to answer all her fan mail.

She still does to this day. Her first fan was an eighty year-old veteran of the 
Royal Flying Corps of WWI, named 
Pat Terry. When he first wrote, he was paralyzed from the waist down and had to write lying on his back with a notepad held at arm’s length. With such dedicated fans as he, it was not at all hard to find the time to respond. As the numbers of her fans increased, my mother had to spend less time responding to fan mail – or else spend less time writing the new books every letter clamored for! 

I remember her proudly showing me her copy of the F&SF magazine with 
The Lady in the Tower
 in it. All I saw was a magazine with a picture of a banana floating on a field of stars - nothing at all like the picture of a cat romping in a spacesuit on the Moon. 

As the years passed - and her covers got better - I became a voracious reader of 
Anne McCaffrey. I even claim the distinction of being the very first person to read the individual pages of 
The White Dragon
 as it came out of Mum’s IBM Selectric typewriter.

Pern – met

Fax – cried with joy for the smallest dragonboy – marveled at 
Robinton’s wit and humor – laughed with 
Menolly and her gay ways – you haven’t heard the stories behind the stories.

“I see,” the mayor said. “And that other ship? Pirates?”

“No, sir,” Cody said, “we think they’re aliens.”

“Really?” the mayor said dubiously. “And how old are you, son?”

“And we need to train ring watchers,” Ellaz said, glancing to Edie who nodded in agreement.

“‘Ring watchers?’ What’s that?”

“It’s like a ring tuner only on ship,” Edie said.

“To watch the ring all the time?” Tom said. “Isn’t that… wasteful?”

“Not if you want to live,” Ellaz told him.

“Well, I’m glad I’m not going —” Tom began. “Wait a minute, you want me to fly in one of those?”

“We’re recruiting,” Cody said. “Those who don’t make the cut can stay behind, maybe try to build a full-size freighter.”

Tom Walker’s eyes went wide at that thought. “But — but you’ll come back, right? Or send someone for us?”

“Yes,” Edie said.

“That’s the plan,” Cody agreed. “In the meantime, we need someone to help supervise the bots.”

“Bots?” Tom said. “You have bots building the ships?”

“Well, we don’t have ten thousand trained techs,” Ellaz said. “So we work with bots.”

“We double-check their work but they do all the heavy-lifting,” Edie explained.

“Bots,” Tom muttered to himself, shaking his head.

#

Fortunately, Tom Walker was not typical of the other survivors. The babies — the under threes — were added to the nursery. That left sixteen people, from age four up to age thirteen. Brenda Hogg was the next eldest and nothing at all like Tom Walker.

“Sure! Show me what to do,” she said when they’d explained their plans to her. Her mother had been the captain of Farley’s Ghost and she was planning to become a captain herself one day. She got the job sooner than she’d expected, when Cody, Clive, and Edie agreed to assign her to the second ship.

“What’s its name?” Brenda had asked.

“That’s for you to decide,” Clive Bamber told her with a grin. The question of Bamber becoming captain was settled when he flat out turned it down. “I’m better with machines,” he’d said, holding up his hands defensively. “Make me the engineer. And my wife, of course.” Because Moira Collins had actual experience on starships whereas Clive Bamber had rapidly moved into management.

“Revenge,” Brenda said immediately, her expression fierce. She looked to Cody. “What are you calling yours?”

“Hope,” Ellaz said. She cocked her head up to Cody. “Right?”

So? I’m a Captain. I’m ordering you to copy yourself to the shuttles. Spread your memories out among them if you have to. Or, better, put a copy of you on each of them.

Ellaz was silent for several seconds. Then, It could work. I’d have to use a compression algorithm and I’d lose more memories but — yes, it could work.

Do it, Cody ordered. Maybe if all that’s left is you, that’ll be enough.

Are you being romantic? Ellaz teased. I don’t do that, you know. I never did.

“Cody?” Nora said. “We need to tell the others.”

“Sure,” Cody said. Ellaz, can you keep us alive?

Ha-ha! Sure, go talk to the normies!

Cody pulled off his helmet. “Ellaz is minding the ship, let’s get everyone together.”

“And eat,” Gail said emphatically.

#

They met in Whisper which was the name that Franny Harper had given the nursery shuttle. Shuttles could hold twenty-five in the main cabin and two in the cockpit. But with the babies and the nurse bots, getting just the twenty-four of them all together was daunting.

Fortunately, at least half the babies were sleeping. Franny, Johnny, and Ginny shoved a wide-eyed baby into the arms of everyone who entered. It took a good ten minutes to sort out the chaos before Cody could get everyone settled — and baby Lindsay to sleep in his arms.

“Okay,” Cody whispered, “we’re just about ten and a half hours away from Deneb.”

Eric Doohan blinked. “Is that why we went to Warp Nine point One?”

Cody nodded. “And we found their ships. They’re ahead of us. Twenty-six of them.”

“We think we know how they’re going to attack,” Nora said. “And we’re going to be two hours too late.”

“So why did we speed up?” Mandy Barquess asked.

“Because we think it’ll take them three hours to finish their attack,” Cody said. “If they repeat their attack at Meath, we’ll be able to save at least one spacehab.”

“How?” Tom Wong asked.

“We think we can use the warp field as a lance,” Gail said. “And use the lance to stop the attack on the spacehab.”

“The lance would destroy the alien ship attacking the spacehab,” Jacob chimed in.

“You’re worried, aren’t you?” Dorit Williams said, as she watched standing next to him.

“Of course,” Cody said when she didn’t stop looking. “She’s a great friend.”

“And you love her,” Dorit said. She saw the way his shoulders tensed and bumped herself against him. “Like you love Ellaz and Gail and Jacob and… your family, Cody.”

“Yeah,” Cody agreed. He looked around. “I’ve got to get going.”

“I know,” Dorit said, wrapping him in her arms. “And you’re my family, too. Don’t forget.”

“Yes, ma’am,” Cody told her. She scowled at him and he grinned back, unrepentant. She let him go, pushed him back and lifted her wristcomm. “Attention on base! Now departing, Wasp, Admiral Ford.”

Cody was surprised to hear a loud cheer reach up from every corner on their cramped base.

“Get going, kick their butts, come back,” Dorit said, turning him around and pushing him toward the door.

#

“Admiral on board!” Georgie Cummings, his XO, called out as Cody turned to close the airlock behind him.

“We good?” Cody said.

Huh! Impressive, Cody thought. And how soon until we can build one of these?

Title: Cody's War - Flight of the Wasp 12pt 5x8
Chapter: OEBPS/Cody's_War_-_Flight_of_the_Wasp_12pt_5x8-11.xhtml

Passage:
“I might sir,” Chitty told him with a wink. “I might.”

“Thanks but it’s months away,” Cody said.

“With babies, you can never be too early,” Juan told him.

“Well, sir, we’ll let you get back to work,” Chitty said in what was clearly a dismissal. “And we’ll be sure to bring Susan and Henry up to speed.”

Susan and Henry Lucks were a brother and sister pairing. Cody couldn’t believe that they were fifty-five and fifty-seven years old. Not that that was very old — even for a spacer — but it would be another forty years before he’d be close to their age. The two had volunteered, had come out of retirement, in part because they were good at their jobs and, sadly, because the rest of their family had been lost on the surface of Deneb.

“Sure, thanks,” Cody said.

“And if you ever want a game of chess…” Chitty offered.

Cody smiled and waved as he turned back to negotiate the tubing from ECLSS back up to his shuttle, Wasp.

#

Days and nights blurred together as Cody and his “crew of imaginary friends” — as ghost Nora liked to say — worked and reworked their plans for the upcoming fight.

“Cody, Cody, Cody!” Ellaz yelled the morning of their eighth day.

“Ellaz, Ellaz, Ellaz!” Cody repeated back, pushing off his covers and looking around — only to realize that she’d been talking over the speakers. “Is there an emergency?” He was pretty sure that she would have reacted differently if there had been — like fixing the problem and then letting him know later in her cocky, self-assured manner.

“No, of course not!” Ellaz replied. “But I’ve got it!”

“Got what?” Cody said, moving to the back of the main cabin and heated up some coffee and a breakfast tray. “And can it wait?”

“Well,” Ellaz sighed, “yes. It’s going to have to wait.”

“So why couldn’t I sleep longer?”

“Because I had to tell you,” Ellaz said. “I’ve got the tachyon communicator.”

Cody’s eyes went wide. “You do? Now?”

“No!” Ellaz said, irritated. “I’ve got the design. Do you want to see?”

“Can I eat and get dressed first?”

“I suppose,” Ellaz grumbled.

Passage:
Moira and Clive exchanged looks but Ellaz ignored them.

“I should be back in three days,” Moira said.

“Here,” Ellaz said, pulling a chip out of the computer’s reader, “this is a list of who you want at the controls.”

“Controls?”

“Twenty-one survivors — nineteen there, of whom ten are watch-qualified, five are on probation, and the last four are recruits,” Ellaz said. She saw Cody flinch at the last word but didn’t pay it any attention — the shuttle pilot was just weird, she knew that. And touchy. Implants?

“As soon as we get Wasp empty, I’ll head out and get an amsee,” Cody said.

“‘Amsee?’” Ellaz said.

Cody nodded. “Anti-Matter Container. AMC. Amsee.”

“Get three if you can,” Edie said. Cody blinked at her. “Take two shuttles and slave them to you, okay?”

“Okay,” Cody said dubiously. “But why three?”

“Redundancy,” Clive Bamber said, smiling at Edie. Then, with a frown, “You’re not thinking of building more?”

“Just being cautious,” Edie Crump assured him. Ellaz shot a look to Cody who answered it with a shrug.

“When you get back, we’ll have enough space for all of them,” Bamber promised, moving over to kiss his wife on the cheek.

“Well, I’d best get going,” Moira said, waving to the others and sealing her helmet.

Moments later the newly-christened shuttle Spite was arcing away from the moon Carlow.

#

“Rest,” Edie Crump’s voice came to Cody, breaking into his reverie. “And eat.” Cody pulled his helmet off and looked around. He was in the command center. Ellaz was slumped in a seat not too far away. Clive Bamber was somewhere else, probably helping the over-worked Nora with the babies.

Cody stumbled as he got to his feet, bumped into Ellaz who jerked, pulled off her helmet and glared at him.

“I was thinking!”

“Do you snore when you think?” Cody asked her with a grin.

She scowled at him then her expression softened. “Sometimes.”

“Edie’s sending us to get food and rest,” Cody said. “Maybe we should check on Nora —”

“Isn’t Bamber with her?” Ellaz asked. When Cody nodded, she continued, “Well, then, we should let them be.” She sniffed and Cody guessed that she wanted to keep her nose from being assaulted by diaper smells.

I don’t think so, Cody thought, checking with the computers to see if they needed to swerve back or if they might be safer continuing on their course. It would mean flying at a slight angle relative to their original course, so that they arrived at the same location rather than some distance above it.

And when we get there? Ellaz prompted.

We should start planning, Cody said.

I’m ahead of you, Ellaz told him. That was part of the “project.”

Ways to defeat the aliens?

Ellaz scoffed. If there are aliens.

They used a lance, Cody thought even as he said out loud, “We’re okay! Stand down! We had to dodge a clump, that’s all.”

“Thanks for the update,” Nora replied, sounding both relieved and a bit tetchy at the late report.

Could we make our bow into a lance? Cody thought to Ellaz.

He could feel her smile as she thought, File Twelve.

Cody pulled up File Twelve and “read” through it quickly. Yeah, this could work.

But we won’t know until we try it, Ellaz added.

And we shouldn’t try it without a target, Cody agreed. Without a target — something to hit — the warp lance might be more than a little dangerous to Hope herself. Cody glanced at their forward display and frowned. How come the monitor didn’t —?

I may have missed it, Ellaz told him. Sorry.

Cody waved off her apology. He thought for a moment. Is there a way to deflect a warp? Like shield or a mirror?

A warp mirror? Ellaz repeated thoughtfully. No one’s ever tried. The math alone — she broke off, then added more enthusiastically — Cody, let’s do the math!

Cody frowned and then his expression changed as all around them there appeared the mathematical equations that described their warp bubble. He pointed to some terms, copied them, squeezed them with his mental “hands” and showed how they could create a warp lance.

And if we could squeeze a bit off — Ellaz said, grabbing the equations eagerly and manipulating them — we could make a warp dart!

I like that! Cody thought in agreement. But the mirror!

“I’ve got a better idea,” Ellaz said, around her gum. She fired up a comm link and set the shuttle’s main antenna searching. “We tap into the comms and see what we can see.”

“What? Why?” Cody said, blowing another bubble. He pulled it of his mouth, frowned at it critically, then threw it behind him, high in the air.

“Ew! What did you do that for?” Ellaz demanded.

“Going to microgravity. Don’t barf,” Cody said, adjusting the controls.

Ellaz closed her mouth tightly, glaring at him and chewing furiously.

“Is that gum ready?”

“How should I know?” Ellaz complained.

“Can you blow a bubble?” Cody said, repeating himself.

Ellaz tried. It burst. Cody shook his head and reached a hand out to her. “Give it to me.”

“What? You’re a barbarian!” Ellaz said. Cody ignored her, reaching into her mouth and pulling out the gum. With a frown, he popped the half-chewed piece into his mouth, passing her another stick.

“Get that one going,” Cody said, chewing and blowing out another bubble. He examined it, pulled it out of his mouth and threw it behind him.

“Patches,” Ellaz said with sudden enlightenment. “Why didn’t you say so?” She started chewing furiously on her new piece even as Cody started on a fresh stick.

“No time,” he told her.

“Does that really work?” Ellaz said. “I thought it was just a spacer story.”

Cody, turned the pack of gum to her. It was labeled, “Ford’s Fancy.” The fine print added, “Refreshing Life-saver. Guaranteed.”

“Any of the bubbles find an air leak and they’ll stretch out, dry up and change color,” Cody said with a hint of pride.

“Did you do that?” Ellaz asked, impressed.

Cody shook his head. “My grandsire.” He adjusted the cabin circulation to blow more air. “But it works.”

Ellaz offered him her next chewed piece. Cody took it, blew out his bubble and took her chewed gum to create a fourth floating balloon.

“They just killed everyone,” Ellaz said.

“I was there,” Cody said.

“No, I mean they went after any atmosphere, destroying it,” Ellaz said. “They didn’t care about any survivors, just the main infrastructure.”

“They got our ship,” Cody countered.

Passage:
“Because I’m supposed to be a male only clone line,” Cody said, surprised that she hadn’t figured it out. “That Dad made a girl —” he stopped and shook his head. “So we needed to get you out and couldn’t let anyone know.”

“That sounds awfully elaborate,” Ellaz said. “And the first DNA sample they take —”

“Are you any good with computers?” Cody said.

She frowned. “You mean break in and reprogram the results?” Cody nodded. “Why not tell them the truth?”

“How well is the Whirly line known?” Cody asked.

Ellaz was silent for a moment. Then, “You’re right.”

“So you’re Ellen Ford, my adopted cousin from the outlands,” Cody said. “Dad took you on because he was being a good citizen —”

“But I thought you said —!”

“That’s the front story, when they get through that, we’ll go to the other story,” Cody said. Then he added thoughtfully, “If they get to that.”

“Just so they don’t ask about my line,” Ellaz agreed. Then, “They aren’t going to be weird that you’re a Ford?”

Cody smiled and shook his head. “I’m a shuttle expert, exactly what they want.”

The shuttle rotated, deployed its landing skids and thudded onto the landing pad. A moment later the pad started sinking beneath the horizon. In a few seconds they were in darkness as the overhead doors slid slut.

Then lights blared from outside and the controller called, “Prepare for exit.”

“How soon can we refuel?” Cody asked. “There are people dying out there.”

“Your equipment is standard, we’ll start immediately,” the controller replied. “First, we’ve got some questions for you.”

Cody turned to Ellaz. “Can you hack in from here?” Ellaz shook her head. Cody smiled at her, “Good thing I can.” He started punching commands on his keyboard. “I’m going to see what’s what… and maybe speed things up.”

#

Two minutes later there was a loud rap on the outside of their airlock hatch. Cody got up and nodded to Ellaz, “You stay here. You’re spacesick and need to hunker down.”

Cody went to the main cabin, cycled the airlock and returned the sharp salutes given him by the two men on the other side.

Passage:
“And why we mute the fricking alarms in the nursery!” Mandy said, glancing to Franny Harper who had become the leader of the nurses. Franny nodded in agreement, glanced to Johnny and Ginny who nodded in acceptance.

“Okay, so… are you ready for more?” Cody said to Nora.

“Sure, bring it!” Nora said. They trooped back into the Sim Lab and donned their VR gear for another round.

#

When they were done, they all — everyone except for the babies and the nurses, of course — suited up and wandered out to their ship. Hope looked like a really weird maze with tubes wandering all around the outside of the ECLSS, power, AMC, and propulsion units. There were also two big radio dishes — outsized because they were stolen from the hulks of freighters — attached fore and aft of the AMC.

“It looks like a bowl of spaghetti,” Nora announced as they stopped just short of the construction zone. “When are we placing the shuttles?”

“And the ring?” Ellaz added.

“We’re going to jack her up later tonight,” Cody said, checking the construction schedule. “Then we attach struts and slip the ring on them.”

“And the shuttles?”

“Day fourteen,” Cody said. “Then day fifteen —”

“We fly!” Nora said.

“Um, after we get all the supplies on board,” Cody said.

“I thought we’d agreed to put them in the shuttles,” Nora said.

“Food, consumables, yes,” Cody agreed. “But soil, plants, that sort of stuff —”

“If we’re just going for five days, do we really need that?” Jacob asked.

Cody shrugged. “Who says we’re only going to be gone five days?”

Jacob raised his spacesuit helmet up to peer at Cody.

“Yeah, Jake,” Ellaz added, “who says?”

“It’s best to be prepared,” Nora said in agreement. She glanced at her comm. “Okay, we’ve been out long enough, everyone back inside.”

“Oh, do we have to?” Gail complained. She waved a hand toward the ship. “I mean, she’s so pretty!”

“Radiation, squirt,” Nora said to her. “You don’t want to get too much.”

“Or you’d get sick,” Cody said. He turned back to the airlock.

Ellaz stumbled behind him, was steadied by Jacob and then grumbled, “I’m okay! I’m okay!”

Who named a system Perky, anyway? Gail wondered.

That would be Dorothea Parker, Ellaz told her. Apparently she was six and given the honor of naming the new home world.

She’d just lost her cat, so she named the system after her, Cody added. It was a story told everywhere and often, being beloved by many. The system lived up to its name and, nearly two hundred years after its founding, was one of the leading lights in the Fifth Quadrant.

Old Earth had expanded mankind out into a wild shape rather like a starfish with five arms. Eighteen worlds — more or less — were part of each quadrant. The Fifth Quadrant got its name because some newsie had decided to name it thus and the name, despite all objections, stuck. But the Fifth Quadrant was really no different from the First Quadrant, aside from the obvious bragging rights.

They may have scouted the whole Fifth Quadrant, Nora thought.

Well, they only have twenty-five ships, Cody reminded them. And we’re going to do something about that.

Oh, yeah! Gail agreed.

Chapter One

It was a 
dark and grey day, cold with the first of what promised to be a bitter spring, just a fortnight after the New Year. It was the 14th day of January, in the year of Our Lord 1745.

“Bessie,” I nudged the girl in bed beside me. “Bessie, get up! The cock didn’t crow!”

Bessie mumbled and tried to move away from me. I shoved her. “Bessie, get up now! Father will be wanting his tea.”

Behind me Jamie rumbled in his sleep and I elbowed him in the ribs.

I pushed Bessie out of the bed, following her into the cold morning air, my breath misting as I said, “You get the fires and the candles, I’ll see to the forge.”

“But —“ Bessie protested, even as she pulled on her dress and apron.

“Go!” There was no time for subterfuge, father would be waking soon and if there wasn’t something warm in front of him and a hot forge afterwards, there’d be sore backsides for certain.

Bessie ducked her head in submission and took off down the narrow staircase to the kitchen to start the fire and put on the kettle.

In the distance I could hear the horses in the far fields neighing and whinnying to each other. Belatedly one of the dratted cocks crowed with a desultory, almost abashed noise.

“Foul rooster!” I muttered to myself as I turned to the back door and rushed across the yard to the forge, thinking that that particular bird was soon for the pot. Probably, I thought, it’d turn out gamey.

I was delighted to see a burst of flame in front of me.

“We just put the coals on now Bess —“ a young boy’s voice piped up only to cut short as the child was elbowed into silence by another hissing, “That’s not Bessie!”

“No, it isn’t,” I said, “now get going.” I moved away from the voices even as the urchins scattered and closer to the forge. Looking at it, I decided that they’d done a good job getting the fire going again. I glanced at the pile of coal I’d left for feed and saw that they’d been good — they hadn’t pilfered any or used it up during the night.

“That was a girl!” a boy’s voice hissed loudly under the archway as the urchins scarpered. That remark was answered by muffled guffaws from the others.

My secret was safe, I could tell.

“And mother of your children!” Nora added gruffly, pulling away from him.

“Oh, of course!” Hanlan said, barking a laugh. “Because half a dozen new babies is no problem for —”

No one knew how fast the aliens could travel in warp. As it was, they’d been gone for twelve days now, and it’d be twenty-one before Hope would arrive at Deneb. At the earliest.

And there was no way that Cody could pilot the ship by himself. He glanced up as someone dropped a tray beside him. Ellaz. She gave him a nod and slumped into her chair.

“Sorry,” Ellaz said grumpily. “I’m worried. I didn’t sleep well.”

Cody nodded.

Tom Walker strode in, looked for Brenda Hogg and marched over to her, standing above her with his tray in his hand while he rattled off a quick bunch of comments.

Cody frowned. Brenda seemed to sag under Walker’s tirade. She spotted Cody, grit her teeth and shook her head — begging him not to get involved.

He didn’t have to; Clive Bamber and Moira Collins came over and started talking with Walker. A moment later, Clive and Tom left the cafeteria and Moira sat next to Brenda, patting her soothingly on the shoulder.

#

They ran through the usual list of space disasters — micro-meteor punctures, failed systems, problems with sanitation and hydroponics — the lot.

Nora and the four engineers handled them with growing confidence even as the three nursery attendants managed the twelve babies with aplomb. Of course, the nursery was on-going, the only difference was that they added the chatter from the emergencies to the mix, to see how the kids would handle it.

“We are going to mute that klaxon!” Mandy Barquess said when they came up to their first debrief. “It set all the babies off.”

“But what if it was a real emergency?’ Scott Ellis replied. “What then?”

“Um,” Nora began slowly, “in the case of a catastrophic emergency in warp…”

“We die,” Ellaz said. She shrugged. “I mean, we’ve got all the shuttles as lifeboats but… well, we’d best not have that sort of emergency.”

“Because we’d be drifting somewhere in interstellar space,” Nora agreed with a slow sigh. Then she brightened, “Which is why we practice.”

“What about Ellaz?” Franny Harper asked. “We’ve got her body here on Whisper.”

“We should move it,” Cody said with a lump in his throat. “She’s slightly radioactive and… well, there’s nothing more we can do for her.”

“Put her in Shuttle Ninety,” Scott Ellis suggested. “Let her go down with the ship, if we have to.”

“I think we should move her regardless,” Nora said, giving Cody an apologetic look.

“And what about her ghost?” Thomas Wong asked.

Cody shot him a look.

Thomas smiled. “Do you think we didn’t know?”

The others smiled and exchanged glances.

“She’s kind of a busy-body, you know,” Eric Doohan said. “She sent me messages, after she’d died.” He shrugged. “I didn’t have much to do, so I traced them. To the ship’s core memory.”

“I’ll explain later,” Cody promised. “But, please! Don’t call her a ghost. The longer she can feel real, the longer she’ll last.”

The others considered that and nodded. “Right,” Eric Doohan said to himself, “I won’t think about that too much, if you don’t mind.”

“In the meantime,” Cody said, “I’d like to have everyone think about abandoning ship.” He raised a hand. “It’s a last resort but we should be prepared.”

“Okay,” Franny said. “So we keep the babies here. The bots stay with them. But I don’t know how to navigate or fly this shuttle.”

“We’ll get you help if it comes to that,” Cody said. He turned to Jacob. “Jacob?” Jacob nodded.

“And if we get the alien ship with the lance? And the others flee? What then?” Eric Doohan asked.

Cody shook his head.

“Then we’ve won,” Nora said, smiling at them all. “We’ll deal with it after.”

“We win, we’ll be heroes,” Eric noted.

“We win, we’ve got to send someone back to Meath,” Thomas said.

“And we’ve got to send someone on to Quark, just in case,” Gail added.

“And we’ve got to fight back,” Cody said. “We win and I’m going to get them. All of them.”

Passage:
But the greater the rewards, the greater the risks. Particularly for ships carrying information. Pirates could catch them, steal their information, and use it for their gain. Which is why most couriers carried a squad of armed men and some even carried small space lasers. Of course, pirates didn’t need live crews if they could get a ship’s computers intact.

Deneb and Meath had made an agreement that they would provide some warships to patrol the normal warp routes. What that usually meant was that a warship would take on the identity of a regular courier — and woe to any pirate that tried to stop them!

Sixty-seven ships reported missing or lost. And that was up from forty-eight the year before and thirty-seven the year before that. The only reason they had the data was because it was a standard part of all ships’ downloads — a list of missing ships so that possibly they might be found.

Okay, this is getting nowhere, Cody thought to himself. Do we have any increases in specific routes or —

Cody broke off as a display appeared to his left and he saw plots of the reported missing ships as lines in three-dimensional space. All that was known was point of departure and point of non-arrival. Nothing popped out at him.

But, Ellaz, who had popped up the display, added, here are the same losses ordered by time.

The view changed. What was particularly alarming was that the older reports were further away from Meath. The newer reports were beyond Deneb in the other direction.

Scouts, Cody thought. They sent scouts.

To steal ships, Other Cody agreed. Cody looked up at him and saw Nora standing beside him, smiling.

We want to look at the oldest reports, Cody thought. Those nearest the warp line from Meath to Deneb but backwards, away from —

Ellaz changed the display. There were three dots. They’re all recon ships.

Title: Cody's War - Flight of the Hope 13pt 5.5x8.5 Glossary Cast
Chapter: OEBPS/Cody's_War_-_Flight_of_the_Hope_13pt_5.5x8.5_Glossary_Cast-9.xhtml

Passage:
It’s a nursery rhyme, Cody replied. Then, It’s from the time of the Bubonic Plague.

Ellaz looked at Cody and a tear dripped down her eye. They’re sad!

Right, Cody replied. They got pulled down by their worries.

No time, Ellaz thought, rushing over to the taller of the two girls and wrapping her arms around her. Come on, it’s time to go home!

Home! Home? No home! All gone! Edie’s childlike voice came back to them. She started howling in despair. Beside her, Jasmine added her wails.

Edie, Jasmine, come on, it’s time to get out of here, Cody thought. We’ll get you drinks and some rest —

He and Ellaz shared an instant gestalt thought, running through data that the simulator provided like a flood, and realizing that Edie hadn’t had nearly enough rest in the past several days. Also, she was an adult, she felt the loss of so many billions of people more thoroughly than either of them.

They pulled the two out of the doldrums and back to reality.

Red flashing computer lights stopped flashing and the room got quiet. Cody pulled off his helmet, raced to the small fridge and pulled out two drinks just as Ellaz was pulling the helmet off of Jasmine.

“Here,” Cody said, passing one drink to Edie and the other to Ellaz who fed it to Jasmine.

“We’re doomed,” Edie said as she tugged a desultory sip from her drink. “Doomed.”

“No, we’re not!” Ellaz said. “You two got sucked into a hole, that’s all.”

“We’re not compatible,” Edie said, tears flowing down her cheeks as she looked to her daughter. “I’m sorry! I never thought that —”

“It’s okay, Mommy,” Jasmine said with forced humor. “It was our first time, we’ll work it out.”

“No,” Edie said, “at least not right now.” She turned to Cody. “You two are the only ones watch rated.”

“So we split up, Cody on one ship and —”

“No,” Edie said. “That won’t work. You’re going to need two of you, one has to sleep sometime, you know.”

“We could take stimulants —” Ellaz said.

“No,” Cody said. “There are too many side effects.”

Ellaz pursed her lips but said nothing.

“We don’t need two ships,” Cody said. “One was a spare.”

Passage:
She’s right on the probabilities, Ellaz admitted. There’s a far greater chance that this is one simple traitor and not a whole world or combine. She waved a hand toward the main cabin. Go on, get your coffee! You’re no use without it.

Cody nodded, turned around and walked through the virtual world back to the main cabin with his helmet on. He found the coffee, grabbed it and — his hands slipped through it.

Cody, you’ve got to bring a copy into the virtual world with you, Other Cody told him.

Cody reached again, imagining the real cup and its simulation together. This time he felt the warmth of the cup and picked it up. He raised it to his lips and sipped. Ah!

Thanks, OC, Cody thought to his ghost.

My pleasure, OC thought back.

Back in his seat, Cody pulled up the first of the virtual files. He skimmed all sixty-seven missing ship reports, some dating back to fourteen months prior.

Traders and scouts were a rare breed. Cody’s freighter, Hornet, was part of a corporation with set routes, times, and cargoes. The traders were much smaller ships — usually not more than two hundred k-tons. They carried rare cargo and traded information. They flew at higher warps than freighters because time was money, particularly when it came to selling information to the highest bidder. Most traders rarely went faster than Warp Six which still gave them a nearly two week advantage in time over regular freighters. So they could carry news quicker. Those ships willing to risk — and pay for — Warp Seven could have a nineteen-day advantage over regular freighters.

Some small ships were used as couriers, particularly by the larger interstellar corporations that spanned multiple worlds and they’d even go as high as Warp Eight which would get them the twenty light-years from Deneb to Meath in just seven point one days — not quite the five days that Hope had done at Warp Nine but still very respectable, especially when compared to the twenty-nine point two days required at Warp Five.

Passage:
“Commodore Wright will have the center,” Cody said. “Commodore Hartman will lead the right section, until he is relieved and then Captain Connors will take over.” Cody had been surprised when Don Hartman had offered his exec to command one of the ships. They’d worked together flawlessly but Hartman was right in saying that she deserved a command chair, and they’d managed to find someone — Jackie Quinn — who’d been more than willing to swap. They’d given her Whirly for her command. She’d worked her butt off with her new XO, Simon Schlachter until even Ellaz was impressed. “And I’ll have the left section with Captain Eber as my second.” Gail smiled at him. After her, they’d put Jacob on Glorious — his name for his first command.

“Now, as soon as we reach Quark, we’ll detach Commodore Hartman in Hermes and head back out to deploy our arrays,” Cody reminded them. “Once the arrays are established, we’ll rotate our ships out — one in three — for rest and refueling if required.” He paused. “We’re hoping that we’ve got a six to eight day lead on them.” Heads nodded. “After that, when we’ve detected them and verified that they’ve passed, we’ll go into warp and chase after them stealthily. Our plan is to hit them two to three days before they’re due to arrive at Quark. With luck, we’ll hit them fast, hard, and unseen.” He smiled. “And then, when we’re done with them, we get down to the real business.”

“Finding their homeworld,” Derval Connors growled.

“And putting an end to it,” Eric Doohan added fiercely.

Cody waited a moment. “Any questions?” He glanced around. “No? Well, back to work, people! And don’t forget to rest!”

The group roared with laughter and then rose, dispersing to their various duties.

#

They worked all night, sleeping in shifts. By dawn, twenty-six ships were ready to be lifted up into lunar orbit. The other four would follow on in the next few days.

Nora insisted that her Phoenix was first. Cody let her go, hugging her before she boarded her ship. He watched with mixed emotions as the tugs lifted the warship off the docking yard and into space.

“Well, sir, the way I see it there are three possibilities,” Jacob said, thrilled to be distracted and doing something useful.

“Yes?”

“First, we arrive in time to warn Deneb,” Jacob said. “Second, we are too late. Third, we arrive just as they’re being attacked.”

“If we’re too late?” Cody asked.

“The first thing we need to do, sir, is see if we can get refueled. Second thing, resupplied,” Jacob said. A glowing list appeared in the simulation in front of Cody’s eyes. “After that, I recommend Search And Rescue but —”

“We used gum to find the holes,” Cody said. “We put proper patches on when we’d found them.”

Edie looked impressed.

“Shuttle pilots do stuff like that,” Cody said to Jasmine triumphantly.

“Quick thinking,” Edie agreed, nodding to Cody. “I’ll bet you were a great help on ship.”

Cody grinned, not wanting to admit that he’d barely been on the ship before there was no ship to be on.

“Okay,” Clive said. “I think what we need to do is start a more comprehensive inventory, looking for food and air.” The others nodded. “The spaceport here is a good place to start.”

“Because it’s not nearly as trashed as the rest of the base,” Ellaz agreed.

“I’ve got a couple of possibilities,” Jasmine said. Cody and Ellaz shot her a look. “That’s why I was using the cameras,” she explained.

“Do we have a list?” Edie said, turning to Moira Collins. “Supplies, quantities?”

“For what?” Moira said. She waved a hand around. “Adding in these twenty-one, we’ve got five hundred and forty-six survivors.”

“And food for five hundred,” Clive added somberly.

“What will they do with the babies?” Nora asked, eyeing the others nervously. No one answered. “They can’t — they just can’t —”

“Cryofreeze?” Moira asked. Then she frowned. “But we don’t have the facilities and —”

“If we go back, Mr. Bamber, what’s going to happen to these kids?” Nora asked. “Should we go back?” Then her mouth tightened. “I’m not going back if I can’t save the kids.”

“Right,” Cody said. He looked around. “So what we need —”

“Is a ship!” Ellaz said, turning to him and beaming.

“We’ve got a ship,” Cody reminded her, pointing to the deck of the Wasp.

“No, a real ship!” Ellaz said. She turned to Edie. “Could we make one?”

Edie was silent for a long moment. Then, she said, “You’d need —”

“We’ve got a shipyard,” Cody said. “What else do we need?”

“About ten thousand trained engineers,” Clive Bamber said.

“How big a ship do we need?” Ellaz asked. “Enough for a hundred, maybe?”

Ellaz shook her head in disgust.

Nora came rushing down four hours later, flushed with worry only to find Ellaz saying, “Pawn to Queen Four. Again.”

“How are the babies?”

“It was an old naval thing,” Nora explained. “A boat with two wooden paddles that you could move in tandem.” She frowned. “But you had to face to the rear.”

“That seems… awkward,” Ellaz said. She yawned. Then she added, “And we took a look —”

“Sorry about your mother,” Cody said.

“And your family,” Ellaz added, glaring at the older boy.

“Yeah,” Cody said.

“Oh!” Nora said in a small voice. “I hadn’t — I mean, there were the babies and — there was no time —”

“I know,” Ellaz said. “But you didn’t mention that your mother was the base commander!”

Nora’s lips twitched. “She wanted me to take over.”

“You’d do a good job,” Cody said comfortingly.

“Except that there’s no base anymore,” Nora said. She shot a look to Cody. “Can I come with you?”

“Well, someone has to watch the babies!” Ellaz said.

“I think, what she means to say is that we’d be delighted,” Cody said, shaking his head at Ellaz. “She has no tact, you see.”

“What’s tact?” Ellaz demanded.

“Later,” Cody said. “Nora, do you think you can manage for a bit? We’ve got to check on the construction.”

Nora turned back to Cody. “What did you do?”

“We,” Cody said, nodding toward Don Hartman, “brought the President up to date.”

“But you didn’t sign anything, did you?” Nora persisted.

“We were just getting to that,” Ed Hanlan said, shooting an amused look to Hartman.

“I might mention that Miz Wright is the daughter of the late Chloe Wright of Carlow Shipping,” Don explained.

“Chloey?” Ed exclaimed, rising from his seat and rushing over to Nora. “Your momma was Chloey?”

Nora nodded, looking surprised. She squeaked when President Hanlan grabbed her, lifted her off her feed and engulfed her in a bear hug. Cody shot a look to Hartman, wondering if he should rescue Nora but Don Hartman shook his head, eyes watering. Finally President Hanlan set Nora back on her feet, leaning forward to kiss the top of her head.

“Your pardon, young lady but your mother —” his voice broke and it was a moment before he could speak again “— she was something.” He shook a look to Cody. “Where did you find her?”

“She was baby-sitting a nursery,” Cody explained.

“I was only supposed to do it while my —” Nora forced herself to choke back a sob “— mother was in a meeting.”

“And then the aliens came,” Don Hartman said.

Nora nodded. “We had three hours’ worth of air left when Cody arrived.”

Hanlan glanced between her and Cody. “I see.” He waved her toward a seat and reclaimed his. “So, I understand that you’re here to rescue us.”

“That’s the plan,” Nora agreed. She glanced to Cody. “Did you eat?”

Cody shook his head.

“And where are my manners?” President Hanlan said, slapping himself on the forehead for show. “Well —” he broke off as someone knocked on the double doors and they opened, revealing a squad of servers, wheeling in two food carts. He broke into a grin, “Here they are!”

He had the servers set up and got them to provide Nora with the first pick, Cody second, Hartman third before gesturing to a server and saying, “The usual, if you please.” A tray arrived in front of him with a salad and a roast beef sandwich. “Imported from Meath, you know,” he said. “Best beef on the hoof.”

“Boom!” Edie cried. “You didn’t dodge fast enough! And your warp core shredded.”

Shredded? Cody thought.

“You died,” Jasmine explained.

So what do we do? Ellaz thought.

“Whenever you find yourself in a warp stream like that, the smart course is to offset your course and stick to it. It means you’ll have to recompute your astrogation, of course.”

I thought the routes were safe, Cody replied.

“They’re safe at Warp Five,” Edie explained. “Everything comes faster — and thicker — at Warp Nine.”

Why aren’t there routes for Warp Nine? Ellaz wondered.

“If there are, only the military has them,” Edie said. “Regular freighters don’t need them and mapping such routes… it’s expensive.”

In time or in ships? Cody wondered.

“Both,” Edie told them. “Okay. Again. Warp Nine.”

They did two more runs before Edie pulled them out. She and Jasmine passed them drinks.

“You are getting it,” Edie assured them.

Cody and Ellaz exchanged looks. “Excuse me,” Ellaz said, “but as near as I can tell, all we’re getting is dead.” Cody nodded in agreement.

“But you’re getting really good at that!” Jasmine teased.

#

Outside, Jacob and Gail waited with lists of disasters. Although, Cody noted, some of the disasters were crossed off his list. He glanced to Ellaz’s list and smiled.

“What?” Ellaz demanded, still grumpy from their exertions.

“Our aides are doing their work,” Cody said, pointing to the eliminated items.

“We talked it over,” Jacob admitted, “and asked ourselves what you would do.”

“Good work,” Ellaz told him with a grin. She gestured for his touchpad and peered down at it. “Now… we’ve got the supplies, the diapers, the formula. What about water?”

“Handled,” Cody said, pointing to his list. “What about soil?”

“We won’t be needing that until the ECLSS units are complete,” Gail said. “And that’s not for another three days. And then they have to power them up —”

“And where are we on power?” Cody asked, looking at his list.

The “quarters” had been offices previously with only two rest areas but, with the judicious use of mass, the tables had been moved to form hard-surfaced beds, softened by whatever they could scrounge. There was a food area with a microwave, assorted dinners, and a refrigerator. Trash, sadly, was just thrown out, not recycled.

Cody found a dinner he could tolerate, heated his, grabbed some cutlery and found a table with chairs still around it. Ellaz joined him a moment later. Edie came over, glanced around and sat with them.

“So… implants?” Edie said in a quiet voice while stirring up her meal. She nodded to Cody. “Starship?”

“We were hoping,” Cody admitted.

“And energy?” Edie said, glancing to Ellaz. Ellaz hissed in surprise, forced her mouth to work in an attempt at a reply but was cut off by Edie’s raised hand. “I’m a ring master, I keep my eyes open.”

“And a single ring?” Ellaz shot back. “Do you know how —?”

“No, why don’t you tell me?” Edie broke in.

Ellaz glared at Cody, then sighed when she looked back to Edie. “I’ve been running the math.”

“N-space manifold, right?” Edie guessed, tapping her temple implants for emphasis.

“Well… yes,” Ellaz admitted. She shot a quick look to Cody, adding, “Mother and I were examining some interesting —”

“Mother?” Edie broke in. She glanced between Cody and Edie. “I thought you were clones.”

“Yes,” Cody said.

Edie considered that, her eyes narrowed as she examined Ellaz’s face. “You’re a Whirly!”

“I —!” Ellaz began in protest. But the look on Edie’s face told her that she wouldn’t get away with it. “Yes, but it’s classified.”

“Who was your mother?” Edie asked in a softer voice. “I’ve worked with some Whirly’s in my time.”

“Elle Dann Triple Vonn,” Ellaz said.

Edie’s eyes went wide. “EDTV?” Ellaz nodded. “And you are…?”

“Ellaz Conn Venier Four,” Ellaz replied. Cody blinked at her. “The other names are mutation listings.”

“Aren’t the CV4’s supposed to be really good at math?” Edie said. Ellaz nodded. “And you?”

“I’m still learning,” Ellaz admitted.

“You’ve got implants,” Edie told her.

“I earned them,” Ellaz said testily. “I scored out of regular interfaces.”

Cody?

Yes?

The Whirly family secrets. The energy converter, Ellaz said.

You had better call the medics, a voice came to him.

Medics? Cody repeated. The voice sounded like Ellaz but… different.

She has failed, the voice replied.

“Nora!” Cody shouted over his mike. “Nora! Medical emergency!”

I have the conn, the voice inside Cody’s helmet informed him.

Who are you? Cody demanded.

I’m her ghost, the voice replied. Systems are nominal. I have the conn.

“In no pain?” Cody repeated dully. “Is she —?” he started to ask hopefully.

Nora shook her head. “She’s gone, Cody. The radiation was too much for her.” She frowned. “She’d been taking iodine pills for days now but —”

“Iodine?”

“We know that they’ve got to be searching forward to look for mass clumps,” Nora added. “But we don’t think they’ll be looking to the rear.”

“Possibly,” Admiral Cartwright agreed.

“I told you we needed rear reach,” Emma Forster murmured. She nodded to Nora. “Our standard operating procedure is to turn inside our warp bubble to search rearwards at irregular intervals.”

“Has it worked?” Cody asked, intrigued. He glanced to Nora who nodded — they would adapt the procedure themselves.

“So far we’ve seen nothing,” Emma admitted. “But we’re mostly pirate hunting.”

“How many ships have you lost?” Nora asked. “In the navy, I mean?”

Emma looked anxious.

“We’ve been tracking disappearances,” Cody said. “We have evidence to indicate that the aliens have planted a spy — maybe more.”

“What evidence?” President Hanlan said.

Cody pursed his lips. “Sir, if there’s a spy…”

“Right,” Hanlan said. “But I’ve known these people or they’ve been vouched for by people I trust.”

“In one scenario — a likely scenario — the spy was coerced with the threat of death to his family,” Cody said. Nora hissed in surprise.

“Which ship?”

“Have you heard of the Maru? Captain Mayhew?” Cody asked.

Emma raised a hand, tapped a command on the keypad in front of her and leaned back when she got a hit. She waved copies to the displays of everyone at the table.

Admiral Cartwright read it and grunted. “Crazy loon,” he muttered. “But… what other ships are missing?” He spread the question equally between Cody and his grand-daughter.

“We ran a search, sir,” Cody said. “We can make our results available to you. In fact, we were hoping —”

“Done,” Admiral Cartwright said. “So, this ship, how did they get it?”

“We don’t know,” Cody said. “We don’t know even if the ship was pirated. Boarded.”

“Alienated?” Emma Forster asked, her eyes gleaming. President Hanlan snorted.

Cody coughed and shook his head. He turned to Admiral Cartwright. “We’ve got a possible twenty-five alien ships en route, due here in thirteen point eight days, we have a plan to ambush them three days out, we need to get our ships refueled, repaired and on station —”
