“No,” Georgie said. “You want us to lie doggo with the AMCs beyond us. When the aliens pass us by, we start following. They run up to our AMC wall, trigger it and — if we time it right, while they’re looking forward, we’re attacking from the rear.”

“How many AMCs and how many tachcomms?” Cody wondered.

“Well, I’m a bit worried about how we’d hook one on,” Georgie said. “For that matter, how we’d drop them off, too. And we’d have to deploy this brand new tachcomm sensor array. Which is untested —”

Cody snorted. “What isn’t?”

Georgie agreed with a nod. “I’d say, let the wonder team tackle the issue,” Georgie said. She yawned. “If you don’t mind —”
“Of course,” Cody said, waving her out of the command seat. It was the end of her watch, the start of his. “But it was a good idea.”

“Thanks,” Georgie said. Then, “Which one?”

“All of them.”

#

“Quark Approach this is Wasp, inbound with a convoy of —” Cody broke off and glanced to Ellaz in the virtual world. She pointed to a display. It read 24. Two ships were missing. “— twenty-four. Request clearance for Space Dock Genny.”

“Unknown ship, say type and origin,” A voice called back.

“Wasp and the convoy are experimental craft out of Deneb,” Cody replied.

“Hey, jerkface! Who let you on the comms?” Captain Don Hartman called. “Didn’t you retire?”

“Who is — unknown caller —”

“Cut it, Ed, you know who it is!” Don Hartman said. “And, I’ve gotta say, it’s good to hear your voice.”

“Don?” Quark Approach replied. “When they said they had a strange convoy coming out of Deneb, I never expected — Don, what the hell happened?”

“We got reamed,” Don Hartman said. “We got attacked by ships we’ve never seen before —”

“How many? How’d you fight them off?” ‘Ed’ asked.

“We didn’t,” Don Hartman replied. “Elantra is all that’s left. And it’s only alive because Cody Ford here and his crew damn near suicided to defend us.”

“I… see,” ‘Ed’ replied. “Huh. We’ve got a read on your ships, now. What the hell are they? I’ve never seen such shoddy workmanship!”

“Are there others?” Cody asked while he took the data and fed it into his navigation computers.

“You’re the first,” the controller replied ninety seconds later.

Cody and Ellaz exchanged dismayed looks. Cody recovered first. “We’re on profile, systems on automatic, we’ve got sixty-three minutes until rendezvous.”

“Pawn to Queen Four,” Ellaz said a moment later.

#

An hour later, Deep Space One called out to them, “Wasp, you are on profile, cleared to land.”

“Roger,” Cody said. He’d actually won two games against Ellaz. She’d decided that she was tired afterwards but Cody was pretty sure that her ego had been bruised. He sent her back to get vac rats — rations designed for eating in microgravity. He also checked their inventory. That had been on his list, just after he’d finished clearing the fuel valve but… the world had ended.

Ellaz came back with four rats — two drinks and two smoothies. She glanced at the labels and passed two to Cody. A spinach smoothie and a vanilla drink. Cody didn’t bother to ask about the rations she’d chosen for herself, he was sure she was still miffed about losing her chess game.

“We’re bringing you inside, so don’t do anything until we’ve cleared you,” DS1 added.

“Wilco,” Cody said tersely, watching his displays as Wasp turned on her tail and slowly began the descent to a waiting platform. He would have to straighten her up to deploy her landing gear but that wouldn’t be until the last few seconds. “They didn’t really have to put us on our tail,” Cody said to Ellaz.

Ellaz nodded. “Um —”

“Let’s not say anything about your power converter,” Cody suggested. Ellaz shot him a surprised look but nodded. Cody kept a smile to himself — apparently he’d guessed what she was going to say. Well, clones tended to be more paranoid than others. “Do we need an alias for you?”

Ellaz considered that and shrugged. “What do you think?”

“I think… I think it’s best if you’re my little sister,” Cody told her. “I was getting you out of the bay where I’d had you stowaway because we needed to get you out-system.”

“Why?”

Cody nodded, his movements reflected in their virtual world. He reached out a hand… and found Nora’s shoulder. Surprised, he patted her on the shoulder reassuringly.

“Seven minutes, forty-three seconds,” Nora said.

“I hate waiting,” Cody muttered.

“Try being me,” Ellaz said. Then, a moment later, she added, “Or not.”

“Okay,” Cody said, “so if this doesn’t work —”

“What?” Ellaz demanded.

“We split off the ship,” Cody said. “All the empty shuttles are programmed to take different evasion routes, that will hopefully prevent the aliens from noticing us.”

“We shut down, go dark like the last time, right?” Ellaz asked.

“Yeah, then we head to the nearest moon, and set up shop,” Cody said.

“We build another ship,” Nora guessed. “But we’ll be faster this time because —”

“You’ll be slower because you won’t have the same numbers,” Ellaz corrected acerbically.

“We’ll find survivors,” Nora said optimistically. “Like you found me.”

“We could start a passive search the minute we separate,” Cody agreed. “And then —”

“Six minutes, thirty-nine seconds,” Ellaz interjected. Then, “Oh, don’t mind me! I won’t be coming, so you two just talk among yourselves.”

“We made copies —!”

“I made copies,” Ellaz corrected. “And they’re distributed. You’re keeping — what — four, maybe five shuttles? Out of eighteen? So that’s twenty-two percent. It’s not viable, all you’ll get is a… well, maybe you’ll get a shadow.” She let that sink in. “So I won’t be coming but I’m already dead.”

“It might not come to that,” Nora protested.

“Even if it doesn’t, I’m gone,” Ellaz said firmly. “I can feel it — hell, you’ve noticed!”

“We’ve got copies, we can —”

“Cody, you don’t know what you’re talking about!” Ellaz protested. “I’m just glad —” she broke off and sobbed “— I’m just glad we could be together this long.”

Cody was silent for a moment. “Yeah, me too.”

“Five minutes fifty-two seconds,” Ellaz reported. Then she said, “Cody? Can I talk with you in private?”

“Sure,” Cody said. “Nora?”

“Go, I’ve got the ship.”

Okay, Cody thought, I’m here.

I’m sorry for being an ass, Ellaz thought. I wish I hadn’t gotten killed.

“Right,” Cody said, thrusting them down to the moon’s surface. “Let’s see what’s what.”

#

The shuttle landed thirty meters away from the blinking light. Clive elected to go first, followed by Edie Crump. The rest stayed inside the shuttle.

The light came from a section of the spaceport, on the ground level. There was debris around it — metal girders, bits of smashed ships and building materials — which Clive navigated easily.

“We’ve got an airlock!” Clive cried triumphantly. “I’m banging on it.”

A moment later the flashing light went out.

“What’s going on?” Jasmine asked. “Why aren’t —”

“This is weird,” Clive said. “Captain, can you do a thermal scan?”

“You’re in the way,” Cody warned. “All I’d get is your suits.”

“Right, backing up,” Clive said.

A moment later, Cody fired up the sensors in infrared, looking for warm spots. “Okay,” Cody said. “I’ve got a number of small spots, nothing major but —” he broke off and turned to Ellaz “— I think they’re kids.”

“Kids?” Clive said. “Okay, we’re going in.”

“I need to go to them,” Ellaz said, unbuckling herself. “They’re going to need me.”

“Why?” Cody said.

“Those are kids,” Ellaz said. “I’m a kid. They’ll need me to talk with them.”

Cody frowned. “Have you ever talked to kids?”

“Sure, loads of times!” Ellaz swore. Cody gave her a look. “Well, no,” Ellaz said, “but they’re at the spaceport which means either they worked there —”

“Not likely,” Edie interjected.

“Or they were on a tour,” Ellaz finished. “Which means they are interested in construction —”

“What’s that got to do with you going there?”

“Skills assessment,” Ellaz said, putting on her helmet and walking into the airlock.

“And none of us can do that?” Clive Bamber demanded.

“Probably,” Ellaz said, “but I’ll be quicker.”

Cody shook his head. The girl was so conceited.

“We’re going in,” Clive said. “You can come when we’ve cleared the area.”

“Of course,” Ellaz agreed. “There’s no point in me risking my life.”

“Is she always like this?” Jasmine Crump asked, bustling up to the cockpit and dropping into the co-pilot’s seat. She glanced at the displays, tapped a window and redirected one of their outside cameras.

Moira and Clive exchanged looks but Ellaz ignored them.

“I should be back in three days,” Moira said.

“Here,” Ellaz said, pulling a chip out of the computer’s reader, “this is a list of who you want at the controls.”

“Controls?”

“Twenty-one survivors — nineteen there, of whom ten are watch-qualified, five are on probation, and the last four are recruits,” Ellaz said. She saw Cody flinch at the last word but didn’t pay it any attention — the shuttle pilot was just weird, she knew that. And touchy. Implants?

“As soon as we get Wasp empty, I’ll head out and get an amsee,” Cody said.

“‘Amsee?’” Ellaz said.

Cody nodded. “Anti-Matter Container. AMC. Amsee.”

“Get three if you can,” Edie said. Cody blinked at her. “Take two shuttles and slave them to you, okay?”

“Okay,” Cody said dubiously. “But why three?”

“Redundancy,” Clive Bamber said, smiling at Edie. Then, with a frown, “You’re not thinking of building more?”

“Just being cautious,” Edie Crump assured him. Ellaz shot a look to Cody who answered it with a shrug.

“When you get back, we’ll have enough space for all of them,” Bamber promised, moving over to kiss his wife on the cheek.

“Well, I’d best get going,” Moira said, waving to the others and sealing her helmet.

The two huge tugs lowered themselves above Wasp, hooked on with magnetic cables, verified the connections, and slowly pulled the ship up into the lunar darkness.

Twenty minutes later, Wasp was in orbit. She was joined ten minutes later by the second ship in his group, Gail’s Persephone. The other two groups were getting their ships up at the same rate in ten minute intervals.

Ninety minutes later, all twenty-six starships were in orbit.

“All ships, report ready for warp,” Cody called out. He watched as the ship displays showed the green ready lights. “Very well, Control this is Wasp. We are ready in all respects for our mission.”

“Godspeed and good luck, Wasp. You are cleared for warp,” Dorit Williams called back.

“Thanks,” Cody told her. Then, “All ships, Warp Nine in three…two… one… engage!”

#

Are we there yet? Ellaz whined as she moved a huge queen up from level one to level two. “Check.” She turned to another board and moved another piece, saying to Georgie, “Mate in three.”

Georgie Cummings swore. “Cody, is she always this mean?”

“No,” Cody said, turning from his human-high virtual 3D chessboard where he was playing Nora. “Sometimes she’s meaner.” Then, he said to Ellaz. “What’s the clock say?”

“That we’ve been in Warp Nine for the past three hours,” Ellaz said. “And I’m bored.”

Cody looked up to the display they’d built in simulation space and saw that it did, indeed, have a flashing “I’m Bored” display beneath the time.

“How are you getting on with that project?” Cody asked as he moved his knight to protect from her queen.

“You mean how to communicate ship to ship in warp?” Ellaz asked. “Or how to locate the enemy homeworld?”

“I thought we’d agreed that their homeworld was destroyed,” Gail’s ghost added from where she was seated, reading up on quantum physics.

“Possibly,” Ellaz agreed. “But they could also be refugees, thrown out by their homeworld. Or pirates.”

If we could change our speed, we could use that as a simple signal, Ellaz thought.

If only we’d thought of it sooner, Other Cody agreed.

We were kind of busy, Cody thought to his copy. He felt a hand touch his and turned to see the ghost of Ellaz smiling at him. He smiled back at her.

#

“Okay, so we’re pretty sure that Quark is not a traitor,” Cody said to Georgie when she came on duty the next morning.

“I should hope so! I’ve got family there,” Georgie replied, taking a sip of her tea. “But what makes you say that?”

“Well…” Cody began slowly, “we’re pretty sure that there was a person — or alien — onboard our freighter, Hornet, when we were attacked.”

“Why?”

“That’s who shot Ellaz, and killed one of the crewmen,” Cody told her. He gestured for her to put on her helmet, then he put his on and waited for her to join him in the simulation.

What do you want to show me? Georgie thought, sipping her tea. She was sipping her tea in the real world and in the simulation. Cody was impressed, it was a talent he hadn’t quite mastered but he was working on it.

This, Cody thought, replaying his memory of the attack through their mind-link.

Was that a human inside the suit? Georgie asked in a small voice. A traitor? And why?

What if they were bribed by the aliens? Cody replied. What if the aliens wanted to be certain that this particular technology was destroyed?

What happened to the human? Georgie replied. How did he get away?

He was wearing a warp bubble, so he wouldn’t have been affected —

But, after? Georgie pressed. How did he get away after?

I don’t know, Cody replied. Then he had a horrible thought. Ellaz? What if the traitor was Edie?

Edie? Ellaz thought immediately.

She was the only adult we rescued, Cody replied.

But she gave us the single ring! Ellaz replied. And… I mean, she was nice! Helpful! Why would she do that?

I don’t know, Cody replied.

What if it wasn’t her? How did they get away? Georgie interjected.

“And feed them,” Cody shouted back only to find that Ellaz had rushed back and was now staring at him in amazement. “I can do it in one hour. Can you be faster?”

“Well…”

“Whoever is faster gets the job,” Cody said, pointing to the baby. “The other gets to —”

“Thirty minutes!” Ellaz cried, whirling about and racing away.

“Clock’s started!” Cody called after her.

Nora gave him a grateful look. “That won’t be a problem, will it? I mean, do we have enough?”

“There were enough to build twenty starships,” Cody told her. “I think we can spare a few.”

Nora smiled at him. She forced herself up to her feet, glancing around at her charges and muttering, “I’m never having babies!” As if in answer, a baby started crying.

#

Ellaz beat her time, arriving twenty-eight minutes later with three small cleaning bots.

“Let’s see how they do,” she said, pursing her lips tightly. “I mean —”

“If they don’t work, don’t worry,” Cody told her with a broad grin. “You can stay with Nora while I get it sorted out.”

Ellaz glowered at him then motioned to one of the bots. “I’m going to start with this one, he can smell.”

“‘He?’”

“Whatever,” Ellaz said. “As far as I’m concerned anything that can do this should be a ‘he.’”

‘He’ — the robot “Sammy” — actually could do it. In fact, he had diapered three babies in the time it took Cody to do one. And, from the looks of the babies, ‘he’ had done a better job.

“And feeding?” Cody said. “And supplies?”

“They’re linked into the main computer,” Ellaz said. “They keep inventory of stock on hand and they can order more.” She jerked her thumb as a fourth robot came bustling in with two boxes of diapers on its arms. Ellaz patted the bot as it moved past, “That’s Stan.”

“Sammy? Stan?” Cody said with a raised eyebrow.

“Simon, Seth,” Ellaz said, pointing to the other two. “Is that a problem?”

“Why ‘S?’” Nora asked.

“I dunno, it rhymes with stupid,” Ellaz said, glaring at Cody. “You know, boys.”

“Thanks,” Cody said.

“And, before that, we have to figure out what to do with the second ship,” Ellaz said.

“Oh, no problem!” Edie said. “Your little monitor’s been able to take everything I threw at it — you — so I think we’re safe on that.”

“Not Warp Nine,” Cody said.

“Warp Five,” Edie agreed. “We’re safe at Warp Five.”

“Backup,” Ellaz said in her usual terse speech. She took another sip from her drink.

“But then you’re thirty days away,” Cody objected. “The whole idea is to warn them!”

“This is true,” Ellaz agreed.

“And we won’t be thirty days out, we’ll be eighty-two and a half days out,” Edie said.

Cody blinked.

“You’re going to Quark,” Ellaz guessed. Edie nodded. “Smart. Bypass Deneb, head to the next nearest star.”

“That spreads out our chances of warning someone,” Cody agreed. “Does Bamber know?”

Edie shook her head. “I’m trying to figure out a good time to tell them.” Cody blinked. “Him and his wife.”

“Then we’ll go to Fafnir,” Cody said. Edie blinked at him. “After Deneb.”

“Yes, okay, that makes sense,” Ellaz said. “Of course, we have to make it to Deneb first.”

“Yup,” Cody agreed.

“In the meantime, I want to start training the rest of the crew,” Edie said. “Get them in here for two hours each. Then train you two with your crew and us —” she waved a hand to include her daughter “— with the other crew.”

“Well, they’ll have it easy,” Ellaz said.

“They will?” Cody said.

“The crew, I mean,” Ellaz said. “We’ve done all the hard stuff.”

“Oh, no we haven’t!” Cody said, shaking his head and grinning at her.

“And if you fail, son, what then?” Admiral Cartwright asked quietly.

“Well sir, we can’t,” Cody told him. “But we’ve got some new tricks to add to our mix —”

“The tachyon comm, right?” Admiral Cartwright guessed.

“The AMC mines, sir,” Cody replied. “We position them closer to Quark, and lie hidden on the far side behind them. When the aliens trigger the mines, we attack.”

“We’re going to position a grav array to detect them,” Nora added. “We’ll put that in normal space, spread out on their likely course. We should be able to detect them at least five hours before they approach, maybe more.”

“And when you get behind them, what then?”

“Well, we devised two new weapons,” Cody said. “The warp mirror which we used to defeat the ship at Deneb and —”

“The warp lance,” Nora said. “And Cody, we’ve been talking and we think we can extend the lance out to a hundred thousand kilometers, maybe more.” Cody knew that “we” included Nora’s copies of the virtual versions that lived in the Mark 60 computer on her ship Phoenix.

“Oh, and one more thing,” Cody said. “It’d really help if we could get upgraded to StarDyne Mark 120 systems.”

“I didn’t know they had a one twenty,” Cartwright murmured.

“We’ve got the specs for that, as well,” Cody said, nodding to the President.

“Hold that thought, sir,” President Hanlan said in reply. He raised a finger. “Jo?” He said to a very trim young woman seated opposite Cody. “You got all that?” She nodded. “Good, then issue a system-wide alert. Don’t lie to people but don’t send them all screaming to me, either. Can do?”

“Yes sir,” the woman said, smiling at him and rising from her seat.

“And make sure that you greenlight anything and I do mean anything that the Deneb Fleet requests, and expedite,” President Hanlan called after her as she opened one of the double doors. She nodded and waved a hand in agreement. Hartman snorted and Hanlan shot him a look. “She’s my grand-niece, if you have to know, and she’s gunning for my job.”

“So you’re working her to death,” Nora guessed.

The smell of his stale helmet woke them and Gail took it, found some wipes and cleaned it up, chattering at him gaily.

“Thirty-six hours,” Gail said, passing Cody a pair of pajamas. She scrunched her nose. “No offense, Captain, but you smell.”

Cody smiled at her, took the hint and went back to the restroom to clean himself off with wipes and change into the comfy pajamas. They weren’t all that different from the overalls they had, he decided, so he could wear them in the pilot’s seat.

Gail got him settled into a bed, pulled a privacy curtain around him and dimmed the lights.

“Four hours, no more!” Cody ordered.

“Aye Captain,” Gail said, giggling.

#

Cody woke when the ship lurched around him. He pulled down the privacy curtain and scrambled to the flight deck, grabbing his helmet as a wide-eyed Gail passed it to him. “Strap down!”

He got to his seat and pulled on his helmet. Ellaz? No answer. Ellaz!

Here! I’m here! Ellaz replied a moment later, slapping his hand with hers. It just came out of nowhere!

Cody could see it. They had swerved around one dark clump of matter and now — Pull up! He put his mind to work and they pulled the ship up and up. He felt the ship strain to change position and then, slowly, Hope rose in the nothing of warp space. A moment later, Cody checked their view forward and blew out a sigh of relief.

And you didn’t see it coming? Cody thought to Ellaz. She didn’t reply. Ellaz?

Um… I might have dozed off, Ellaz confessed. I was working on my project and I lost track of time.

Project? Cody repeated. Are you trying to figure out a new way to beat me at 3D chess?

Ellaz scoffed. No! Why would I?

Well, I did beat you once, Cody reminded her. Although, truth be told, he thought she was off form for that last game. Distracted. Tired.

Fifty-seven more hours, right? Ellaz thought, pointing to the mission timer. We didn’t lose any with that swerve?

“What about Ellaz?” Franny Harper asked. “We’ve got her body here on Whisper.”

“We should move it,” Cody said with a lump in his throat. “She’s slightly radioactive and… well, there’s nothing more we can do for her.”

“Put her in Shuttle Ninety,” Scott Ellis suggested. “Let her go down with the ship, if we have to.”

“I think we should move her regardless,” Nora said, giving Cody an apologetic look.

“And what about her ghost?” Thomas Wong asked.

Cody shot him a look.

Thomas smiled. “Do you think we didn’t know?”

The others smiled and exchanged glances.

“She’s kind of a busy-body, you know,” Eric Doohan said. “She sent me messages, after she’d died.” He shrugged. “I didn’t have much to do, so I traced them. To the ship’s core memory.”

“I’ll explain later,” Cody promised. “But, please! Don’t call her a ghost. The longer she can feel real, the longer she’ll last.”

The others considered that and nodded. “Right,” Eric Doohan said to himself, “I won’t think about that too much, if you don’t mind.”

“In the meantime,” Cody said, “I’d like to have everyone think about abandoning ship.” He raised a hand. “It’s a last resort but we should be prepared.”

“Okay,” Franny said. “So we keep the babies here. The bots stay with them. But I don’t know how to navigate or fly this shuttle.”

“We’ll get you help if it comes to that,” Cody said. He turned to Jacob. “Jacob?” Jacob nodded.

“And if we get the alien ship with the lance? And the others flee? What then?” Eric Doohan asked.

Cody shook his head.

“Then we’ve won,” Nora said, smiling at them all. “We’ll deal with it after.”

“We win, we’ll be heroes,” Eric noted.

“We win, we’ve got to send someone back to Meath,” Thomas said.

“And we’ve got to send someone on to Quark, just in case,” Gail added.

“And we’ve got to fight back,” Cody said. “We win and I’m going to get them. All of them.”

“Cody, Cody, Cody!” A voice woke him up, sounding urgent.

“Here,” Cody called back immediately. He recognized the voice. Edie.

Cody never heard “one.” He’d pressed the controls on the sides of his helmet, closed his eyes and —

“Hi!” A young voice came to him. “Who are you?”

“I’m Cody,” he said. “And you are?”

“Wow!” Cody said. “That’s the ring, isn’t it?”

“Cody, Cody! What are you doing here?” Another voice came to him. Cody started to reply but the voice pressed on, “Don’t answer! Just look at this and memorize it. It’s important!”

“Why don’t I just download it to the extruders?” Cody said, glancing at the huge, mirror-finished ring in front of him. It was like nothing he’d ever seen before. The curves in the ring itself, the sections the —

“Cody!” the voice pulled him back to his senses. “I said, yes! Did you download it?”

“Uh…” Cody thought. “I’ll do it again.”

“It’s not just a question of people, it’s a question of duration,” Edie said. “Are we traveling for a month, a year, what?”

“How long is it to the nearest star?” Cody said. “Double that for safety and that’s our duration.”

“If you can build a warp drive,” Edie said.

“If we can build a warp drive, mother,” Jasmine said, grinning at her. “And aren’t we the best two warp tuners in all the system?”

“Jazzy, we’re the only two in the system,” Edie Crump reminded her.

“My point exactly!” Ellaz said, grinning at them. She turned to Bamber and Wilson. “So, what else do we need?”

“We can get the plans from the computers,” Cody said, jerking his head to the spaceport outside. “And they’ve got to have remotes, right? We can use them.”

“Son,” Clive Bamber said, “you want to build a starship here, in the middle of a ruined spaceport?”

“Do you think we’ll do better at Jurgens?” Cody asked. Jurgens was the other major shipyard on the moon.

“Let’s see what we’ve got here first,” Moira Collins suggested. She turned to their new crewmate, “Nora, can you watch the babies?”

Nora was practically asleep on her feet. “Uh, sure?”

“I’ll stay with her,” Ellaz volunteered, shooting a look toward Cody. “You get suited up.” Cody nodded but had the feeling that he was missing something, some signal the girl was trying to relay to him. “And while you guys are out there, I’ll start building a list.”

“Well, no matter what, we have to check for supplies,” Clive Bamber agreed, glancing to his wife who nodded in agreement.

#

It took hours just to get a bare inventory of the spaceport. They found several caches of food, all still edible, not so much oxygen, and plenty of materials in mostly untouched storage bays scattered around the shipyard.

An hour later the monitor program beeped, Cody and Ellaz looked up and languidly steered Hope around the latest mass clump. A moment later they put her back on their new course. Then they went back to their “work.”

It’s not a perfect mirror, Ellaz thought as they admired their handiwork hours later.

It’s more like a reflector than a mirror, Cody thought in agreement. It’ll take a warp field and reverse it back on itself.

If there’s a ship inside —

It would be destroyed, Cody agreed. And… we don’t know if this will work.

Only one way to find out, Ellaz agreed. She blew out a sigh. I need a break.

Go! We can watch the ring!

“We?” Ellaz asked.

Me and the monitor, Cody replied.

Oh! Sure, Ellaz thought back, sounding relieved. He could feel it when she dropped out of the mind-link.

Cody peered forward to the warp space in front of them.

#

“Nora, where’s Ellaz?” Cody called out loud.

“I’m just sending her up now,” Nora said. Cody frowned. She sounded stressed.

“Is everything okay?” Cody asked.

“She’s on her way,” Nora said.

“Okay,” Cody replied, returning his attention to the simulation and the warp field in front of them.

A moment later, he felt Ellaz’s hand on his. Do you need a break?

No, I’m fine, Cody thought back. What about you?

Oh! Nothing, Ellaz… lied.

Why did you just lie? Cody asked her. You know I can tell, now, right?

I do now, Ellaz confessed, mentally sighing. We’ve got thirty-one hours, right?

Minus a few minutes, Cody thought back in agreement.

We’re almost there, Ellaz thought, distractedly.

What is it? Cody asked. He felt a sense of dread in the pit of his stomach. Something was wrong. Something was wrong with Ellaz. She’d been sick, had thrown up, had — That converter, Cody thought suddenly.

It was experimental, Ellaz thought back. It absorbed the energy.

There was a blue flash, Cody recalled. That means that it didn’t absorb all the energy. And you fell to the deck.

Yeah, it wasn’t perfect, Ellaz agreed. So?

What aren’t you telling me? Cody said. The belt. Where is it?

It’s safe, Ellaz said. Inert. It did its job and now it’s just melted components.
